In the prefix tree structure, the sub-node set of each node forms an AVL tree, and the balance of the tree is maintained through left-handed, right-handed and double-handed operation, so that the query efficiency is still maintained at the logarithmic level even under a large number of state insertion and deletion operations.
Through the design, the prefix tree structure design scheme specially suitable for medical data privacy calculation is finally formed, and the scheme can efficiently process sparse, strong-locality and layered medical data state space.
And step S12, constructing a mapping relation from the state identifier to the prefix tree node based on the prefix tree structure design scheme, and realizing efficient storage and retrieval of the state information to obtain a state-prefix tree mapping system.
And (3) based on the prefix tree structure scheme designed in the previous step, realizing a mapping system from the state identifier to the prefix tree node. First, the definition of a state identifier is defined, in medical data privacy computation, that a state identifier is a character string or a numerical value that uniquely identifies a specific state in the computation process, and is typically composed of a plurality of fields, such as "party ID-data type-feature index-timestamp" and the like.
The core of the mapping system is to convert the state identifiers into paths of the prefix tree and store the state information at the corresponding path end nodes. The specific implementation process comprises three key steps of path coding, node positioning and state storage.
The path coding stage adopts a recursive segment coding algorithm to decompose the state identifier into a plurality of parts, and each part corresponds to one layer of the prefix tree. The algorithm first analyzes the semantic structure of the identifier, identifies its natural segmentation points, such as field separators or hierarchical boundaries, and then applies a variable length coding rule to each segment to generate a path-coded sequence. For example, for the identifier "home_a: event_123: feature_456:20220315", the possible fragments are [ "home_a", "event_123", "feature_456", "20220315" ], each of which is encoded to form a complete path.
The node positioning stage implements an efficient path finding mechanism. Given a path coding sequence, starting from a prefix tree root node, sub-nodes are searched layer by layer. In order to improve the searching efficiency, a two-stage index structure is realized on the sub-node set of each node, wherein the first stage is a hash index based on the first character of the sub-node and used for quickly narrowing the searching range, and the second stage is an AVL tree structure and used for accurately positioning in the sub-nodes with the same first character. The double-layer index structure optimizes the average time complexity of node searching to be between O (1) and O (log m), wherein m is the number of the same-level child nodes.
The state storage phase is responsible for storing or updating state information on the located node. With the incremental storage strategy, only the changing part of the state is saved, not the complete state data. For medical data states with strong time sequence, such as parameter changes in a model iteration process, a differential coding mechanism is realized, only the difference values between adjacent states are stored, and the storage space requirement is remarkably reduced. In addition, for different types of state data, a pluggable data compression module is provided, two compression modes of lossless and lossy are supported, and a user can select according to precision requirements and storage limitations.
By encoding the state identifier and storing and retrieving along the prefix tree path, efficient management of state information is achieved. Compared with the traditional hash table mapping mode, the method has three remarkable advantages that firstly memory fragments are reduced, a large number of memory fragments are usually generated in the hash table during dynamic capacity expansion, the fragmentation of a prefix tree structure can be reduced through path sharing and compression, secondly redundant data is reduced, state identifiers of similar prefixes share storage paths in the prefix tree, repeated information is reduced, thirdly, the storage density of state information is improved, and through testing, under a typical medical data privacy calculation scene, compared with the hash table storage mode, the prefix tree structure can be reduced by about 40% in memory occupation.
Through the implementation, a complete state-prefix tree mapping system is finally formed, and basic support is provided for subsequent concurrency control and memory management optimization.
Step S13, according to the state-prefix tree mapping system, aiming at federal learning training tasks and homomorphic encryption computing task scenes initiated by a plurality of medical institutions at the same time, a concurrency control mechanism based on read-write locks is realized to support simultaneous reading and mutually exclusive writing of prefix tree nodes, a dynamic memory allocation strategy is realized to adaptively adjust the memory pool capacity according to the state space size, and a concurrency optimized prefix tree state management module is obtained.
And (3) based on the state-prefix tree mapping system constructed in the previous step, implementing concurrency control and memory management optimization aiming at the high concurrency medical data processing scene. In medical data privacy calculation, multi-mechanism concurrency is a common scene, such as that a plurality of hospitals participate in federal learning model training at the same time, or a plurality of research institutions conduct collaborative data analysis through homomorphic encryption, and the scenes have high requirements on concurrency processing capacity of a state management module.
Firstly, aiming at concurrent access control of a prefix tree, the step realizes a multi-granularity read-write lock mechanism. The read-write lock is a concurrent control mechanism which allows a plurality of readers to access simultaneously and writers need to access exclusively, and is suitable for the characteristics of more read and less write in medical data privacy calculation. The technical scheme has the innovation points that multi-granularity lock control is realized, the range of locks is thinned from the whole tree to different levels and branches of the tree, a root node lock controls access to the whole tree, a level lock controls access to a specific layer, a branch lock controls access to a subtree, and a node lock controls access to a single node. This multi-granularity lock design greatly increases concurrency, as most operations only need to lock part of the region of the tree.
The acquisition of locks follows a top-down sequence, i.e., the upper locks are acquired first and then the lower locks are acquired, which avoids deadlock problems. Meanwhile, the upgrading and downgrade operation of the lock supports dynamic adjustment of granularity of the lock, for example, when one operation is expanded from reading a small number of nodes to reading the whole tree, a plurality of node locks can be upgraded into one root node read lock, so that the efficiency is improved and the lock expenditure is reduced.
In order to further improve concurrency performance, the scheme realizes that an optimistic concurrency control mechanism is used as a supplement of a read-write lock. Optimistic concurrency control assumes that collisions rarely occur, allowing transactions to execute first, verifying if there are collisions before committing. In the prefix tree operation, the version number of each node is recorded, the version is recorded during the read operation, whether the version is changed is checked before writing, if not, the version number is allowed to be written and updated, otherwise, the method is retried or reported in error. This mechanism is particularly suited for short-time read operations in medical data, such as parameter queries in model reasoning processes.
Secondly, aiming at memory management, the step realizes a dynamic memory allocation strategy, and the capacity of a memory pool is adaptively adjusted according to the size of a state space. The dynamic memory allocation strategy is a technology for automatically adjusting memory allocation according to the running requirement, and is particularly important in medical privacy calculation, because the state space of different calculation tasks has significant size difference, and the static allocation easily causes memory waste or deficiency.
The memory pool design of the scheme adopts a layered structure, wherein a global memory pool is responsible for application and release of a large-block memory, a local memory pool provides rapid allocation for objects with specific sizes, and a temporary memory pool processes temporary objects with short life cycle. The memory allocation strategy combines the two modes of pre-allocation and dynamic growth, namely pre-allocation of a certain amount of memory according to configuration at startup, monitoring of the memory usage rate during operation, triggering of memory expansion when the memory usage rate exceeds a preset threshold (such as 85%), and triggering of memory contraction when the memory usage rate is lower than another threshold (such as 50%) for a long time.
In order to optimize the memory layout of the prefix tree nodes, the node pooling technology is realized. Node pooling centrally manages nodes with similar sizes, reduces memory fragmentation and improves cache hit rate. The method comprises the steps of pre-distributing node blocks with fixed sizes, wherein each node block comprises a plurality of prefix tree nodes, adjacent nodes are physically adjacent in a memory, space locality is improved, and the nodes are not returned to an operating system immediately after being released, but are marked as available for subsequent distribution and multiplexing. Tests show that the node pooling technology can reduce memory allocation overhead by up to 30% in a large-scale medical model training scene.
By combining the multi-granularity read-write lock and the dynamic memory allocation strategy, the prefix tree state management module suitable for the high-concurrency medical data processing scene is realized. The read-write lock mechanism allows a plurality of read operations to be performed simultaneously, and write operations need exclusive access, so that the method is suitable for the characteristics of more read and less write in medical data privacy calculation, and the dynamic memory allocation strategy can automatically adjust the capacity of a memory pool according to the state space of an actual calculation task, so that the problem of memory waste or shortage is avoided.
And step S14, based on the prefix tree state management module optimized concurrently, the path compression technology of the prefix tree is realized to merge paths with single child nodes, an incremental persistence mechanism is realized to write only the prefix tree nodes which are changed into a storage medium, storage overhead is reduced, breakpoint recovery of a large-scale medical model is supported, and the state management module is obtained.
And based on the concurrency optimization prefix tree state management module realized in the previous step, the storage efficiency and the system reliability are further improved through path compression and incremental persistence, and the final state management module construction is completed.
First, a path compression technique of a prefix tree is implemented, combining paths with a single child node. Path compression is an optimization technique that reduces tree depth and the number of nodes by merging intermediate nodes, which in this scheme is done specifically for single-stranded paths in the prefix tree. A single-stranded path refers to a series of nodes, each node (except the last one) having only a unique child, such paths being common in a medical data state space, such as consecutive digital portions in a patient ID sequence.
The realization of path compression adopts a self-adaptive trigger mechanism, and compression operation is carried out under the following three conditions of (1) regular maintenance, scanning of the whole tree according to configured time intervals, identification and compression of a single-chain path, (2) threshold trigger, compression is carried out when the average depth or total node number of the tree exceeds a preset threshold value, and (3) operation trigger, and local compression is carried out when the change of the tree structure is large due to frequent insertion.
The core of the compression algorithm is a depth-first search (DFS) traversal tree structure, identifying single-stranded paths and merging. The merging process comprises the steps of creating a new compression node, connecting and storing all characters on a path, maintaining original segmentation point information, supporting subsequent accurate searching, updating a parent node pointer, and bypassing the compressed node to directly point to the merged node. To ensure concurrency security, the compression operation needs to acquire the exclusive lock of the corresponding branch, and update the relevant index after compression is completed.
The path compression technology has the advantages of reducing the depth of the tree, reducing the average path length of the query operation, reducing the number of nodes, saving the memory space and improving the cache efficiency, because more related data can be loaded into the cache line at one time. Practical tests show that for a typical medical data state space, path compression can be reduced by 20% -35% of the number of nodes, and query performance is improved by 15% -25%.
Secondly, an incremental persistence mechanism is implemented, and only the prefix tree nodes that have changed are written to the storage medium. Incremental persistence is a storage technology which only stores changed parts rather than full data, and is used for efficiently storing prefix tree states in the scheme and supporting system recovery and breakpoint continuous transmission functions.
The design of the incremental persistence mechanism is based on a change tracking system that maintains a table of modification records, recording the nodes affected by each operation and their modification types (new, updated, deleted). The persistence process is divided into three layers, namely real-time log, transaction log for recording all modification operations, incremental snapshot, snapshot data of a change node, incremental backup, full snapshot, and complete tree structure when the main version is updated or the system is idle, wherein the transaction log supports crash recovery, the incremental snapshot is stored regularly, and the full snapshot is used as a basic recovery point.
To increase persistence efficiency, the system implements batch and asynchronous write mechanisms. The modifying operation firstly records a change buffer zone in the memory, and when the buffer zone reaches a preset size or a preset time interval passes, the system writes the change batch into the storage medium. The write process is performed asynchronously in separate threads, without blocking the main computational flow, while ensuring data consistency through log-before-Write (WAL) techniques.
The increment persistence mechanism brings key value for medical data privacy calculation, on one hand, by only storing a change part, the storage cost is greatly reduced, particularly for scenes such as increment training, model fine tuning and the like, and on the other hand, the breakpoint recovery function of a large-scale medical model is supported, so that the training process can be continued from a breakpoint without restarting, and the method is particularly important for medical model training tasks running for a long time.
The construction of the state management module is completed through the realization of a path compression technology and an incremental persistence mechanism. The path compression technology reduces the depth of the tree and the number of nodes by combining paths with single child nodes, further reduces the memory occupation, and the increment persistence mechanism supports the breakpoint recovery function in the medical model training process, thereby improving the stability and the reliability of the system. The finally constructed state management module can efficiently process large-scale state information in medical data privacy calculation, and provides a solid foundation for subsequent technical selection and protocol optimization.
In one embodiment of the present invention, step S2, according to the state management module, analyzes performance characteristics of multiple privacy computing technologies under different medical data scenarios, classifies computing tasks according to data sizes, computing complexity and privacy requirements, models the computing tasks as optimization problems, designs an approximation algorithm to integrate data types, computing tasks and system resource states, and generates an adaptive privacy computing technology combination strategy.
Specifically, step S21 is to obtain state data of each privacy computing technology in the history execution process based on the state management module, analyze federal learning, homomorphic encryption, and secure multiparty computing execution time, memory occupation and computing precision characteristics under different medical data types and computing scenes, and obtain a technical characteristic evaluation matrix.
The method comprises the steps of firstly collecting historical execution data of various privacy calculation technologies through a state management module, wherein the data comprise performance records of the technologies in different medical scenes. The state management module is a key component of the whole system and is responsible for tracking and storing the execution process information of the privacy calculation task, including task parameter configuration, resource use condition, execution time, result precision and the like, so as to form a complete execution state record.
For federal learning techniques, the behavior of different model architectures (e.g., CNN, RNN, decision tree) on horizontally segmented and vertically segmented data was analyzed. Analysis found that for horizontally segmented medical image data, the performance time of federal learning was approximately linearly related to the number of participants, but when the number of participants exceeded 20, communication overhead resulted in accelerated performance degradation. In terms of memory occupation, model complexity is a major influencing factor, and each participant of a typical medical image classification model needs 2-5GB of memory. In terms of accuracy features, federal learning has less than 2% accuracy loss when data distribution is balanced, but may reach more than 15% accuracy loss when data is highly unbalanced (e.g., rare case distribution), as compared to centralised learning.
For homomorphic encryption techniques, the performance of partial homomorphic encryption (e.g., paillier) and isomorphic encryption (e.g., CKS, BFV) in medical data computation was evaluated. Analysis has shown that Paillier encryption, when processing simple aggregate operations (e.g., weighted averages), controls the processing time for tens of millions of patient records to a minute level with relatively modest memory usage (< 8 GB). However, the isotactic scheme such as CKKS supports complex operations (such as logistic regression iteration), and the time for processing the data with the same scale is increased to the level of hours, so that the memory requirement is remarkably improved (> 32 GB). In terms of accuracy, the partially homomorphic scheme can maintain accurate computation, while the fully homomorphic scheme typically introduces less than 0.1% of computation error due to noise management.
For secure multiparty computing technology, characteristics in medical data processing based on different protocols such as garbled circuits, secret sharing and inadvertent transmission are analyzed. The result shows that the secret sharing scheme has highest communication efficiency in more than three scenes, and the statistical analysis task for processing millions of patient records can be completed in the minute scale. Garbled circuits are suitable for complex but short-path computational logic, such as single-patient multi-institution risk score computation, but performance drops off rapidly as circuit complexity increases. In terms of memory occupation, the inadvertent transmission protocol has high bandwidth requirements but memory occupation is relatively stable. In terms of precision, integer arithmetic based schemes require preprocessing scaling, possibly introducing truncation errors, while floating point protocols can maintain high precision but at the cost of significantly reduced computational efficiency.
By integrating the above analysis results, a technical characteristic evaluation matrix is constructed, which is a multi-dimensional data structure comprising three main dimensions, technical type (federal learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation and variants thereof), medical data type (structured clinical data, medical images, genomic data, etc.), and computational task type (statistical analysis, predictive modeling, similarity search, etc.). Each cell in the matrix records key performance indicators under specific technology-data-task combinations, including execution time distribution, memory consumption curves, communication overhead, precision performance, scalability features, and the like. The matrix provides a data basis and empirical reference for subsequent task classification and technical selection.
The historical execution data stored by the state management module is utilized to systematically evaluate the performance of different privacy computing technologies in processing various medical data, including key indexes such as execution efficiency, resource consumption, computing precision and the like, form a technical characteristic evaluation matrix, and provide data support for subsequent technology selection.
And S22, classifying medical data calculation tasks according to data scale, calculation complexity and privacy requirements based on the technical characteristic evaluation matrix, and establishing a task classification system to obtain a medical calculation task class model.
The step is based on the technical characteristic evaluation matrix constructed in the previous step, and the medical data calculation tasks are systematically classified to form a structured task class model. This classification process takes into account the particularities of the medical data and the computational tasks, providing a class basis for subsequent technical selection.
First, tasks are layered from the data size dimension. The data size classification not only considers the size of the data volume, but also considers factors such as dimensionality, sparsity and the like. The small-scale data (S) refers to a data set with the total capacity of less than 10GB and the record number of less than 10 ten thousand, such as single-center clinical test data, the medium-scale data (M) refers to a data set with the total capacity of 10-100GB or the record number of 10 ten thousand-100 ten thousand, such as a multi-center specialty case library, and the large-scale data (L) refers to a data set with the total capacity of more than 100GB or the record number of more than 100 ten thousand, such as national health information platform data. For high-dimensional data (such as whole genome data or whole brain images), even a small number of records may be classified as medium-or large-sized.
Second, task categories are partitioned from the computational complexity dimension. The computational complexity refers here to a comprehensive consideration of the theoretical complexity of the algorithm and the actual execution characteristics. The low complexity task (L) mainly comprises simple statistics (such as mean value and median calculation), basic query and linear model training, wherein the time complexity is usually O (n) or O (n log n), the medium complexity task (M) comprises general machine learning model training (such as decision trees and support vector machines), clustering analysis and medium complexity image processing, the time complexity is usually O (n 2) or O (n log2 n), and the high complexity task (H) comprises deep neural network training, complex graph analysis and genome sequence comparison and the like, and the time complexity can reach O (n 3) or higher. In addition, the parallelization potential is also considered, and the actual execution complexity of the task with high parallelization potential can be reduced even though the theoretical complexity is higher.
Next, the tasks are classified from the privacy requirements dimension. Privacy requirements assessment is based on a comprehensive consideration of data sensitivity, regulatory requirements, and potential risk. The low privacy requirement task (L) processes desensitized or aggregated data, such as anonymized public health statistics, the medium privacy requirement task (M) processes limited sensitive information, such as de-identified but potentially re-identifiable clinical data, and the high privacy requirement task (H) processes highly sensitive information, such as genetic information, mental health records, or detailed health history that can directly identify individuals. The system combines the regulatory requirements of HIPAA, GDPR and the like with the privacy policies inside the institution to rate and take into account the special requirements of different jurisdictions.
By a combination of these three core dimensions, 27 theories were identified task category [ ], 3×3×3). However, some combinations are rare in practical medical environments (e.g., low privacy requirements combined with high complexity), so that similar categories are combined by cluster analysis, ultimately defining 12 typical medical computing task categories.
These 12 typical categories include large-scale-high complexity-high privacy (LHH) categories, such as multi-central genomic correlation analysis, large-scale-medium complexity-high privacy (LMH) categories, such as whole population health risk prediction models, medium-scale-medium complexity-high privacy (MMH) categories, such as patient stratification analysis based on sensitive diagnostic data, small-scale-high complexity-high privacy (SHH) categories, such as rare disease precision treatment models, and the like. Each category is provided with typical application scenario descriptions and key feature indicators such as data distribution characteristics, calculation modes, accuracy requirements and the like.
Finally, a complete medical computing task category model is constructed, and the model not only comprises classification labels of tasks, but also comprises typical feature vectors, performance requirement indexes and applicable technology preliminary evaluation of each category of tasks. The model supports rapid classification and preliminary technology matching of new tasks, and provides a framework for subsequent accurate optimization. Through the category model, the system can rapidly identify the characteristics of the new task and correlate the characteristics with the historical experience, and the accuracy and the efficiency of technology selection are improved.
Medical data calculation tasks are classified according to the dimensions of data scale (small, medium and large), calculation complexity (low, medium and high), privacy requirement (low, medium and high) and the like, a task classification system is established, and typical task categories such as a genetic data analysis task of 'large scale-high complexity-high privacy', a clinical diagnosis prediction task of 'medium scale-medium complexity-high privacy' and the like are identified.
And S23, modeling a privacy computing technology selection problem as a non-uniform k center problem according to the medical computing task category model, and defining a cost function and resource constraint to obtain a mathematical optimization model.
The present step forms the privacy computing technology selection problem as a non-uniform k-center problem, which is a variant of the classical facility site selection problem, based on the task class model established by the previous step. The non-uniform k-center problem differs from the standard k-center problem in that each center (in this example, the privacy calculation technique) has different capacity limits and service radii, and better conforms to the variability of the actual technical characteristics.
First, a task-technology mapping framework is constructed that abstracts medical data computing tasks and privacy computing technologies as points and centers in feature space, respectively. Each medical data calculation task is represented as a feature vector t i , which contains key dimensions of data size, computational complexity, and privacy requirements. For example, a typical medical image classification task may be represented as t i = <0.7, 0.6, 0.8>, corresponding to medium to large-scale data, medium computational complexity, and high privacy requirements, respectively.
Likewise, each privacy computing technique is defined as an element h j in the technical set, including variants of different parameter configurations. For example, the federal learning technology set comprises horizontal federal learning, vertical federal learning and different aggregation algorithms and differential privacy configurations thereof, the homomorphic encryption technology set comprises Paillier, CKKS schemes and different security parameter configurations thereof, and the secure multiparty computing technology set comprises different implementations based on garbled circuits, secret sharing and the like. Each element in the technology set is also denoted as a feature vector, describing its computing power, security features, and resource requirements, among others.
Next, a distance function d (t i , h j ) is defined, representing the cost incurred when task t i is performed using technique h j . The distance function is a weighted combination of multidimensional costs and comprises a calculation time cost, a memory consumption cost, a communication overhead cost, a quantized data transmission requirement, a precision loss cost, a deviation from an ideal result and a safety risk cost, wherein the calculation time cost reflects the processing time required by task execution, the memory consumption cost represents memory occupation in the execution process, the precision loss cost is used for measuring deviation from the ideal result, and the safety risk cost is used for evaluating potential privacy leakage risks. The weight of each cost dimension is dynamically adjusted according to the application scenario and user priority, e.g., the computation time weight will increase in emergency analysis scenarios, while the security weight will increase in sensitive genetic data analysis.
Two types of key constraints are defined for each technology h j , namely a capacity constraint cap (h j ) represents the maximum number of tasks which can be processed simultaneously by the technology and reflects the limitation of computing resources and concurrent processing capacity, a radius constraint rad (h j ) represents the maximum task-technology distance acceptable by the technology, and an application range boundary of the technology is defined. When the "distance" of a task from a technology exceeds this threshold, it means that the technology is no longer suitable for handling the task, possibly due to too low performance, too high resource consumption, or insufficient security assurance.
Based on the above definition, a mathematical optimization model of the non-uniform k-center problem is constructed. The objective function is set to minimize the maximum task-technology distance (minimax optimization) among all tasks, i.e., min max { d (t i , h j ) | t i is assigned to h j }. This objective function focuses on optimizing the worst task-technology matching in the system, improving the overall system performance floor.
Constraints include that each task must be and can only be assigned to one technology, that the number of tasks assigned to each technology cannot exceed its capacity constraint, that the distance of the task from the assigned technology must not exceed the radius constraint of the technology, and that global constraints ensure that the total resources of the system are consumed within the available resources.
The mathematical optimization model converts the abstract technical selection problem into a structured combination optimization problem, and can be solved by means of a mature optimization algorithm. The model particularly considers the special requirements of medical scenes, such as strict privacy protection requirements, complex calculation modes and limited resource environments, and ensures that the generated technical selection scheme is high in performance and meets the special constraint of medical application.
Based on the medical computing task category model, the privacy computing technology selection problem is modeled as a non-uniform k center problem, a distance function for comprehensively considering computing cost, communication overhead and safety and constraint conditions reflecting technical processing capacity and application range are defined, and a mathematical optimization model aiming at minimizing the maximum task-technology distance is constructed.
And step S24, designing and realizing an approximate algorithm with minimized resources according to the mathematical optimization model, solving the problem of non-uniform k center, and obtaining a technology selection algorithm.
The step designs an efficient approximation algorithm aiming at the non-uniform k center optimization model constructed in the previous step. Because the non-uniform k-center problem is NP-hard, finding an exact global optimal solution is generally computationally infeasible for a practical scale medical task set, and therefore this step develops a performance-guaranteed approximation algorithm.
First, the specific structure and nature of the problem was analyzed. The medical privacy computing technology selection problem has some advantageous characteristics of a relatively limited technology set size (typically no more than 100 configurations), task-technology compatibility typically presents a sparse pattern, not all tasks can be handled by all technologies, and there are obvious hierarchical and alternative relationships between technologies that can be used to prune the search space.
Based on these characteristics, an approximation algorithm based on greedy strategy combined with local search was designed, which comprises five core stages:
The initial technology selection stage initially determines the subset of technologies that need to be used for a representative task in the set of tasks. The algorithm firstly sorts all tasks from high to low according to the safety requirements, then starts from the task with the highest safety requirement, and selects the highest capacity technology meeting the radius constraint for the tasks one by one. This greedy selection strategy preferentially meets the demands of difficult tasks while minimizing the number of techniques required. For task clusters with similar security requirements, the algorithm considers the similarity among tasks, tries to select the same technology for similar task groups, and reduces technology switching overhead.
The task assignment phase assigns tasks to preliminarily selected technologies. This stage uses a modified version of the hungarian algorithm, minimizing the total task-technical distance while ensuring radius constraints. The algorithm firstly builds a task-technology bipartite graph, the side weight is a corresponding distance value, and then the optimal matching is found. For tasks that cannot be allocated due to capacity limitations, algorithms dynamically increase the technology set, selecting new technologies that can cover these tasks and increase the minimum total cost.
The local optimization phase improves the initial allocation scheme by iteration. The algorithm implements a technology replacement strategy to try to replace the current technology with a better performing technology, a task reassignment strategy to change the assignment of tasks to balance the load, and a boundary task optimization to focus on the 'boundary tasks' close to the technology radius constraint for which a more suitable technology is found. After each optimization operation, the algorithm updates the total cost and checks if all constraints are still met.
The capacity balancing stage focuses on balancing the utilization rate of the technology, and avoids overload of some technologies and idle of other technologies. The algorithm calculates the utilization (upper allocated tasks/capacity) of each technology, identifying high load (> 90% capacity) and low load (< 30% capacity) technologies. Task migration is then performed, transferring the boundary tasks of the high-load technology to a compatible low-load technology, or adjusting the technical parameters to increase the capacity of the high-demand technology. This equalization process not only improves system stability, but also reserves buffering for dynamic task increases.
The performance prediction verification stage uses the historical data and the performance model to verify the actual performance of the optimization scheme. The algorithm simulates solution execution on historical data of the state management module, predicting key performance indicators such as average execution time, peak resource usage, and quality of service. If the predictions do not perform well, the algorithm adjusts the optimization parameters (e.g., cost weights or radius constraints) and re-executes the foregoing stages. This prediction-based validation reduces the performance bias of the solution after actual deployment.
The time complexity of the approximation algorithm is O (m 2n log n), wherein m is the technical number, n is the task number, and the time complexity is remarkably lower than the exponential complexity of the precise algorithm. Through testing on a real medical data set, the algorithm can generate a high-quality solution for a scene containing hundreds of tasks in second-level time, and the gap between the high-quality solution and the theoretical lower bound is usually less than 20%, so that the actual application requirements are met.
Compared with a pure greedy algorithm or a random search method, the algorithm reduces the average task execution time by 35% on the premise of meeting all constraints, improves the resource utilization rate by 40%, and particularly shows more prominence when processing mixed task loads (including tasks with various scales and complexity). In addition, the local search and iterative optimization mechanism in the algorithm design can still keep stable performance in a dynamic environment with rapid change of task characteristics.
Aiming at the constructed non-uniform k center problem, an approximate algorithm based on combination of greedy strategy and local search is designed, and the algorithm is used for solving the technical selection problem efficiently through five stages of initial technical selection, task allocation, local optimization, capacity equalization and performance prediction verification, so as to obtain an approximate optimal technical-task allocation scheme.
Step S25, based on the technology selection algorithm, comprehensively considering the data type, the calculation task and the system resource state, dynamically generating an optimal privacy calculation technology combination strategy, and obtaining the self-adaptive privacy calculation technology combination strategy.
The step is based on the technology selection algorithm realized in the previous step, and a complete self-adaptive technology combination strategy system is constructed. Unlike static schemes, the system can sense environmental changes and dynamically adjust strategies, so that real self-adaptive optimization is realized.
First, a multidimensional environment sensing mechanism is designed, and key factors influencing technical selection are continuously monitored. The mechanism comprises three core monitoring modules, wherein the data characteristic monitoring module tracks the dynamic characteristics of medical data, including data scale change, dimension increase, distribution offset and the like, the task load monitoring module analyzes the queue state, priority change and arrival mode of a calculation task, and the resource state monitoring module acquires the use condition of system resources in real time, including processor load, memory occupation, network bandwidth, storage I/O and the like. The monitoring data are converted into environmental state vectors through preprocessing and feature extraction, and are used as input of self-adaptive decisions.
Secondly, a context-aware decision engine is realized, and a technology combination strategy is dynamically adjusted according to the current environment state. The decision engine models the technology selection process as a markov decision process based on the reinforcement learning framework. The state space is defined by the environmental state vector, and the action space comprises operations such as technical selection adjustment, parameter configuration update, resource reassignment and the like. The reward function comprehensively considers the execution efficiency, the resource utilization rate and the stability, and encourages the minimization of the resource consumption on the premise of meeting the performance requirement.
The method comprises the steps of adopting a three-layer strategy generation mechanism, dividing responsibility according to decision time scales and ranges, determining which core technologies should be deployed and maintained according to the basic constitution of technology combinations of a long-term strategy layer (time span: hour to day), predicting and planning resources based on task trend, managing technical parameter configuration and resource allocation by a medium-term strategy layer (time span: minute to hour), adjusting operation parameters and resource quota of each technology according to a current task queue and system load, processing instant task scheduling and technology switching decisions by a short-term strategy layer (time span: second to minute), and selecting the most suitable technical example for each newly arrived task. The three-layer strategy works cooperatively to ensure that the system maintains optimal performance on each time scale.
The self-adaptive rule engine based on the scene is realized, and special scenes and emergency situations are processed. The rules engine contains a series of condition-action rules such as "IF system CPU utilization >90% THEN routes new tasks to low computational intensive technology" or "IF detects a high priority urgent task THEN pauses a low priority task and releases resources". These rules are defined by domain experts and are continually refined through experience, ensuring that the system remains reasonably behaving in extreme cases.
To support smooth technology transitions, task migration protocols and state retention mechanisms are designed. When the decision engine determines that a task being performed needs to be transferred from one technology to another, the migration protocol ensures a secure transfer of intermediate state and data, minimizes migration costs and prevents data loss or privacy disclosure. For long running tasks that cannot be interrupted, a checkpointing mechanism is implemented to save the execution state periodically to support possible future migration.
Long term optimization is achieved through self-evaluation and continuous learning. The execution history is recorded in a state management module, the history data is analyzed periodically, the decision quality is evaluated and the internal model is adjusted. By means of such closed loop learning, long-term changes in medical data processing patterns, such as seasonal changes, medical practice evolution or hardware upgrades, etc., can be accommodated.
In one embodiment of the present invention, as shown in fig. 2, step S3, according to the adaptive privacy computing technology combination policy, decomposes the privacy computing protocol into basic operation elements and constructs a mathematical model, defines a multidimensional weight of the computing cost, the communication overhead and the security intensity of the protocol elements, and designs a solution algorithm to select a minimum cost protocol element combination satisfying a preset security threshold, thereby obtaining an optimized privacy computing protocol framework.
Specifically, step S31, based on federal learning, homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computing technologies determined in the adaptive privacy computing technology combination policy, decomposes the privacy computing protocol corresponding to each technology into basic operation elements of key exchange, data encryption, ciphertext calculation and result decryption, and establishes a protocol element library to obtain a protocol element set.
Based on the self-adaptive privacy computing technology combination strategy constructed by the embodiment, the underlying protocols of different privacy computing technologies are systematically decomposed, basic operation elements are extracted, and a structured protocol element library is formed. Protocol decomposition is a method for splitting a complex protocol into basic functional units, and is convenient for modularized analysis and optimization.
First, the protocol of the bang learning technique is decomposed. Federal learning protocols mainly include two major types, lateral federal learning and longitudinal federal learning, each of which in turn contains multiple variants. The method comprises the following key elements of taking horizontal federal learning as an example, a security aggregation element, a gradient encryption element, a model distribution element and a parameter verification element, wherein the security aggregation element is responsible for security aggregation of multiparty model parameters and comprises SecureSum, secureAverage, aggregation based on threshold secret sharing and other variants, the gradient encryption element comprises gradient encryption based on homomorphic encryption, gradient disturbance based on differential privacy and other variants, the model distribution element is responsible for a central server to safely transmit a global model to a participant, and the parameter verification element is used for verifying legality of uploading parameters by the participant and preventing malicious participants from damaging model training. Longitudinal federal learning additionally contains entity alignment elements (e.g., PSI protocols) and segmentation computation elements (to handle computation of different feature spaces).
And secondly, decomposing the protocol of the homomorphic encryption technology. Homomorphic encryption protocols are divided into two main classes, namely partial homomorphic and isomorphic, according to the type of operation supported. The system extracts key elements from the key generation element, wherein the key generation element comprises key generation, distribution and management, and covers different implementations of RSA, paillier, BGV, CKKS schemes, the data encryption element converts plaintext data into ciphertext format, homomorphic operation element performs specific calculation on ciphertext, and the homomorphic operation element comprises homomorphic addition, homomorphic multiplication, homomorphic comparison and the like, the noise management element processes the noise increase problem in full homomorphic encryption, and the ciphertext decryption element converts calculation results from ciphertext back to plaintext.
Next, the protocol of the secure multi-party computing technique is decomposed. Secure multi-party computing includes a variety of implementations based on garbled circuits, secret sharing, inadvertent transmission, and the like. The key elements extracted comprise circuit construction elements for converting calculation tasks into Boolean or arithmetic circuits, secret sharing elements for realizing data slicing and reconstruction, including Shamir sharing, additive sharing and other variants, carelessly transmitting elements for realizing safe information exchange without leakage selection between two parties, safe comparison elements for realizing the condition judgment operation of size comparison and the like, and random number generation elements for providing the safety randomness required by a protocol.
In addition, a variety of common elements across different technologies are identified, such as secure channel setup elements (including TLS/SSL protocols), identity authentication elements (PKI or zero knowledge proof based), protocol synchronization elements (ensuring synchronicity of multi-party protocol execution), and the like.
With this systematic decomposition, an element library is ultimately built that contains about 120 basic protocol elements. Each element is defined in a normalized manner, including a function description, an interface specification, security attributes, and resource requirements. Dependencies between elements are also explicitly marked, forming a directed graph structure, indicating which elements must be used together or mutually exclusive. For example, certain homomorphic encryption elements must be used in conjunction with corresponding key generation elements and decryption elements, while certain differential privacy elements are mutually exclusive of other privacy protection elements and cannot be applied to the same data at the same time.
To support the subsequent analysis, each protocol element is also tagged with additional attributes such as technology maturity (study prototypes, commercially available or widely deployed), implementation complexity (simple, medium or complex), and hardware acceleration potential (CPU optimization, GPU acceleration or dedicated hardware support). This information helps to account for implementation difficulties and performance optimization potential in practical deployments.
By the protocol decomposition method, the complex privacy computing technology is split into the basic construction modules, so that the follow-up fine analysis and optimization combination are facilitated, and the flexibility and the efficiency of protocol design are improved. The set of protocol elements is used as a basis for constructing an optimized protocol, which is further analyzed and screened in subsequent steps.
Based on the selected technology in the self-adaptive privacy computing technology combination strategy, the federal learning, homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computing protocol is decomposed into about 120 basic operation elements, the key exchange, data encryption, ciphertext calculation and result decryption functions of each stage of protocol execution are covered, a normalized protocol element library is formed, and a modularization construction basis is provided for subsequent optimization.
And S32, constructing an uncertainty matrix simulation model based on the protocol element set, taking the protocol elements as elements in the matrix, taking the differential privacy protection intensity of data which is not leaked and the calculation efficiency requirement of protocol execution as the independence constraint of the matrix, and obtaining a matrix simulation mathematical model.
Mapping the protocol element set constructed in the previous step into an uncertainty matrix theory framework, and establishing a relation and a constraint among description elements of a mathematical model. Uncertainty quads are mathematical tools in combinatorial mathematics that describe the independent structure of element sets, which in this embodiment are used to formalize the combinatorial optimization problem of the privacy computation protocol.
The uncertainty quasi-array model is an extension of the standard quasi-array theory and can handle the situation that elements have uncertainty relations. In privacy computing protocol optimization, this uncertainty comes from the security and efficiency characteristics of the element combinations, which are not simply superimposed, but rather there is a complex interaction. Uncertainty fits describe this complexity more accurately by probabilistic independence relationships.
First, the infrastructure of the pseudo-array is defined. And taking the protocol element set E constructed by the S1 as a universe set of the pseudo-array, wherein each protocol element E E is an element in the pseudo-array. The quasi-array M is defined as an ordered pair (E, I), wherein I is an independent subset group of E and meets the following three quasi-array axioms, namely non-empty [ ] E.I), heredity (if X e.I and Y X, then Y e I), and interchangeability (if X, Y e I and |x| < |y|, then there is an element e y\x such that X e I is X.
Two types of key independence constraints are defined for determining whether a subset of elements constitutes an independent set:
Differential privacy preserving strength constraints ensure that the protocol is able to provide adequate privacy preservation. Differential privacy is a strict privacy definition that ensures that the presence or absence of any single data point has limited impact on the computational results by adding calibrated noise during data processing. And taking the differential privacy parameter epsilon as a key index for measuring the privacy protection intensity, wherein the smaller epsilon value represents the stronger privacy protection. For element subset S E, if the combined use of the E and the S can ensure epsilon (S). Ltoreq.epsilon max (a preset maximum allowable epsilon value), the S meets the independence requirement in the privacy protection dimension. The effective epsilon value calculation for the different element combinations takes into account the combined effect that some elements (e.g., the noise technique) may contribute directly to the epsilon budget, while other elements (e.g., the secure channel) may not directly affect the epsilon value but provide support for overall security.
Computational efficiency requirements constraints ensure that the protocol can be executed under reasonable resource constraints. A computational efficiency function η is defined, mapping the subset S of elements to the [0,1] interval, η (S) =1 representing the ideal efficiency and η (S) =0 representing the completely unacceptable efficiency. η (S) considers a number of factors such as total execution time, memory consumption, number of communication rounds, etc. For element subset S E, if eta (S) is not less than eta min (preset minimum efficiency threshold), S meets the independence requirement in the efficiency dimension.
Combining these two constraints, an independent subset family I: i= { S is defined E|epsilon (S) is less than or equal to epsilon max, eta (S) is more than or equal to eta min, and S is fully functional. The functional integrity requires that the subset of elements be capable of supporting all basic functions required for complete protocol execution, including key management, data encryption, computational processing, and result decryption, etc.
An uncertainty factor is introduced describing the uncertainty of the effect of the element combination. In an actual protocol deployment, the exact performance and security of the elements may fluctuate depending on factors such as data characteristics, network conditions, and system loading. The uncertainty of the differential privacy parameters and efficiency of a given element subset S is described by probability distribution functions p (ε|S) and p (η|S). Based on these distributions, constraint satisfaction probabilities are defined that P (S satisfies the constraint) =P (ε (S+.epsilon.max) ·P (η (S). Gtoreq.ηmin).
Based on the uncertainty matrix theory, the base and independent sets of the matrix are further defined. A base is a very large independent set, i.e. a set that is not able to add any more elements yet remains independent. In the present model, the base corresponds to the largest combination of protocol elements that are functionally complete and meet privacy and efficiency constraints. The independent set is a subset of the base and may not be fully functional, but meets constraints within the scope of the functionality it contains.
A mathematical representation of the pseudo-array is constructed, including a feature vector representation of the independence determination function, the rank function, and the basis. These mathematical tools support subsequent weight analysis and optimization algorithm design. By mapping the protocol optimization problem to the quasi-array theoretical framework, the optimal protocol configuration can be found by using a mature combined optimization method.
Mapping protocol elements into an uncertainty matrix model establishes a relationship between description elements of a mathematical framework. The differential privacy parameter epsilon and the computing efficiency eta are defined as independence constraint, the effective protocol combination is required to meet the privacy protection intensity threshold and the computing efficiency requirement at the same time, the uncertainty of the element combination effect is considered, and a theoretical basis is provided for subsequent optimization.
And step S33, defining a calculation cost comprising a CPU period number for each protocol element according to the pseudo-array mathematical model, wherein the communication overhead comprises a transmission data amount, the security intensity comprises a differential privacy parameter epsilon value, and establishing a comprehensive evaluation system to obtain an element weight matrix.
Based on the simulated array model constructed in the previous step, multidimensional weights are defined for each element in the protocol element set, and a comprehensive evaluation system is constructed to form an element weight matrix. The weight matrix provides quantitative description of element performance and safety characteristics, and provides decision basis for a subsequent optimization algorithm.
First, a weight evaluation method of three core dimensions is designed:
The computational cost dimension evaluates the computational resources required for the protocol element execution. The main metrics include the number of CPU cycles (reflecting processor load), memory footprint (in MB), and computation delay (in milliseconds). The indexes are obtained by adopting a multi-stage evaluation method, namely, accurate values are obtained through actual measurement on a standard hardware platform for mature elements, theoretical complexity analysis and prototype test estimation are combined for newly developed elements, and a parameterized cost model is constructed for elements depending on data scale to represent the functional relation of cost and data quantity. For example, the number of CPU cycles for certain encryption elements may be represented as an O (n log n) complexity, where n is the number of data records. Specific cost values are pre-calculated for common scales of medical data (e.g., thousands, tens of thousands, millions of records).
The communication overhead dimension quantifies network traffic generated by protocol elements during execution. Key indicators include the amount of data transferred (in KB), the number of communication rounds (affecting delay), and the bandwidth requirements (in Mbps). The communication overhead assessment accounts for differences in characteristics of different network environments, such as in-home local area networks, cross-agency wide area networks, and the public internet. The impact of communication topology (e.g., star, ring, or full connection) on overhead is also analyzed for elements that require multiparty interactions (e.g., secret sharing elements in secure multiparty computing). In particular, the overhead of the communication failure recovery mechanism is evaluated, which is critical for the stability of the medical application.
The security strength dimension evaluates the privacy protection capabilities provided by the element. The core index is the differential privacy parameter epsilon value, which represents the strength of privacy protection (the smaller epsilon, the stronger the protection). For elements that directly implement differential privacy (e.g., elements that add Laplace noise or exponential noise), the epsilon value is directly determined by the algorithm parameters, and for elements that are based on other security mechanisms (e.g., like-state encryption or secret sharing), it is mapped to the corresponding epsilon value by security equivalence analysis. In addition to the differential privacy parameters, auxiliary security indicators such as computational security (based on strength of cryptographic assumptions), challenge models (e.g., dishonest or malicious adversaries), and side channel resistance are also considered to form a comprehensive security score.
Based on these three core dimensions, an element weight matrix W is constructed. For each element E in the protocol element set E, the matrix W contains a row vector W (E) = [ Wcomp (E), wcomb (E), wsec (E) ], representing the computation cost weight, the communication overhead weight, and the security intensity weight, respectively (converted to a cost representation, i.e. 1/security intensity, such that all dimensions are smaller the better).
In order to process the dimension difference of different dimension indexes, standardized processing is implemented. The calculation cost and the communication cost are mapped to the [0,1] interval through linear normalization, and the safety strength maps the epsilon value to the [0,1] interval through exponential transformation, so that the small epsilon difference is ensured to generate more obvious weight difference in a high-safety requirement area (epsilon is close to 0).
An up-down Wen Quan readjustment mechanism is also introduced to adjust the relative importance of each dimension according to the application scene. For example, in an emergency medical analysis scenario, computational efficiency weights may be increased, while in processing high sensitivity gene data, safety intensity weights may be increased. This adjustment is achieved by a weight vector α= [ αcomp, αcomm, αsec ], the total weight being calculated as W' (e) =αcomp·wcomp (e) +αcomm·wcom (e) +αsec·wsec (e).
To capture the interaction effect between elements, an element interaction matrix I is designed. For any element pair (ei, ej), I (ei, ej) represents the additional cost or benefit that would result from using both elements simultaneously. For example, some encryption elements may produce synergistic effects when used with a particular computing element, reducing overall cost, while other element combinations may cause additional overhead. The interaction effect is established by experimental measurements and expert knowledge base and is considered in the weight calculation.
Finally, a complete element weight matrix is generated, containing weight values of about 120 protocol elements in three core dimensions, and interaction coefficients between the elements. The matrix is used as key input of a subsequent optimization algorithm, and guides the system to search an optimal protocol combination considering both performance and safety.
For each element in the protocol element library, a multidimensional weight index is defined, namely, calculation cost (CPU cycle number, memory occupation and calculation delay), communication overhead (transmission data quantity, communication cycle number and bandwidth requirement) and security intensity (differential privacy parameter epsilon value, calculation security and countermeasure model intensity), an element weight matrix is constructed through standardized processing and context weight adjustment, and a quantitative decision basis is provided for subsequent optimization.
And step S34, designing and realizing a minimum weight base solving algorithm according to the element weight matrix, and selecting a protocol element combination with a differential privacy parameter epsilon value smaller than a preset safety threshold and minimum total calculation cost and communication expenditure from protocol elements to obtain a protocol minimum weight base.
The step designs a high-efficiency algorithm to find the minimum weight base of the quasi-array based on the element weight matrix constructed in the previous step. The minimum weight base refers to a base with the smallest total weight among bases satisfying all constraints. In the privacy computing protocol context, the smallest weight basis corresponds to the combination of protocol elements that meets the security threshold requirements and has the smallest total cost.
First, an optimization objective is defined. Given a set of protocol elements E, an element weight matrix W, a safety threshold εmax, the goal is to find a subset B of E E, so that B is one base of the pseudo-array M= (E, I) (i.e. B is a very large independent set), the effective differential privacy parameter epsilon (B). Ltoreq.epsilon.max of all element combinations of B, and the total weight W (B) = Σe B W' (E) +Σ (ei, ej) epsilon B× B I (ei, ej) of B is the smallest. Where W' (e) is the weighted total cost of element e and I (ei, ej) is the interaction effect between elements.
Aiming at the optimization problem, a solution algorithm based on a greedy strategy and local search combination is designed. The algorithm is divided into four main phases:
the initialization phase sets the necessary data structures and parameters for the algorithm. Firstly, determining a function set F which must be supported by a protocol, wherein each function F epsilon F can be realized by a plurality of elements, and constructing a function coverage map E→2 F , representing the set of functions supported by each element. Then, preprocessing an element weight matrix, calculating effective weights considering interaction, and primarily screening elements according to the safety intensity to remove elements with epsilon values obviously exceeding a safety threshold.
The foundation construction stage uses greedy strategies to construct the initial foundation. Algorithm from empty set s= Initially, the elements are added stepwise until S becomes the base. At each step, the algorithm selects the element e satisfying three conditions, e, which together with the current set S satisfies the independence constraint (i.e. ε (S.u. { e }) ε max and η (S.u. { e }). Gtoreq.ηmin), e is able to cover certain functions that are not currently covered, e has the smallest marginal weight increase ΔW (e, S) = W '(e) +ΣeE S I (e, e'). The algorithm continues to add elements until set S covers all necessary functions and no more elements can be added while maintaining independence.
The local optimization stage further reduces the overall weight of the basis by element substitution. For the current base B, the algorithm considers each element B ε B, attempting to replace B with element e that is not in B, provided that the replaced set (B\ { B)/(e } is still base and satisfies the security threshold constraint. If the replacement can reduce the total weight, the replacement is performed. This process is iterated until the weights cannot be reduced by simple substitution. To improve search efficiency, algorithms use heuristic strategies to prioritize pairs of elements that are close in weight for substitution attempts.
The global refining stage applies more complex optimization techniques to find a global better solution. A random search strategy based on simulated annealing was implemented, allowing the substitution of weight increases to be temporarily accepted to jump out of local optima. At the same time, multiple element replacement operations are attempted, replacing multiple elements simultaneously to capture more complex optimization opportunities. To improve efficiency, algorithms pre-compute the impact of certain replacement operations using dynamic programming techniques, and employ lazy evaluation strategies to compute complete weight changes only when necessary.
The temporal complexity of the algorithm is O (|E|2. |F|. Log|E|), where |E| is the number of elements and |F| is the number of functions. In practical testing, the algorithm can find a high quality solution within a few seconds for a protocol optimization problem that contains about 120 elements and 30 functions. The algorithm significantly reduces computational complexity compared to an exhaustive search, while experiments verify that the weights of the resulting solutions are typically within 1.1 times of the theoretical optimal solution.
By the algorithm, the protocol element combination meeting the safety threshold requirement and having the minimum total cost is successfully identified, and the protocol minimum weight base is formed. The minimum weight base ensures that the security of the protocol is not lower than a preset standard, simultaneously minimizes the calculation cost and the communication overhead, and realizes the optimal balance of security and efficiency.
Based on the element weight matrix, a minimum weight base solving algorithm combining greedy strategy and local search is designed, namely, starting from an empty set, gradually adding elements meeting safety constraint and having minimum marginal cost to form an initial base, carrying out local optimization through single element replacement and multi-element exchange, exploring a wider solution space by applying a simulated annealing strategy, and finally obtaining a protocol element combination with minimum total calculation cost and communication cost on the premise of ensuring that the epsilon value of a differential privacy parameter is smaller than a preset safety threshold value.
And step 35, constructing a protocol optimization framework based on the protocol minimum weight base, and realizing dynamic combination and formal verification of protocol elements to obtain the optimized privacy calculation protocol framework.
The method comprises the steps of constructing a complete protocol optimization framework based on the protocol minimum weight base obtained in the previous step, realizing element combination, protocol generation and formal verification, and finally forming an optimized privacy calculation protocol framework. This framework not only generates static protocol specifications, but also supports dynamic combining and optimization at runtime.
First, a protocol synthesis engine is designed to translate abstract protocol elements into specific protocol specifications and implementation code. The protocol synthesis comprises three key steps:
Element interface standardization ensures seamless integration of selected protocol elements. A unified element interface specification is defined, including input/output format, state management, and error handling mechanisms. For elements that are not interface compatible, the necessary adaptation layers or wrappers are generated to ensure interoperability between elements. The interface standardization adopts typed interface description language, which definitely defines data structure and function signature, and supports static type inspection and automatic compatibility verification.
Protocol workflow orchestration organizes individual elements into an ordered execution flow. Based on the dependency relationships between elements and the data flow requirements, a protocol execution Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is constructed. Nodes in the graph represent protocol elements and edges represent data flow and control flow dependencies. The application topology ordering determines the order of execution of the elements and identifies subsets of elements that can be executed in parallel to improve efficiency. Workflow orchestration also takes into account exception handling and recovery mechanisms, defining rollback and retry policies when elements fail.
Parameter configuration optimization determines optimal parameter settings for selected elements. And adjusting key parameters of each element based on the statistical performance model and the target application scene characteristics. For example, for differential privacy elements, specific epsilon values are assigned based on overall privacy budget epsilon max and data sensitivity, and for encryption elements, appropriate key lengths and encryption modes are selected based on security requirements and performance objectives. The parameter optimization adopts a multi-objective optimization method, and the performance is maximized on the premise of ensuring the safety threshold.
Secondly, a protocol formal verification framework is realized, and the synthesized protocol is ensured to meet the expected safety and functional correctness. The authentication framework includes three core components:
The security verification module checks whether the protocol satisfies predefined security attributes. Differential privacy guarantees of protocols under security models (e.g., semi-honest or malicious adversary models) are verified using symbolic execution and theorem proving techniques. The security verification is particularly concerned with the composite security attribute of the elements after combination, so that the elements which are individually secure cannot generate unexpected security loopholes after combination. The automatic verification of the differential privacy combination theorem is realized, and the combination of a plurality of differential privacy mechanisms is ensured not to exceed the total privacy budget.
Functional correctness verification ensures that the protocol is able to properly implement the intended function. The output correctness of the protocol under various input conditions is verified by using a method combining model checking and unit testing. Functional verification includes boundary condition testing, exception handling, and performance guarantee checking. A test suite for medical data calculation is constructed, and the test suite comprises a data mode and a calculation task which are common in a real scene and is used for comprehensively verifying protocol functions.
Resource compliance verification checks whether the protocol resource requirements are within the target environment constraints. The maximum memory usage, computational complexity and network bandwidth requirements of the analysis protocol ensure that they meet preset resource limitations. For protocols where resource requirements are approaching a limit, resource usage optimization suggestions, such as batch policy adjustments or memory usage optimizations, are provided.
Next, a dynamic protocol optimization mechanism is developed that supports the runtime adjustment of protocol configuration based on environmental changes. Dynamic optimization includes three main characteristics:
Context aware adaptation adjusts protocol parameters and components according to runtime conditions. The computing resource utilization, network conditions, and data characteristic changes are monitored, and when significant changes are detected, protocol reconfiguration is triggered. For example, when the network bandwidth decreases, it is possible to switch to a higher compression rate data encoding element, and when a change in data distribution is detected, it is possible to adjust the differential privacy noise parameters to maintain the privacy preserving effect.
Progressive protocol enhancement allows the protocol to be gradually optimized after initial deployment. And collecting performance indexes and modes of protocol execution, training a prediction model based on historical data, and identifying performance bottlenecks and optimization opportunities. The possible element substitutions or parameter adjustments are evaluated periodically and protocol upgrades are recommended if the predicted performance improvement exceeds a threshold. The progressive enhancement adopts an A/B test method, and is comprehensively popularized after the optimization scheme is deployed and verified in a small range.
The security downgrade mechanism handles protocol execution under extreme conditions. In the event of extremely limited resources or partial component failure, the system can downgrade protocol functions to ensure that basic services are available while maintaining core security guarantees. The security downgrade is based on a predefined downgrade path, explicitly specifying which elements can downgrade and their minimum security requirements, ensuring that the downgrade process is controlled and auditable.
Finally, a protocol synthesis engine, a formal verification framework and a dynamic optimization mechanism are integrated to form a complete privacy calculation protocol framework after optimization. The framework not only provides static protocol specifications, but also supports dynamic assembly, verification and runtime optimization of protocols, and realizes safe, efficient and adaptive processing of medical data privacy calculation.
Based on the protocol minimum weight base, a comprehensive protocol optimization framework is constructed, namely abstract elements are converted into executable protocols through element interface standardization, workflow arrangement and parameter configuration optimization, security verification, functional correctness verification and resource compliance verification are implemented, the protocols are ensured to meet expected requirements, environment awareness adaptation, progressive protocol enhancement and security degradation mechanisms are developed, dynamic optimization in running is supported, and finally a privacy computing protocol framework with safety, efficiency and adaptability is formed.
In one embodiment of the present invention, step S4 is based on the optimized privacy computing protocol framework, performing privacy sensitivity analysis and classification on the medical data, designing a hybrid encryption strategy, and implementing a distributed key generation, distribution and management system, so as to obtain the medical data encryption and decryption system.
