I. Intrusion Detection System
An intrusion detection system (IDS) can be defined as a surveillance system that detects abnormal activity and sends an alert when it is found. It analyzes the metadata contained in network packets and determines whether to allow or deny traffic based on preset rules. It sets up a barrier to prevent some traffic or procedures from passing through. An effective IDS provides three most important security measures: (i) data confidentiality, which determines whether data is stored on a secure server; (ii) data availability, which determines whether data is easily accessible to authorized users; and (iii) data integrity, which checks whether data is accurate and consistent with other data in the system.
Initially, deployment and detection are the two categories into which intrusion detection technologies can be divided. These two groups are further subdivided into two subgroups within each category. Depending on the deployment technology, IDSs generally fall into one of two categories: host-based IDS (HIDS) or network-based IDS (NIDS).
For example, Open Source Security (OSSEC) is a HIDS and OpenWIGS-ng is a NIDS. IDS approaches can also be classified as signature-based or anomaly-based systems, depending on how they detect intrusions. The first is based on previously established system behavior patterns. For example, Snort is a signature-based intrusion detection system. It operates as a network sniffer and is an open source network intrusion prevention and detection technology. Signature-based IDS cannot be used to identify new or unknown threats. Anomaly-based IDS can recognize any change in system behavior as a potential threat by using specific network traffic features. For example, CrowdSec is a collaborative anomaly-based intrusion detection system.
Figure 1 is a diagram showing the classification of intrusion detection systems.
Referring to Figure 1, there are a total of four intrusion detection methods in the network depending on the distribution and detection method.
The application of machine learning (ML) approaches has shown great success in improving the detection techniques of well-known intrusion detection systems (IDS) by implementing various algorithms (e.g. neural networks) that predict potential threats based on network traffic analysis. For a long time, it has been standard practice in the industry to manage and analyze industrial data generated by IoT systems and store them centrally in databases. This data is processed using machine learning techniques to distinguish between attack traffic and normal traffic.
Figure 2 is a diagram showing the steps of a machine learning-based intrusion detection system (IDS).
A generalized diagram is shown in Fig. 2, which illustrates the steps that occur in an IDS driven by a conventional machine learning method. The input of the experimental data set containing IoT traffic is the initial step, as shown in the figure. The preprocessing of the data set, which combines the normalization and data cleaning steps, is the next step. This preprocessing is necessary because the data set often contains noise, redundancy, and various types of data, which causes serious difficulties in data modeling and knowledge retrieval. The classification of network traffic can be hampered by low-relevance and redundant data features, so the preprocessing, feature extraction, and selection steps follow. The data set after preprocessing, feature selection, and feature extraction is divided into a training data set and a test data set, where the ML algorithm is applied. The ML method used can be evaluated to determine how well the model detects intrusions and normal traffic in the final step.
These centralized techniques for data processing are good for management, but they have difficulties in security and privacy. Recent studies have highlighted the vulnerability of various machine learning models to intrusion detection, where untraceable modifications to input data can lead to incorrect output predictions, thereby fooling machine learning algorithms. In addition, existing centralized methodologies require data to be transferred and processed by a single central entity, which makes them unworkable in some situations, such as large-scale data management for response time, performance, and scalability, due to the lack of availability of private data.
The volume and sensitivity of information shared by some devices in IoT networks can aggravate the above-mentioned issues, thus increasing the need for decentralized solutions for data management. Federated Learning (FL), a collaborative distributed learning approach that addresses the privacy concerns of traditional centralized ML approaches, is introduced, where the end devices (also known as clients or parties) only share updates of the global model assembled by a central unit (aggregator or coordinator). FL never shares user data with the outside world, thus protecting the privacy of the users. Typically, FL allows the ML process to extract information from multiple datasets stored in multiple distributed locations. This approach allows multiple parties to collaborate on model evolution without sharing sensitive information. Some of the industries where FL has been extended are security, telecommunications, Internet of Things (IoT), and healthcare.
Recently, the use of federated learning-based intrusion detection methods has been increasing. The shortcoming of current intrusion detection systems (IDS) is that they are set to identify specific types of attacks and cannot adapt to new threats. The inventors decided to adopt a blockchain-based federated learning approach to improve IDS and attack detection. FL helps to alleviate privacy issues associated with centralized machine learning techniques to some extent. Privacy issues that may arise in the FL process should be closely analyzed to ensure that the function is being used in the right way.
Combining blockchain technology with federated learning can improve intrusion detection. There are clear advantages to using blockchain to achieve decentralized data storage and secure interactions occurring within IoT networks. Blockchain is a peer-to-peer distributed ledger that puts application users at the center of the entire ecosystem and records transactions in a sequential and tamper-proof manner. A group of encrypted nodes can store and manage blocks of immutable data records that are timestamped using blockchain technology. The cryptographic hash of the previous block is used to link the blocks. Since most IoT environments today rely on data-driven research that requires sophisticated machine learning techniques, it is important to protect yourself from all kinds of attacks. Blockchain is being used in many areas such as healthcare, real estate, non-fungible tokens (NFTs), supply chain, personal identification systems, and the Internet of Things (IoT).
Coding is used to specify the rules of a multi-party agreement in a self-executing contract known as a smart contract (SC). It independently performs all or part of the contract-related tasks and generates evidence that can be used to support claims of contract performance. Smart contracts play a key role in managing all interactions and activities in a blockchain network. Smart contract-based blockchain technology can be a great alternative for storing sensitive data and assets due to its tamper-proof and immutable properties. However, storing a significant amount of data on a typical blockchain is expensive and impractical. An effective solution to this problem is provided by the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS). IPFS can store a significant amount of data and provides similar functionality to blockchain. There is also Hyperledger Fabric, a blockchain infrastructure where all participating nodes are authorized and can develop decentralized applications. Using IPFS and Hyperledger Fabric as a decentralized storage system can be very useful for intrusion detection systems.
The present inventors have proposed a blockchain-based federated learning approach (BFLSID) that can accurately detect unwanted intrusions in wireless IoT networks to protect the security and privacy of IoT data. In the proposed method, the machine learning activity is distributed by performing IDS model training within the local client without using a centralized server where devices usually transmit data. Training and inference are completed on the local client, and the information is never transmitted externally. In addition, only the model parameters are shared with a central entity that assigns global model enhancements in subsequent federated learning rounds.
The achievements achieved through the proposed Blockchain-based Federated Learning Approach (BFLSID) are as follows:
○ We propose a unique blockchain-based federated learning approach for IoT intrusion detection that guarantees security by training models on local clients and federating learning.
○ We used the Edge-IIoTset dataset to provide a detailed evaluation covering a variety of real-world data related to distinct attack types.
○ We evaluated the performance using both the existing centralized ML method and the federated learning method proposed by the inventor. The experimental results show that distributing and aggregating models in a FL environment is more effective and competitive than the centralized method.
The remaining sections of this paper are organized as follows: Section 2 provides a literature review of the most recent FL advances in the IoT and intrusion detection domains. The proposed method and its components are discussed in Section 3. Section 4 presents and discusses experimental results and evaluations in detail. Section 5 concludes by highlighting some potential future research directions.
II. Related Research
Since intruders develop new attack types every day, in order to prevent such attempts, intrusion detection systems (IDSs) must be able to recognize them immediately and provide necessary countermeasures. This section highlights the contributions and shortcomings of previous studies in this regard.
II -1. Intrusion Detection in IoT Using ML
Machine learning helps IDSs to detect new and existing attacks efficiently without human intervention by improving the system's feature selection. Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Genetic Algorithms (GA) are some of the machine learning methods that have been recently incorporated into IDSs to improve system security.
The IoT intrusion detection system proposed by Anthi et al. has proven that multiple ML classifiers are effective in detecting network scanner probing and traditional denial of service (DoS) cyber attacks. The dataset was generated by collecting network traffic for four consecutive days using the Wireshark tool. The machine learning classifier was applied using Weka software.
Zhao et al. proposed a system that uses classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques to find IoT traffic anomalies. To prevent the performance degradation of real-time threat analysis due to complex algorithms, dimensionality reduction using principal component analysis (PCA) was used. When the number of features is different, such as 3, 6, and 10, the classifier uses the softmax regression approach to compare with the nearest neighbors (KNN). For multi-class classification, softmax regression, which is a generalization of the logistic regression method, can be utilized. The output probability range is the main advantage of adopting softmax regression. The probabilities range from 0 to 1, and the sum is 1.
Dimensionality reduction (layer 2) and classification module (layer 2) are the basis of the intrusion detection model proposed by Pajouh et al. Also, this approach is designed to detect User-to-Root (U2R) and Remote-to-Local (R2L) attacks. Both component analysis and linear discriminant analysis were used for dimensionality reduction. The entire experiment is conducted using data from the Network Security Laboratory-Knowledge Discovery Dataset (NSL-KDD dataset). Dimensionality reduction makes the model simpler by reducing the least important variables in the model and removing noise from the data. This approach helps to alleviate the overfitting problem.
Vallathan et al. proposed a deep learning-based method to predict the possibility of abnormal behavior in the IoT ecosystem and alert users of such incidents by utilizing video from network monitoring systems. The proposed approach consists of deep neural networks, multi-classifiers, and kernel density functions. However, tracking and identifying numerous irregularities in a real-time setting was not addressed in this study.
Saba et al. presented a CNN-based method for anomaly-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) that leverages the power of IoT and provides the ability to effectively analyze all IoT traffic. The model can detect potential intrusions and abnormal traffic patterns. In another paper, Ferrag et al. proposed a deep learning-based IDS to identify DDoS attacks in systems supporting agriculture 4.0. Experimental results on TON_IoT and CIC-DDoS2019 datasets show that the proposed method exhibits remarkably superior performance.
Ahmed et al. proposed an entropy-based active deep learning and attention-based model for software-defined vehicular network (SDVN) intrusion detection. The experimental results show that the load balancing mechanism they proposed can provide better performance in improving resource utilization and throughput than previous methods. Although some other algorithms provide better performance in some intrusion detection parameters, the proposed active learning improves the detection speed of the system.
Elaziz et al. have presented a novel intelligent intrusion detection system (IDS) technique for IoT cloud scenarios by utilizing the latest advances in deep neural networks and swarm intelligence (SI) methods. The entire process includes utilizing deep neural networks to obtain optimal features from IoT IDS data, and using Capuchin Search Algorithm (CapSA), a recently developed SI optimization tool, for efficient feature selection. The limitation of this work is that CapSA has a slow convergence speed, which degrades the solution quality.
II-2. Intrusion Detection in IoT Using FL
Centralized machine learning models are very effective in reducing the risk of intrusions and other attacks, but because they are based on centralized servers, these technologies still have certain security issues, such as single point of failure (SPOF). Some researchers have proposed federated machine learning-based IDS as a solution to this problem.
Zhao et al. used Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network (RNN) and FL approach to introduce intelligent intrusion detection system. LSTM network integrates cell state and memory state to store essential data in extended data input. This model used Adam optimizer to compare the effectiveness of the proposed method with that of traditional neural network, and achieved F1 score of 99.21 points and accuracy of 99.21%.
Khan et al. developed a FL incentive mechanism using a Stackelberg game-based methodology to improve the connectivity between devices and edge servers. They explain that this technique is suitable for large-scale IoT networks because it can customize various ML computing characteristics according to the capabilities of connected devices. This method is advantageous for large-scale IoT networks because it can customize various ML computing characteristics according to the capabilities of connected devices.
A self-learning anomaly detection method using federated learning techniques to find exploited IoT devices in networks was developed by Nguyen et al. The proposed model is built using Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs). It continuously analyzes the network traffic of devices without human intervention and finds unexpected anomalies in the specified communication patterns of the devices.
We present a federated learning (FL)-based anomaly detection solution that proactively identifies intrusions in IoT networks using distributed on-device data. The method employs a gated recurrent units (GRUs) algorithm with federated learning rounds and communicates the learned weights to a central aggregation server of FL to preserve the data of local IoT devices. Experimental results show that the method outperforms existing/centralized machine learning (non-FL) approaches in protecting user data privacy and provides the highest accuracy in attack detection. However, essential evaluation metrics such as false alarm rate were not used in this study.
Smart Internet of Things (IoT) systems such as smart homes, e-healthcare systems, and cities are vulnerable to cyberattacks. Tabassum et al. proposed a federated deep learning (DL) IDS using GANs to identify such threats. They spread it to IoT devices and trained the GAN network using augmented local data to act as a classifier. The results of comparing the accuracy and convergence of the model showed that it outperformed most standalone IDSs and achieved early convergence.
A novel intrusion detection system for healthcare system security was proposed by Ghourabi et al. The proposed method consists of two components: a malware detection system for data servers and an IDS for medical devices installed in healthcare networks. Two machine learning models were used: an improved LightGBM (Light Gradient Boosting Machine) model and a Transformer model based on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representation). The disadvantage is that multiple solutions need to be installed throughout the healthcare network. In addition, correlation techniques need to be used to compile the results.
II-3. Intrusion Detection Using Blockchain
Blockchain has been used in many areas to promote trust and data privacy by allowing participants to transact and share information while maintaining a high level of trust, integrity, and transparency. As such, blockchain technology offers applications beyond the areas related to financial and economic systems. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and blockchain can be combined in cloud and IoT networks to identify cyberattacks and protect sensitive data.
Alexopoulos et al. introduced an approach to combine CID and blockchain in their study. They presented the idea of using blockchain technology to enhance the reliability of CIDS. They emphasized that the advantages of blockchain include the ability to trust each other and the technology for accountability and consensus. Casado-Vara et al. presented a hybrid IoT architecture that provides decentralized data management using blockchain. This architecture can optimize the connection between IoT and blockchain by integrating computational distribution based on the edge computing paradigm. They proposed a novel algorithm utilizing game theory to improve the quality of data collected from IoT devices and detection of false data. The proposed hybrid design optimizes the existing end-to-end architecture.
Alkadi et al. achieved decentralized intrusion detection in cloud and IoT networks while maintaining the confidentiality of smart contracts using bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) deep learning in blockchain. Experimental results show that the proposed framework outperforms other proposed models related to privacy-preserving intrusion detection methods. A distributed machine learning-based intrusion detection solution for the Internet of Things (IoT) using blockchain technology is presented in the study of Cheema et al. The IoT network is partitioned into autonomous systems (AS) through spectral partitioning, so that traffic monitoring for intrusion detection (ID) can be performed in a distributed manner at selected AS boundary nodes. The IDS is built on machine learning and trains support vector machine algorithms using well-known IoT data sets to enable attacker detection. The use of blockchain technology ensures the integrity of the attacker list and allows for decentralized sharing of information across AS boundary nodes in the blockchain network.
A novel decentralized intrusion detection system (IDS) for identifying DDoS attacks on mining pools in blockchain-enabled networks using fog computing is presented by Kumar et al. The performance of random forests (RF) and an improved gradient tree boosting system (XGBoost) is evaluated by training them on distributed fog nodes. The usefulness of the proposed model is evaluated using BoT-IoT, a real-world IoT-based dataset that covers the latest threats discovered in blockchain-enabled IoT networks. The results show that random forests outperform binary attacks in detecting multiple attacks, while XGBoost outperforms them in detecting binary attacks.
Mansour et al. present an efficient Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) cluster-based intrusion detection system that uses blockchain technology to detect intrusions and enable secure data exchange. Their method uses Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO) based clustering strategy to efficiently select cluster heads (CHs) and create clusters as needed. In addition, the presence of intrusion in the IIoT environment is determined using Chicken Swarm Optimization (CSO) along with GRU-based intrusion detection. Blockchain technology additionally provides secure data transmission from cluster members (CMs) to CHs. They plan to continue their future research to develop multi-path path planning techniques which are not used in this study.
Golomb et al. introduced an IoT-based distributed collaborative anomaly detection framework called CIoTA. Each device has a built-in model to identify malicious activities, and the new detection framework is exchanged by adding a new block to the chain, which is then broadcast to all nearby nodes. Test results show that CIoTA can detect various network attacks, enhancing network and device security. However, when there are many devices in the network, CIoTA, which is built for limited resources, can increase overhead.
The inventors focused on developing IDS in IoT by utilizing blockchain and federated learning. Existing research results detect intrusions, but have poor data storage performance and accuracy. Federated learning was utilized to improve intrusion detection in IoT networks, and in particular, blockchain was utilized to ensure privacy protection of IoT data.
III. Proposed Method
In general, in anomaly detection scenarios, models are developed using training data from simulated participating nodes. However, this method suffers from the IoT paradigm. IoT devices often have a single purpose and a small number of functions, so they do not generate much data. It is challenging to train a model solely with data obtained from the user’s local network, as it may take time to collect enough data to train a consistent model. Therefore, a technique is needed to accelerate the training of a reliable model by aggregating training data from multiple clients into a unified training dataset. Instead of transmitting data to a central location as in a fully centralized training model, each client (e.g., a local WiFi router connected to multiple IoT devices) trains a local model using data that is easily accessible locally in the FL setting. This section describes the workings and explanation of the proposed method. Data storage and protection are handled solely by a blockchain-based aggregation server with the help of a distributed storage system (a combination of IPFS and Hyperledger Fabric). To prevent unauthorized transactions, the activities of the FL distributors are thoroughly managed and maintained by smart contracts. As a result, blockchain-based security forms the basis of the security of the proposed method.
III-1. System Architecture
A federated learning-based approach for IoT network intrusion detection using machine learning and blockchain is proposed.
Figure 3 is a diagram showing a federated learning architecture supporting blockchain for IoT intrusion detection.
Figure 3 shows the architecture of the proposed method for IoT intrusion detection, where multiple IoT devices are deployed in distributed locations and connected to the system. The following subsections describe in detail each of the tasks performed to implement the strategy of the proposed method. The proposed FL model is divided into three layers:
○ IoT client and device layer
○ Smart contract layer
○ Blockchain Layer
III-1.1 IoT Client and Device Layer for Local Training
In this framework subsection, every BC-enabled k FL client (here k [1, …, K]) learns on its own data. This data is accumulated from each connected IoT device. During data learning, the client uses a local model shared by the global server, and a local IDS on the client side is triggered to recognize intrusions. This on-device intelligent learning, through local learning, parameter tuning, and improved inference techniques, enables the independence of local intrusion detection. This layer also ensures the security of local data. Since local transactions are timestamped and immutable, deploying clients with BC minimizes the possibility of forgery.
III-1.2 Smart Contract Layer for FL-Distribution
The client collaborates with a blockchain-based aggregation server to aggregate local models and build a more powerful intrusion detection system with optimal settings. The FL distributor (e.g., a security gateway) handles all communications between the local client and the blockchain-based aggregation server using smart contracts. In the system proposed by the inventors, three types of smart contracts are utilized:
○ FL Client Registration Smart Contract: Registration and authentication of FL clients to participate in the intrusion detection process are handled by this smart contract.
○ Local Learning Upload Smart Contract: Controlling the upload of locally learned FL weights is another important step in the federated learning process. This smart contract is responsible for ensuring that all local weights are successfully transmitted to the blockchain aggregation server.
○ Global Learning Distribution Smart Contract: Authorized clients learn local data using the updated aggregated global model shared by FL-Distributor. This smart contract can control the proper distribution of the global model.
III-1.3 Blockchain Layer for FL Aggregation and Storage
The blockchain-backed aggregation server has high computing power and aggregates the parameters shared by all local clients for global training. This layer has two aspects. The first is the blockchain-backed aggregation server, which collects all local weights before training and updating the global model. The second is a decentralized storage system built with a combination of IPFS and Hyperledger Fabric. This decentralized storage system is responsible for storing the hash data of the updated global model and the intrusion detection results, providing a double layer of protection.
III-2. Adversary Model and Assumptions
Attackers M in IoT systems can be internal or external. Web-based attacks, such as influencing devices equipped with digital devices, inserting malicious content into databases, and stealing personal information, are often carried out by external attackers. If an infected IoT device or other devices connected to the network continue to operate within the network, they may be considered insiders. IoT malware can identify and exploit vulnerable IoT systems and devices, such as exploiting vulnerable devices as platforms for cyberattacks. Malware, traffic congestion, commercial fraud due to inflow of false product data, compromise of inappropriate quality and control systems, Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and Structured Query Language (SQL) injection, and DDoS are some examples of IoT network-based attacks. Additional attacks target IoT protocols as well. Some examples of IoT protocol-based attacks include compromising surveillance systems, GPS spoofing, and manipulating farm machinery to delay or erroneously make decisions.
In this disclosure, several assumptions are made for the proposed method to work:
○ Secure communication between FL clients and devices: For the intrusion detection system to function properly, it must communicate with participating FL clients and IoT devices. It is assumed that this communication is secure and not vulnerable to any form of threats.
○ No malicious IoT devices by design: When IoT vendors first release new IoT products, they may already have security flaws. Nevertheless, these products must not be compromised or compromised in any way during initial use. This allows the system to learn safe patterns by only generating allowed interactions before an attacker (M) can detect and exploit the flaw.
○ IoT clients are not compromised: Since clients are essential for FL learning in IoT systems, we assume that they have no security vulnerabilities. If these clients are exploited, the security of the IoT network is no longer guaranteed.
III-3. Intrusion Detection using FL Classifiers
In the proposed FL model, instead of training and evaluating models on a central server, all K FL clients train their local models by leveraging their personal local datasets along with the global model shared by the same FL distributor. They then send the information collected from these local trainings to an aggregation server using SSL/TSL-compliant channels (e.g., gRPC channels [40]) via a communication manager. The global server aggregates these learnings and provides an improved model with the best possible parameters. The BC support server first selects clients to participate in the FL process using a smart contract connected to an active IoT device that is powered on and connected to the WiFi network. Then, various system participants interact in the following manner to complete the process:
1. The BC support server generates a general global ML model as an intrusion detection model at time t = 0. At this time, the number of neurons, epochs, hidden layers, etc. are calculated. The initial weight of the model can be expressed as w.
2. At this stage, the FL distributor that supports smart contracts downloads the general global model.
3. Each k FL client (here k [1, …, K]) that wants to use the global model downloads the model after receiving approval from the smart contract.

5. The FL distributor only receives updated model weights for the upgraded IDS and does not disclose any information to the client.
6. The smart contract specified in this step monitors and controls the transmission of locally learned weights to the BC support aggregation server.
7. Then, the server aggregates the weights of all the incoming weights to generate a new improved model (Equation (1)). The FedAvg algorithm is used for aggregation, and the parameters are evaluated based on the volume of the node data set.
8. For secure storage, updated model parameters and intrusion detection results are pushed to a distributed storage system.
9. Only the global learning distribution smart contract has the authority to authorize the download of updated global models from decentralized storage and distribute them to local FL clients.
10. The FL distributor deploys the updated and improved global model with the authenticated FL client using the global learning distribution smart contract to ensure that there are no unwanted intrusions.
11. Each client further enhances intrusion detection by using improved model parameters with the help of data generated from each IoT device.
12. Steps 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 are repeated for R FL rounds to continue model learning and global model improvement.
III-4. Complexity of FL Approach
The unique scenarios presented by federated learning variables make FL more sophisticated than traditional ML systems. For example, a key variable is the skewness of heterogeneous data distributed across client devices. In a highly skewed data environment, if each client has only one data label, a multi-class classification problem can occur. Some important FL factors include the number of participating clients, communication and operational costs, and program participation.
Since the performance of the relevant process is greatly affected by the programs used, FL must have low time complexity to operate at the edge layer. Except for the transmission time, which usually varies greatly across networks, the time complexity of the global model depends on the time complexity of the client, the time complexity of the aggregation server, and the complexity of the transmitted parameters.

IV. Experiments, Results and Discussion
In this section, we provide a demonstration of the proposed approach as well as an experimental evaluation of its performance.
Ⅳ-1. Experimental Setup
The basic programming language used for the tests was Python 3, and the tests were performed on Google Colaboratory. Multidimensional arrays and matrices were used with NumPy and several other well-known libraries. Pandas provides powerful functions for analyzing and manipulating data structures. In addition, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) are performed using TensorFlow and Keras. In addition, Scikit-learn provides implementations of various supervised and unsupervised ML methods. In addition, minority classes were oversampled using SMOTE to improve the overall model efficiency.
Ethereum smart contracts are created using the Solidity programming language and are configured and tested using the Remix IDE. The features of these smart contracts are described in more detail later in this specification.
Ⅳ-2. Dataset Description and Pre-Processing
Choosing an appropriate dataset is essential because IoT networks require datasets for training and testing IDS. For Industrial IoT (IIoT) and IoT applications, there is an Edge-IIoTset dataset that has been widely used in cybersecurity research. This dataset consists of heterogeneous network traffic. More than 10 different types of IoT devices, such as low-cost digital sensors for measuring temperature and humidity, ultrasonic sensors, water level sensors, pH sensor meters, soil moisture sensors, heart rate sensors, and flame sensors, were used to generate IoT data. The testbed was attacked in 14 different ways, including DDoS attacks, backdoor attacks, man-in-the-middle attacks (MITM), ransomware, and password attacks. Due to the lack of FL-specific datasets, we used existing public datasets with manufactured divisions to mimic data federation in our experiments.
As the first step, we remove redundant or missing information such as “NAN” (Not a Number) and “INF” (Infinite Value) from the dataset. Then we remove additional flow features such as tcp.connection.rst, tcp.connection.fin, tcp.checksum, tcp.payload, tcp.options, tcp.len, tcp.flags.ack, tcp.flags, tcp.ack raw, tcp.ack, arp.dst.proto ipv4, etc. After data preprocessing (cleaning and splitting), Table 1 shows the 80/20 ratio data selected for the ML model along with the training and test datasets.
[Table 1]
To evaluate the effectiveness of FL, we conducted several experiments where 4 to 12 clients participated in model training. The results showed that the local model for each client needs to be trained for a total of 20 epochs and 20 FL rounds. We examined how effective the system is for different numbers of clients while generating the federated models. The training data from the distribution dataset was distributed to each client, and was randomly selected from them. The entire training dataset was distributed to 4, 8, and 12 clients, and three federated models were generated to evaluate potential accuracy loss. The results of these models were then compared with the centralized model.
Ⅳ-3. Evaluation Metric
A confusion matrix is a method to determine the performance of a method. A confusion matrix is a table that is often used to summarize how well a classification model performs when applied to a dataset. This makes it easy to find areas of class confusion. Almost all performance metrics are often calculated using a confusion matrix. Using a confusion matrix, you can define True Positive (TP), False Positive (FP), False Negative (FN), and True Negative (TN) for multiple classes.
True Positive (TP): This represents the percentage of samples correctly identified as attacks among all samples.
False Positive (FP): Reports how many positive samples were incorrectly classified as attacks.
True Negative (TN): Reports the number of neutral samples that can be correctly classified as normal.
False Negative (FN): The number of attack samples that were incorrectly classified as normal.
Accuracy: One measure to evaluate the performance of a classification model is accuracy. The accuracy measure is expressed by equation (5). It measures the proportion of inputs classified correctly among all inputs.
[Equation 5]
Precision: Precision is the ability to make accurate predictions. Precision measures the ratio of the number of positive judgments claimed by the model to the number of actual positive judgments, and is expressed by equation (6).
[Equation 6]
-
Recall: Recall is a measure of the proportion of positives found in the entire data set. It is also called the positive rate. Equation (7) gives the recall for the model.
[Equation 7]
-
F1-Score: The performance of the model can also be evaluated using the F1 score, which represents the weighted average of the model's recall and precision, and is given by equation (8).
[Equation 8]
-
True Positive Rate (TPR): When an IDS recognizes an activity as an attack and actually constitutes an intrusion, this is called a true positive. TPR is also called detection rate and is as follows:
[Equation 9]
-
False Positive Rate (FPR): A false positive occurs whenever an IDS incorrectly identifies an attack as something that is actually normal. The false positive rate is another name for false positive and is determined using the following equation (10):

The centralized model performed relatively well, but was vulnerable to the Single Point of Failure (SPOF) problem.

Ⅳ-4.2 Intrusion Detection Using Blockchain-enabled FL Method
First, we used CNN and LSTM, which are existing centralized ML methods for cyberattack detection, to evaluate the accuracy of the proposed dataset.
In the FL test of the model, three client K sets were distributed: K=4 (first set), K=8 (second set), and K=12 (third set). Table 4 shows the accuracy results of the best client, worst client, and global model in the 1st and 20th FL rounds using the data distribution sets. As can be seen in the figure, the performance of all classes improves as the rounds repeat, and the gap between the best and worst clients narrows. In all client numbers, the gap between the best and worst clients is clearly visible in the 1st round, but the gap narrows as it approaches the 20th round.

Figure 5 shows the learning process and accuracy graphs for both the centralized method and the federated learning method.
As shown in Fig. 5, the gap between the centralized methods (both CNN and LSTM ML methods) and the federated learning method is quite large at the beginning. However, as we move to higher rounds, the gap is minimized, and by the end of round 20, we can obtain quite competitive results. This shows that the FL method proposed by the inventors performs significantly better than the centralized machine learning approach, with some additional advantages that will be discussed in the next section.
Figure 6 shows a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve comparing the actual positive rate (detection rate) and false alarm rate of intrusion detection.

Fig. 7 is a graph showing the training period for the proposed FL approach after 20 FL rounds. Fig. 7 shows the time required for different numbers of FL clients (4, 8, 12). As the number of clients increases, the training time also increases. It can be seen that the CNN method learns faster than the LSTM method.

In this section, we introduce how to successfully deploy the developed smart contract to ensure that only authorized clients can participate in the entire intrusion detection process and manage the upload and download of local and global learning models. As described above, we used the Remix IDE platform to program the smart contract in Solidity programming language and execute it online.
As explained earlier, the FL-clients Registration smart contract is responsible for registering and authenticating FL clients that will participate in the intrusion detection procedure.

Another important element of the federated learning process is controlling the upload of locally learned FL weights. All local updates must be successfully transmitted to the blockchain aggregation server, which is the responsibility of the local learning upload smart contract.
Figure 9 is a diagram illustrating the deployment of a local learning upload smart contract.

As explained earlier, FL-Distributor provides authorized clients with access to the updated and aggregated global model, which can be used to train on local data. The proper distribution of the global model must be supervised by the global training distribution smart contract.
Figure 10 is a diagram illustrating successful deployment of a global learning distribution smart contract.

The inputs, outputs, size, and complexity all affect the amount of gas consumed by the contract function. The execution cost is the cost of completing various activities in the smart contract, while the transaction cost includes the contract deployment and all data moving to the blockchain network. The goal of all smart contract design and implementation is to maximize functionality while reducing costs. As mentioned earlier, Remix IDE, which provides code debugging and runtime error alarms, is used to develop smart contracts. However, it is not enough to prove the reliability of smart contracts. It is essential to check for reentrancy issues, looping, and other prevalent flaws that are particularly vulnerable to malicious attackers. The inventors used specialized security analysis tools to examine the Ethereum smart contracts embedded in the solution to identify code vulnerabilities.

[Table 6]
Ⅳ-8. Discussion
This section briefly discusses the benefits of federated learning and blockchain technology for intrusion detection systems in IoT networks.
Ⅳ-8.1 Blockchain-enabled Security Features
This subsection briefly describes the security features of the proposed blockchain-based IoT network solution.
-
Privacy: Each step of our system is accessible only to clients authorized by the smart contract, and authorization is granted only after thorough review. Access to information stored in storage is restricted to trusted, select users, ensuring privacy.
-
Scalability: The number of participants in a blockchain can be dynamically expanded or reduced based on the demand of decentralized ledger users. As a result, the scalability of the system is improved.
-
Efficiency: The time-consuming reporting process can create a single point of failure for participating clients, but this is reduced through a transparent architecture. As a result, the synchronization of the entire intrusion detection system is improved, improving the overall quality and efficiency of the system.
-
Authentication and Access Control: Participants in the proposed solution can share information with trusted authorities for a predefined period of time and with a limited number of resources, thanks to full authentication and access control technology, without revealing critical security credentials.
-
Cyberattack vulnerability: Blockchain networks use cryptographic hashing to protect transactions. Since blocks are protected by cryptography, attackers cannot target specific blocks. This makes distributed denial of service (DDoS) and man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks more difficult.
Ⅳ-8.2 Benefits of Using Federated Learning in Intrusion Detection
The following are the advantages of the FL-based intrusion detection model proposed in this disclosure.
- Using FL instead of standard ML techniques, IoT devices can provide data with enhanced security and with less bandwidth consumption.
- FL helps reduce latency caused by massive data transfers and detects real-time anomalies using on-client predictions.
- The device can independently predict and detect intrusion attempts even when isolated due to the model's local awareness.
In this paper, we provide a practical and real-world application of blockchain and FL for IoT network intrusion detection. The proposed strategy can serve as a great starting point for developing an architecture that can transition non-FL-based solutions to FL. A detailed study of this paper can accelerate the transition of ML-based products to FL-enabled blockchain in production environments. In addition, distributed training and storage can be used to share resources and enhance the security of end-device data, which can lead to more effective and environmentally friendly ML-based devices.
V. Conclusion
To enhance the security and privacy of IoT networks, the inventors propose a blockchain-based federated learning-based intrusion detection system (BFLSID). We conduct tests using two well-known ML models, CNN and LSTM, in both centralized and federated systems, based on the latest dataset called Edge-IIoTset. The experimental results show that the proposed FL technique can produce results that are competitive with existing centralized models in intrusion detection. For example, the intrusion detection accuracy reaches 92% in the centralized approach, while the proposed FL technique achieves about 91% accuracy.
This approach maintains client-specific data for local model learning, while transmitting local learning updates for IoT intrusion detection to a blockchain-enabled decentralized storage system to aggregate aggregates. All transactions and interactions occurring in the IoT intrusion detection system are properly authenticated and continuously monitored thanks to the FL distributor controlled by a smart contract. In addition, a decentralized storage system consisting of IPFS and Hyperledger Fabric is built to ensure the security of FL model parameters and model results, and to enhance the performance of the blockchain to meet the storage requirements in realistic situations.
To fulfill the potential of malicious IoT and edge node detection in IoT networks, we plan to enhance the proposed approach in follow-up studies. In addition, there are several constraints that can reduce the usefulness of the global model, such as clients with sparse relevant data, devices that terminate during a task, and slow upload and model update times. Finding solutions to these federated learning constraints that significantly reduce the global model accuracy is essential for further research. We will evaluate the success of the proposed method by leveraging real-time data from a device-specific dataset that can classify all known and unidentified IoT device vulnerabilities, which can be improved using an IoT testbed.
VI. Summary of the Disclosures of This Specification
Figure 12 is a flowchart showing a method according to one disclosure of the present specification.
The method can be performed by a system comprising one or more federated learning clients, one or more federated learning distributors, and one or more aggregation servers.
Referring to FIG. 12, one or more federated learning clients can acquire a learning model for detecting network intrusion, and perform learning on the learning model using collected data to generate updated model weights (S110).
The learning model can be generated by one or more aggregation servers. The learning model generated by the aggregation server can be downloaded by one or more federated learning distributors. The downloaded learning model can be downloaded by one or more federated learning clients.
The learning model can be acquired by one or more federated learning clients approved by the smart contract. One or more federated learning clients can train the downloaded learning model using the collected data to update the model weights.
Updated model weights generated by one or more federated learning clients can be transmitted to one or more aggregation servers via one or more federated learning distributors.
One or more aggregation servers can aggregate the updated model weights to generate an updated learning model (S120). The updated model weights can be aggregated by one or more aggregation servers using the FedAvg algorithm.
One or more federated learning distributors can distribute the updated learning model to one or more federated learning clients (S130). The updated learning model can be acquired by one or more federated learning clients approved by the smart contract.
One or more federated learning clients can obtain an updated learning model and perform learning on the updated learning model using collected data to additionally update model weights for the updated learning model (S140).
The examples of the present disclosure shown in this specification and drawings are only specific examples presented to easily explain the technical content of the present disclosure and to help understand the present disclosure, and are not intended to limit the scope of the present disclosure. It will be apparent to those skilled in the art to which the present disclosure pertains that other modified examples are possible in addition to the examples described so far.
The claims set forth in this specification may be combined in various ways. For example, the technical features of the method claims of this specification may be combined and implemented as a device, and the technical features of the device claims of this specification may be combined and implemented as a method. In addition, the technical features of the method claims of this specification and the technical features of the device claims of this specification may be combined and implemented as a device, and the technical features of the method claims of this specification and the technical features of the device claims of this specification may be combined and implemented as a method.

### 📋 Abstract
> The invention relates to the technical field of intelligent manufacturing and computer-aided process planning, and discloses a mechanical CAD drawing recognition-based process flow arrangement system, which comprises CAD drawing analysis and feature recognition, manufacturing information structured storage, a process knowledge base, an intelligent process flow arrangement engine and a man-machine interaction module. The system adopts a vector analysis and visual inspection dual-channel parallel processing drawing, executes feature space alignment and consistency verification, calculates a feature identification risk factor and generates a reconstruction feature vector; and the intelligent arrangement engine dynamically adjusts the matching weight of the processing method according to the risk factor, constructs a process sorting optimization model containing the virtual risk cost, and adaptively supplements forced detection and margin compensation constraints according to the risk level. According to the method, the recognition uncertainty is converted into the quantitative risk index, and the quantitative risk index is fused into the process decision, so that the adaptive fault tolerance and dynamic optimization of the process scheme are realized.

The method also includes structuring the cybersecurity threat intelligence data into one or more threat intelligence tables each having a plurality of fields describing attributes of network security threats. Also, the method includes sampling rows from each of the one or more threat intelligence tables and programmatically generating, from each corresponding row, a plurality of Q/A/R triples, each Q/A/R triple including a Question element, an Answer element, and a Reasoning element derived from one or more fields. Next, the method includes a step of generating a cybersecurity-focused language model from the one or more threat intelligence tables and the plurality of Q/A/R triples, wherein the cybersecurity-focused language model, when trained, is configured to answer network security inquiries.

Description
Translated from Chinese
Performance test data processing method, device, equipment, medium and program product
technical field
The present application relates to the technical field of testing, in particular to a performance testing data processing method, device, computer equipment, storage medium and computer program product.
Background technique
Performance testing is to test various performance indicators of the system by simulating various normal, peak and abnormal load conditions through automated testing tools. Both load testing and stress testing are performance testing, and they can be combined. Through load testing, determine the performance of the system under various workloads. The goal is to test the changes in various performance indicators of the system when the load gradually increases. Stress testing is a test to obtain the maximum service level that the system can provide by determining the bottleneck or unacceptable performance point of a system.
At present, the analysis of performance test results is mainly based on manpower, which greatly improves the entry threshold for quality assurance personnel in performance testing; at the same time, since performance testing is an extremely complex engineering system involving Human monitoring and analysis is time-consuming and labor-intensive.
Contents of the invention
Based on this, it is necessary to provide a performance test data processing method, device, computer equipment, computer-readable storage medium and computer program product capable of improving performance test efficiency in view of the above technical problems.
In a first aspect, the present application provides a performance test data processing method, the method comprising:
receiving a performance test request, the performance test request carrying scene information;
Acquiring service information corresponding to the scene information;
Reading corresponding performance test data from at least one monitoring tool end based on the service information;
Process the performance test data.
In one of the embodiments, before acquiring the service information corresponding to the scene information, it also includes:
Start a pre-test request, the pre-test request carries scene information, link identification and domain name;
At each monitoring tool end, query the service information corresponding to the link identifier;
Obtaining corresponding environment information based on the domain name;
An association relationship among the scene information, the service information, and the environment information is established.
In one of the embodiments, the starting pre-test request includes:
Initiates pretest requests a preset number of times.
In one of the embodiments, the processing of the performance test data includes:
The performance test data is compared with a corresponding threshold to obtain an analysis result.
In one of the embodiments, the analysis result obtained by comparing the performance test data with the corresponding threshold includes at least one of the following:
Compare broiler hardware resources with broiler hardware resource thresholds to get analysis results;
Compare the hardware resource information with the hardware threshold to get the analysis result;
Compare the method time consumption, gateway time consumption, SQL time consumption with the preset SLA to get the analysis results;
According to the results of data analysis on whether the heap memory and off-heap memory can be recovered in time, the analysis results are obtained;
Compare the GC time and times with the target threshold to get the analysis results.
In one of the embodiments, after comparing the broiler hardware resource with the broiler hardware resource threshold to obtain the analysis result, it includes:
When the broiler hardware resource is greater than the broiler hardware resource threshold, output the information of adjusting the broiler hardware resource to retest.

Detailed ways
In order to make the purpose, technical solution and advantages of the present application clearer, the present application will be further described in detail below in conjunction with the accompanying drawings and embodiments. It should be understood that the specific embodiments described here are only used to explain the present application, and are not intended to limit the present application.
The performance test data processing method provided in the embodiment of the present application may be applied to the application environment shown in FIG. 1 . Wherein, the application environment includes a local test platform 102, a tested server 104, and a monitoring tool 106, wherein the local test platform 102 initiates a performance test request, for example, the local test platform 102 receives a performance test request, and the monitoring tool 106 can collect the tested The performance test data corresponding to the server 104, so that the local test platform 102 obtains the service information corresponding to the scene information; reads the corresponding performance test data from at least one monitoring tool 106 based on the service information; and processes the performance test data. In this way, the corresponding service information can be determined according to the environmental information, so that based on the service information, the corresponding performance test data can be directly read from the monitoring tool and processed without manual processing, which improves efficiency. The data storage system can store data that the monitoring tool end 106 needs to process. The data storage system can be integrated on the monitoring tool end 106, or placed on the cloud or other network servers. Among them, the local test platform 102, the server under test 104 and the monitoring tool 106 can be realized by an independent server or a server cluster composed of multiple servers.
In one embodiment, as shown in FIG. 2 , a method for processing performance test data is provided. The application of the method to the local test platform in FIG. 1 is used as an example for illustration, including the following steps:
S202: Receive a performance test request, where the performance test request carries scene information.
Specifically, the performance test request is received by the local test platform, for example, generated by the user directly operating the local test platform, or the local test platform receives the performance test request sent by the user terminal. The environment information refers to the environment where the performance test request is located. When generating the performance test request, the local test platform receives configurations such as corresponding environment information, so that the local test platform generates a performance test request carrying the environment information.
The environment information may include arbitrary environment information, for example, common environment information includes dev environment information, test environment information, stg environment information, and prod environment information.
S204: Obtain service information corresponding to the scene information.
The service information refers to the service information involved in the performance test, such as virtual machine service, SQL service, Skywalking service, Prometheus service, etc., which is not specifically limited here.
One point to be explained is that a scenario can be uniquely determined by the environment information and the performance test request, that is, a performance test, and the service information involved in the performance test is determined. For this reason, the service information corresponding to the scenario is pre-established, so that In the actual test, the corresponding service information can be obtained based on the scene, so that only the performance test data corresponding to these service information can be obtained, and there is no need to obtain the performance test data of all services, which reduces the amount of data acquisition and improves efficiency.
S206: Read corresponding performance test data from at least one monitoring tool end based on the service information.
Specifically, different monitoring tools are used to monitor different performance data, and the monitoring tools may include hardware monitoring tool Prometheus, link monitoring tool skywalking, slow sql monitoring tool, application service monitoring tool (mainly related to JVM), etc., but in the art A skilled person can clearly know that the present application is not limited to the above-mentioned monitoring tools, and may also include other monitoring tools, which are not specifically limited here. In addition, different tests can read performance test data from different monitoring tool ends as needed, without reading all monitoring tool ends, so as to adapt to different tests.
Performance test data includes, but is not limited to, broiler hardware resources, hardware resource information, method time consumption, gateway time consumption, SQL time consumption, data analysis heap memory, off-heap memory, and GC, etc.
In practical application, the local test platform reads the performance test data of the service corresponding to the service information from each monitoring tool.
Specifically, as shown in FIG. 3, FIG. 3 is a flow chart of performance data collection in the performance testing process in an embodiment. In this embodiment, after the scene is determined, the services involved in the scene can be obtained, and then monitoring The tool end can obtain the performance test data corresponding to each service, and store the performance test data, for example, in a relational database ES. In other embodiments, the performance test data stored in the database by different monitoring tool ends The data are located in different data tables to facilitate subsequent queries.
S208: Process the performance test data.
Specifically, after the local test platform obtains the performance test data, it performs intelligent aggregation analysis on the performance test data according to certain algorithm rules to obtain the location of the bottleneck point, which greatly improves the efficiency of performance result analysis.
Optionally, when the local test platform reads the corresponding performance test data from the monitoring tool side, the monitoring tool side queries the full amount of data according to the input information such as service information and time period and returns it to the local test platform. The received full amount of data is preprocessed, such as re-aggregated according to the target dimension, such as time, data category, etc., to obtain the result.
In the above performance test data processing method, the performance test request carries scene information, so that the corresponding service information can be determined according to the environment information, so that based on the service information, the corresponding performance test data can be directly read from the monitoring tool and processed, without Manual processing is required, which improves efficiency.
In one of the embodiments, before obtaining the service information corresponding to the scene information, it also includes: starting a pre-test request, the pre-test request carries the scene information, link identification and domain name; Corresponding service information; obtain corresponding environment information based on the domain name; establish the association relationship among scene information, service information and environment information.
Specifically, as shown in FIG. 4, FIG. 4 is a flow chart of the pre-test steps in an embodiment. In order to establish the association relationship between the scene and the service information, the pre-test is performed in advance, for example, through NPT (a software test platform) After uploading or modifying the test scenario and saving it, NPT will automatically pre-execute one concurrent number at a time to obtain the tested service information by parsing the request domain name and the returned link ID traceID, and establish the relationship between this scenario and the involved service information. connection relation.
Among them, NPT can obtain the tested test cases, and then obtain the tested service information according to the execution of the tested test cases. In addition, in parallel, NPT can obtain the domain name. Since different environments correspond to different domain names, it can be The environment information is acquired according to the domain name, so as to subsequently establish the association relationship among scene information, service information, and environment information.
Optionally, starting the pre-test request includes: starting a preset number of pre-test requests.
For example, start 10 small concurrent pre-tests, which can prevent unexpected interruption of requests or failure of collection tools to obtain services. It is necessary to obtain the service information and environment information under test, because the test will be carried out in different environments (common environments include dev, test, stg, and prod environments), so as to resolve the domain name to obtain the correct environment information, and then get the Accurate Service Information.
In the above embodiment, the association relationship between the scene and the service is established in advance, so that when testing, it is sufficient to read the test data directly from each monitoring tool according to the service, so that only the test data corresponding to the service is read, reducing the reading of data quantity.
In one embodiment, processing the performance test data includes: comparing the performance test data with a corresponding threshold to obtain an analysis result.
In one of the embodiments, the performance test data is compared with the corresponding threshold to obtain the analysis result, including at least one of the following: comparing the broiler hardware resource with the broiler hardware resource threshold to obtain the analysis result; comparing the hardware resource information with the hardware threshold Compare to get the analysis results; compare the method time-consuming, gateway time-consuming, SQL time-consuming with the preset SLA to get the analysis results; analyze the results of whether the heap memory and off-heap memory can be recovered in time according to the data; get the analysis results by comparing the GC time-consuming And the number of times is compared with the target threshold to get the analysis result.
Specifically, after the performance test data is collected, the performance test data needs to be analyzed. Optionally, the analysis process can be automatic or manual, for example, after the performance test data is collected, the analysis of the test results is automatically triggered , or output a prompt after collecting the performance test data, so that the user can manually trigger the analysis of the test result.
Among them, the analysis of the performance test data includes the following types. It should be noted that the following analysis in this embodiment can be performed in the following order, and in other embodiments can also be performed in other orders, but preferably in the following order: The sequence in this embodiment is the main one, specifically shown in Figure 5, and Figure 5 is a flow chart of the performance test data analysis steps in one embodiment:
The local test platform will obtain broiler (pressure initiator) resource occupancy data through ES according to server information, and judge broiler hardware resources (CPU, memory, disk, network IO) and the preset threshold value in the program. In an optional embodiment, after comparing the broiler hardware resource with the broiler hardware resource threshold to obtain the analysis result, it includes: when the broiler hardware resource is greater than the broiler hardware resource threshold, outputting information for adjusting the broiler hardware resource retest. That is, if the threshold is exceeded, the detailed results are returned to the NPT report, informing the user that the broiler needs to be adjusted and retested. If there is no bottleneck, proceed to the next step.
The local test platform will obtain the CPU load, CPU usage, memory usage, whether the swap area is used, disk usage, and disk I/O of the service under test during the test through ES based on service information, test time period and other information. If the CPU load is greater than the number of CPU cores or the CPU usage is greater than 75%, it will prompt the CPU resource bottleneck; if the memory usage is greater than 90% or the swap is not 0, it will prompt that the memory resource bottleneck has an OOM risk; During this test period, the disk usage has obvious changes or the disk I/O util is close to 100%, indicating a disk bottleneck.
The local test platform will obtain the method time-consuming, gateway time-consuming, SQL time-consuming and other data involved in this test through ES according to the service information, test time period and other information, and judge the method time-consuming, gateway time-consuming and preset SLA (performance Before the test is executed, set the SLA for this test scenario on the performance test platform). If the size is greater than the SLA preset value, it will prompt that the response time of this test does not meet expectations and needs to be checked; if the SQL takes more than 1 second, then The SQL xml file is converted into a SQL statement through the mybatis conversion script, and then the SQL statement is analyzed through soar, optimization items are given and optimization suggestions are given in the report.
The local test platform will obtain the jvm configuration and performance test execution data through ES according to the service information and analyze whether the heap memory and off-heap memory can be recovered in time. If it cannot be recovered in time, it will remind the risk of OOM in the report; ) time-consuming and times. If there are too many times of full GC (such as 10 times) in a short period of time (such as five minutes), the report will remind you that there are too many times of full GC, and further manual investigation is recommended.
It should be understood that although the steps in the flow charts involved in the above embodiments are shown sequentially according to the arrows, these steps are not necessarily executed sequentially in the order indicated by the arrows. Unless otherwise specified herein, there is no strict order restriction on the execution of these steps, and these steps can be executed in other orders. Moreover, at least some of the steps in the flow charts involved in the above embodiments may include multiple steps or stages, and these steps or stages are not necessarily executed at the same time, but may be executed at different times, The execution order of these steps or stages is not necessarily performed sequentially, but may be executed in turn or alternately with other steps or at least a part of steps or stages in other steps.
