Translated from Chinese
The invention relates to a multi-objective optimization method and system for urban train operation. First, the speed limit information, ramp information and curve radius information in the actual train line are obtained, and then the sections are divided into unequal divisions according to the above line characteristic information, and then combined with The basic vehicle data of the train is used to construct the longitudinal dynamics model of the train; then, the energy consumption, interval running time, actual parking position, and acceleration change rate of the train are calculated through the dynamic model, and the multi-objective optimization model of the train operation is established; then the multi-objective differential evolution algorithm is used. The multi-objective optimization model is solved to obtain the Pareto optimal solution set of each running interval. Finally, according to the evaluation principle of urban train operation performance indicators, the optimal solution that can comprehensively consider each objective is obtained and the train running speed curve is generated. Compared with other methods, the method of the present invention has fast convergence speed, is not easy to fall into the local optimal solution, and can quickly and accurately search for the optimal working condition transition position.

Description
Translated from Chinese
A multi-objective optimization method and system for urban train operation
technical field
The invention relates to the technical field of rail transit operation optimization, in particular to a multi-objective optimization method and system for urban train operation.
Background technique
Urban rail transit occupies an indispensable and important position in my country's urban public transportation system due to its advantages of safety, comfort, punctuality, environmental protection, and large carrying capacity. With the gradual increase of rail transit operating mileage, the continuous increase of passenger traffic, and the continuous growth of operating energy consumption, energy saving and consumption reduction have become one of the problems that must be overcome in the sustainable development of urban rail transit. In the rail transit system, the traction energy consumption of trains accounts for the largest proportion of the total operating energy consumption. Therefore, how to reduce the traction energy consumption of trains has very important practical significance for maximizing the energy-saving benefits of urban rail transit systems. The urban train operation optimization problem is essentially a multi-objective optimization problem that integrates multiple objectives of safety, punctuality, precise parking, energy saving and comfort. It seeks an "optimal" strategy among many control strategies to ensure train operation. On the premise of safe, punctual, and precise parking, it can also minimize operating energy consumption and maximize passenger comfort, achieving a win-win effect for the railway operation department and passengers. In summary, it is of great practical significance and engineering application value to carry out the research on its optimization method.
At present, many fairly mature research results have been achieved in the field of train operation optimization. Early scholars focused on theoretical research and derivation. The construction of the model was often simplified, and the solution was mostly based on numerical and analytical algorithms. The solution is often a local optimum. , the problem of inability to guarantee convergence. With the development of computers, intelligent optimization algorithms are widely used to solve optimization problems. Many scholars' research regards the optimization of train operation as a single-objective optimization and only takes the operation energy consumption as the optimization objective, failing to consider the train operation process as a whole and realize that it is essentially a multi-objective optimization problem. Some studies also regard it as a multi-objective optimization problem, but some consider the optimization under ideal line conditions, ignoring the influence of actual line parameters, and have little value for practical engineering applications. There are also studies that integrate multiple indicators of punctuality, safety, comfort, and energy saving into single-objective problems for optimization, but they still fail to fully reflect the essential characteristics of multi-objective optimization problems. In addition, most of the solving algorithms use genetic algorithm and particle swarm algorithm, which have problems such as slow convergence speed and easy to fall into local optimum, which cannot achieve the best optimization effect.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The purpose of the present invention is to provide a multi-objective optimization method and system for urban train operation. It is used to seek an "optimal" strategy among many control strategies, and under the premise of ensuring the safe, punctual and precise parking of trains, it can also minimize operating energy consumption and maximize passenger comfort as much as possible. To achieve a win-win effect for railway operators and passengers.
For achieving the above object, the present invention provides the following scheme:
A multi-objective optimization method for urban train operation, comprising:
Obtain the section parameter information of the actual running route conditions of the urban train;
Divide each running section of the urban train into unequal partitions according to the section parameter information, and obtain each running section of the urban train;
According to the basic parameter information and section parameter information of the urban train vehicle, the longitudinal dynamics model of the urban train is obtained;
According to the longitudinal dynamics model of the urban train, the multi-performance evaluation index values of the train running in each running section of the urban train are obtained;
Build a multi-objective optimization model of urban trains according to the multi-performance evaluation index values of train operation;
Multi-objective differential evolution algorithm is used to solve the multi-objective optimization model, and the Pareto optimal solution set of urban trains in each running section is obtained;
The Pareto optimal solution of each running section is selected to focus on the solutions that meet the performance evaluation criteria of urban train operation indicators, and the optimal train running speed curve of urban trains in each running section is obtained.
Optionally, the specific steps for obtaining the longitudinal dynamics model of the urban train include:
According to the basic parameter information of the urban train vehicle and the section parameter information, the force value of the train in each running section of the urban train is obtained;
The longitudinal dynamics model of the urban train is constructed according to the train force value of the urban train in each running section;
The longitudinal dynamics model of the city train is as follows:
Among them, t is the running time of the urban train between stations, s is the position of the urban train when it changes working conditions, v is the running speed of the urban train, μ f is the proportional coefficient of the actual traction force and braking force applied by the urban train, and μ b is the urban train The proportional coefficient between the maximum traction force and the braking force, F ( μ f , v ) is the current traction force applied by the city train, B ( μ b , v ) is the current braking force applied by the city train, W ( s , v ) is the city train The total resistance of the train operation, W 0 ( v ) is the basic resistance of the urban train , Wi ( p ) is the curve additional resistance of the city train, and W c ( r ) is the slope additional resistance of the city train.
Optionally, the multi-objective optimization model is as follows:
Among them, f E is the operating energy consumption value of the urban train, f t is the punctuality index of the urban train, f s is the precise parking index of the urban train, f c is the comfort index of the urban train, and T is the planned stop of the urban train at the station. F is the current traction force exerted by the urban train, v is the running speed of the urban train, α is the punctuality penalty factor, T Z is the actual running time of the urban train between stations, β is the precise parking penalty factor, S Z is the actual parking position of the urban train, S is the planned parking position of the urban train, and J is the acceleration rate of change.
Optionally, the multi-objective differential evolution algorithm to solve the multi-objective optimization model specifically includes:
Use the population initialization strategy to generate an initialized population with N individuals, and the individuals in the initialized population represent the position of the urban train when changing working conditions;
Calculate the objective function value of each running index of the urban train corresponding to each individual in the initialized population;
According to the objective function value of each running index of the urban train corresponding to each individual, the non-dominated sorting of individuals in the initialized population is performed, different individuals are assigned to different non-dominated layers, and the individuals in the first non-dominated layer are selected;
Use the adaptive mutation strategy to perform mutation operation on the individuals in the first non-dominated layer, and then perform crossover and selection operations in the differential evolution algorithm to obtain a new first non-dominated layer individual set;
Process the first non-dominated layer individual set to generate a new evolutionary population by using the evolution strategy based on excellent individuals;
Set the iterative termination condition of the evolutionary population, and judge whether the evolutionary population satisfies the iterative termination condition. If not, return to the step "Using the evolution strategy based on excellent individuals to process the first non-dominant layer individual set to generate a new evolutionary population", if so, according to the evolutionary population The Pareto optimal solution set of urban trains in each running section is obtained.

In the specific application process, the driver can select the train running speed curve corresponding to different solutions according to the actual needs, such as whether the train is early or late, so as to make up for the error in the train running time and ensure that the train can still be on time. to the station.
Compared with other existing technologies, the multi-objective optimization method for urban train operation based on multi-objective differential evolution proposed by the present invention is constructed with the train operation energy consumption index, punctuality index, parking accuracy index and comfort index as optimization goals. Aiming at the problems of slow convergence speed of traditional differential evolution algorithm and easy to fall into local optimum, an improved multi-objective differential evolution algorithm is proposed based on improved initialization strategy, adaptive selection mutation mechanism strategy and excellent individual evolution strategy. For the solution of the multi-objective optimization model of urban train operation, the Pareto optimal solution can be quickly searched. Finally, the corresponding Pareto solution can be selected according to the actual needs of the driver to generate the corresponding train speed curve, which has a good practical guiding significance for the operation optimization of urban train stations.

Title

The invention discloses a multi-objective optimization method for reservoir dispatching based on GCN and NSGA-II, which includes: collecting data related to flood control dispatching of a reservoir, establishing a multi-objective optimization model for flood control; using NSGA-II to obtain primary populations, and performing coding operations on individuals through coding operations. Description
Translated from Chinese
A Multi-objective Reservoir Scheduling Based on Graph Convolutional Neural Network and NSGA-Ⅱ Algorithm
Optimization
technical field
The invention belongs to the field of multi-objective optimal reservoir scheduling in the water conservancy industry, and relates to a multi-objective optimization method for reservoir scheduling based on a graph convolutional neural network and an NSGA-II algorithm.
Background technique
During the flood season, comprehensive factors such as the water level of the reservoir dam and downstream safety need to be taken into consideration in reservoir operation. If only the goal of lowering the water level of the reservoir is considered, it may result in low environmental benefits. Then, it is necessary to consider multiple objectives, adjust the discharge flow at each stage, and obtain a solution set that can make the environmental benefits and flood control benefits non-inferior. The user selects the scheduling scheme as required. In previous research, traditional methods (such as particle swarm optimization and genetic algorithm dynamic programming) are usually used to solve the scheduling scheme. When the model is complex, problems such as dimensional disaster and slow convergence rate usually occur. The GCN_NSGA-II algorithm proposed in the present invention searches for the Pareto frontier and can be used in the multi-objective optimal scheduling model for flood control of the present invention to find the Pareto frontier in the model.
NSGA-Ⅱ algorithm is a multi-objective optimization algorithm based on Pareto non-inferior solution. Inheriting the global search ability of traditional genetic algorithm, and with elite strategy and fast non-dominated sorting, the algorithm has a good effect in quickly finding Pareto frontier and maintaining population diversity. In real life, many data do not have a regular spatial structure, while graph neural networks can use the particularity of graph structure to model data in non-Euclidean space, and capture the internal dependencies of data in mining graph node features. Great advantage.
The patent application (CN110428099A) discloses a method based on particle swarm algorithm to optimize the agricultural scheduling line and urban water supply capacity, and obtain the maximum water supply capacity that meets the requirements of a certain double guarantee rate of agricultural irrigation water and urban water use, and solves the problem that the existing technology cannot handle the multi-level water supply. Target multi-guarantee rate problem. However, the particle swarm optimization algorithm is easy to lose the diversity of the population in the search space, so it falls into the problem of local minimum and cannot guarantee the global search. The patent application (CN109948847A) discloses a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm applied to reservoir group scheduling. The invention improves the traditional third-generation non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGA-III) by performing two rounds of tournament selection and vector angle selection. ), the parent population is randomly selected for reproduction, and a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (VA-NSGA-III) based on reference point and vector angle selection is proposed. However, the method provided by this patent makes the selection operation more complicated during population evolution, and also increases the computational complexity, and is not conducive to the improvement of the convergence speed of the Pareto front.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The purpose of the present invention is to overcome the defects of the prior art and provide a multi-objective optimization method for reservoir dispatching based on graph convolutional neural network and NSGA-II algorithm. The invention is applied to multi-objective reservoir optimization and dispatching, and can quickly provide a reservoir optimization and dispatching scheme set satisfying all objectives, thereby facilitating decision makers to select the optimal scheme.
In order to solve the above technical problems, the present invention adopts the following technical solutions.
A multi-objective optimization method for reservoir dispatching based on graph convolutional neural network and NSGA-II algorithm of the present invention includes the following steps:
Step 1. Collect relevant data of reservoir flood control and dispatch, and establish a multi-objective optimization model for reservoir dispatch;
Step 2. Use the NSGA-II algorithm to obtain the initial population of the multi-objective optimization problem of reservoir dispatching, group the population individuals through coding operations, and label them with categories. Each category is used as a node of the GCN graph structure. The obtained parent-child relationship is mapped as the edge between the nodes of the GCN graph structure, and the GCN graph structure and the preliminary Pareto frontier are obtained;
Step 3. Carry out grouping and labeling on the abscissa of the preliminary Pareto frontier obtained in step 2, and then use the grouping label and the GCN graph structure obtained in step 2 to train the GCN model;
Step 4. Use the trained GCN model to classify the nodes of the GCN graph structure, and then use the NSGA-II algorithm to adjust the uniformity of the Pareto front until the algorithm iteration ends, and a more uniform Pareto front is obtained;
Step 5. According to the more uniform Pareto frontier obtained in Step 4, output a non-inferior set of solutions for the multi-objective optimization problem of reservoir dispatching.
Further, the objectives considered in the flood control multi-objective optimal scheduling model described in step 1 include:
The first is to minimize the upstream water level to ensure that the reservoir maintains a low water level during the flood season, which can effectively ensure the safety of the dam; the second is to minimize the maximum discharge flow of the reservoir. The reservoir stores as much floodwater as possible to ensure downstream safety and minimize inundation losses.
Further, the specific process of step 2 includes:
Step 2.1. Randomly initialize the population of the multi-objective optimization problem of reservoir scheduling, encode the population individuals according to the following encoding method, and use the encoded individual category as the node of the GCN graph structure; through this encoding method, multiple individuals in the population belong to the same group. A category is represented by the same node, so as to avoid the redundancy of graph structure caused by too many individuals in the population;
Coding method: divide the definition domain of the maximum leakage flow Q max into equal distances, then each distance is
Where Q max is the maximum leakage, N is the number of classifications, that is, the number of points in the GCN graph structure, then use
Then, the Pareto frontier is divided into equal distances according to the abscissa, and its interval is defined as 0, 1, 2..., where the 0 node is defined as the elimination node, and the length of the gene sequence in the population is determined by the variable The number is determined;
Step 2.2. Perform crossover and mutation operations on the population individuals described in step 2.1, determine whether the constraints are met, and point the gene sequence code of the eliminated individuals that meet the constraints to node 0; record those that meet the conditions, and at the same time crossover and mutation The parent-child relationship resulting from the operation is defined as the edge of the graph structure.
Further, the specific process of step 3 includes:
Step 3.1. Group and label the preliminary Pareto fronts obtained by the NSGA-II algorithm according to the abscissa, that is, divide the value range of the objective function equidistantly, and define digital labels;
Step 3.2. Set the input parameters, express the relationship between the individuals of the population as the adjacency matrix A∈R N×N of the graph convolutional neural network, and initialize the feature matrix X∈R N×D ;
Step 3.3. The first part is the input layer, N individuals, that is, N nodes of the graph, constitute the N-layer input layer, and the above-mentioned feature matrix X and adjacency matrix A are used as inputs;
Step 3.4. The second part is the convolution layer, which is composed of two layers of graph convolution. The information of the trigger edge is passed between the two layers, and the features of this layer are passed to the next layer through the edge;
Step 3.5. The third part is the output layer, which calculates and transfers the feature matrix X obtained by the above two layers of convolution layers, and then outputs the classification probability of each node through the activation function.
Further, the specific process of step 4 includes:
Step 4.1. The NSGA-II algorithm will obtain a preliminary Pareto frontier during selection, crossover and mutation operations, and during this process, a parent-child tree structure relationship will be generated between the population individuals of the multi-objective optimization problem of reservoir scheduling, and the tree The structure is converted into a GCN graph structure;
Step 4.2. Determine whether the above-mentioned population iteration threshold is met, if so, start training GCN, learn the node characteristics in the population evolution relationship graph network, and correspond the node classification results to the categories of the Pareto frontier;
Step 4.3. Use GCN to classify the nodes, and then use the NSGA-II algorithm to iteratively adjust the individuals in the Pareto frontier. The specific steps include:
Step 4.3.1. Use GCN to classify nodes and supplement the preliminary Pareto frontier;
Step 4.3.2. Traverse the nodes of different categories in the Pareto frontier, delete redundant nodes of the same category, increase the population of a small number of categories, and increase the difference;
Step 4.3.3. Then use the NSGA-II algorithm to perform crossover and mutation operations on the nodes with good performance obtained by GCN classification to obtain new nodes;
Step 4.3.4. Determine whether the node satisfies the constraint condition, and keep it if it does.
Compared with the prior art, the present invention has the following advantages and beneficial effects:
1. The present invention is aimed at the multi-objective optimization problem of the reservoir during the flood season, taking into account the two objectives of the lowest water level in front of the dam and the smallest discharge flow, and taking into account the safety of the reservoir and the ecological health of the downstream. This is also the multi-objective optimization problem of the reservoir dispatching in the flood season. main consideration. Due to the conflict between these two objectives, and this problem needs to consider a series of constraints, it cannot be simply treated as a single-objective problem. The NSGA-II algorithm has been used to deal with multi-objective optimization problems and is widely used. The algorithm proposed by the invention inherits the advantages of the NSGA-II algorithm, such as the advantages of fast convergence in the early stage of the algorithm and strong global search ability, etc., which also makes the algorithm of the invention have a good effect in dealing with multi-objective optimization problems of reservoir dispatching in flood season, A satisfactory Pareto solution set is obtained.
2. The present invention introduces a graph convolutional neural network, and transforms the parent-child relationship between individuals generated in the multi-objective optimization problem population evolution process into nodes of the GCN graph structure through encoding operations, thereby training the GCN model. The graph convolutional neural network can well mine the relationship between the nodes of the graph structure, learn the node features, and thus accurately classify, thereby improving the problem of poor local search and slow convergence in the NSGA-II algorithm. The NSGA-II algorithm uses GCN classification in the later stage, instead of using the NSGA-II algorithm to calculate the crowding distance and other strategies, which achieves the purpose of reducing the computational cost and improving the speed. Pareto front, ensuring the uniformity of Pareto front. The invention can quickly provide a set of optimal dispatching schemes for flood season reservoirs that meet all the objectives.

As shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3, the multi-objective optimization method for reservoir scheduling based on graph convolutional neural network and NSGA-II proposed by the present invention is applied to the multi-objective optimal scheduling problem of Xiaolangdi Reservoir flood control, and the pareto frontier of the multi-objective optimization problem is obtained. .
As shown in Figure 1, the method according to the embodiment of the present invention includes the following steps:
Step 1. Collect data such as Xiaolangdi Reservoir storage capacity, maximum discharge capacity, water inflow during flood season and natural water demand, and establish a multi-objective optimal scheduling model for flood control, including:
1.1. Collect data such as reservoir storage capacity, maximum discharge capacity, water inflow during flood season and natural water demand, as follows:
The Xiaolangdi Water Control Project is located on the main stream of the Yellow River 40km north of Luoyang City, Henan Province. The upstream is the Sanmenxia Water Control Project, and the downstream is the Huayuankou Reservoir in Zhengzhou. The watershed area controlled by the dam site is 694,000 km 2 , accounting for 95.1% of the watershed area above Huayuankou. The purpose of Xiaolangdi Reservoir is mainly to prevent floods and reduce siltation, as well as water supply, irrigation and power generation. The designed normal water storage level of the reservoir is 275m (the Yellow Sea elevation), the check flood level is 275m once in 10,000 years, and the design flood level is 274m once in a thousand years. The total designed storage capacity is 12.65 billion m 3 , including 7.55 billion m 3 for sand blocking, 4.05 billion m 3 for flood control, and 1.05 billion m 3 for water and sand regulation. The maximum flood control water level of the reservoir is 275.0m, and the corresponding storage capacity is 9.422 billion m 3 .
1.2. Establish a multi-objective optimal scheduling model for flood control:
1.2.1. The lowest water level in front of the dam: MinF 1 =Min{MaxZ t }, wherein, the water level in front of the dam in the Z t period.
1.2.2. The maximum discharge flow is the smallest: MinF 2 =Min{MaxQ t }, where Q t represents the discharge flow of the reservoir in the t-th period of the dispatch period.
1.2.3. The constraints are as follows:
1. Water level constraint in front of the dam: Z t,min (230m)＜Z t ＜Z t,max (275m), where Z t,min and Z t,max represent the lowest and highest water levels in the t-th period of the reservoir operation period, respectively constraint; Z t is the water level before the dam of the reservoir in the t-th period.
2. Reservoir balance constraint: V t =V t-1 +(I t -Q t )Δt, where V t is the storage capacity of the reservoir in the t-th period; I t and Q t are the inflow of the reservoir in the t-th period, respectively and drain flow.
3. Discharge capacity constraint: Q≤Q max (14900m 3 /s), where Q max is the maximum discharge capacity of the reservoir under the corresponding water level.
Step 2. The graph structure of the graph convolutional neural network (GCN) is established by multiplying the offspring through the NSGA-II algorithm;
Step 2.1. Randomly initialize the number of individuals in the population to 50, and encode the population according to a certain encoding method, as shown in Figure 2;

The individual is encoded by the method, N is selected as 26, that is, it is divided into 26 categories, that is, the first category is Q t ∈ [0,573]; set the algebraic threshold to be 40, and if more than 40 generations, the pareto frontier is divided according to the abscissa equidistant length 0.00016 , initialize the 0 node as the elimination node, [1, 2, 3, 4] are the categories on the pareto frontier, and the 5 nodes 0-4 are the source nodes, and the length of the gene sequence in the population is determined by the number of variables. 72.
Step 2.2. Perform crossover and mutation operations on the individuals of the population, determine whether the constraints are met, and point the gene sequence code of the eliminated individuals that meet the constraints to node 0; record those that meet the conditions, and record the results of crossover and mutation, that is, father and son the individual relationship of the generational relationship;
Step 2.3. According to the population obtained by the NSGA-II algorithm, transform the parent-child tree structure into the graph structure required by GCN, which is the population evolution relationship graph network G.
Step 3. GCN mines the relationship between nodes, and continuously enriches the features of nodes to train GCN, as shown in Figure 3;
Step 3.1. Set the input parameters, the relationship between the individuals of the population is expressed as the adjacency matrix A of the graph convolutional neural network, and the specific feature matrix X is determined by the reachable length of the path in the graph;
Step 3.2. The first layer is the input layer, 50 individuals, that is, 50 nodes in the graph and 5 source nodes form 55 to form the input layer, and the above feature matrix and adjacency matrix A are used as inputs;
Step 3.3. The second layer is the convolution layer, which consists of two layers of graph convolution, and the transmission between the two layers is based on the following propagation rules:
By triggering the information transfer of the edge, the features of this layer are passed to the next layer through the edge, as shown in Figure 4.
Step 3.4. The last layer is the output layer. The feature matrix Z obtained by the calculation of the above two layers of convolution layers is output through the softmax function, that is, the classification probability of each node;
Step 4. The GCN nodes are classified, and the nodes with good classification results continue to multiply through NSGA-II to adjust the performance of the nodes.
Step 4.1. Through the individual evolution process (crossover, mutation and elimination) in the NSGA-II genetic algorithm, the evolution process is modeled into a population relationship network diagram;
Step 4.2. Determine whether the population iteration threshold is satisfied (the threshold is 100 generations), and if it is satisfied, use the graph convolutional neural network provided in step 3 to learn the direct relationship between the nodes, and set the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.01. Give the adjusted and classified results of the given points;
Step 4.3. Use GCN to classify the nodes of the population, and the classification results supplement the initial Pareto front to obtain a more complete Pareto front, and then use the NSGA-II algorithm to adjust the nodes in the Pareto front to make the distribution more uniform . The specific steps include:
Step 4.3.1. Use GCN to classify nodes, classify nodes according to the classification results, the number of nodes in each category will be supplemented, and the Pareto frontier will be more complete;
Step 4.3.2. Calculate the number of node categories in the above-mentioned more complete Pareto frontier, then delete some nodes in the category with more nodes, and generate some nodes for the category with fewer nodes, and the generation rules are shown in Figure 2;
Step 4.3.3. Use the NSGA-II algorithm to perform crossover and mutation operations on the above Pareto fronts to obtain a more uniform and accurate Pareto front;
Step 4.3.4. Determine whether the node satisfies the constraint condition, and keep it if it does.
Step 5. The Pareto frontier is obtained by satisfying the termination conditions, that is, the result of multi-objective optimization is obtained, and the benefit of each objective and the set of reservoir dispatching schemes are determined.
The method proposed by the present invention is applied to the multi-objective optimal scheduling of Xiaolangdi Reservoir during flood season. Taking four hours as a small scheduling interval and the total duration of 72 hours as an example, the NSGA-II algorithm and the NSGADE algorithm are compared. It can be seen from Figure 5 The Pareto solution set obtained by the method of the present invention is superior to the NSGA-II algorithm and the NSGADE algorithm. And by comparing the IGD value and HV value of the three algorithms, it also shows that the algorithm proposed by the present invention has obvious advantages in convergence speed, wherein the IGD value measures the closeness between the real Pareto front and the Pareto front obtained by the algorithm. to evaluate the convergence and diversity of the algorithm, and the HV value is used to measure the range covered by the Pareto solution set obtained by the algorithm in the target space, which can measure the convergence and diversity at the same time. The smaller the IGD value, the better the convergence of the Pareto fronts obtained by the algorithm and the more uniform the distribution. The larger the HV, the better the convergence of the Pareto fronts obtained by the algorithm and the more uniform the distribution. The detailed comparison is as follows:
To sum up, the present invention models the multi-objective optimization problem of reservoir dispatching in flood season, and considers the influence of two objectives, water level before the dam and maximum discharge volume, on the reservoir dispatching scheme in flood season. According to the specific factors such as the specific reservoir and the surrounding environment, a specific model is further established. Using the algorithm proposed in the present invention, a set of dispatching schemes that meet all the objectives can be obtained. A reasonable reservoir dispatching scheme can not only maximize benefits for many parties, but also It can ensure less damage to the ecological environment.

Title
Building HVAC system with multi-objective optimization control

Abstract
A controller for heating, ventilation, or air conditioning (HVAC) equipment operable to affect an environmental condition of a building is configured to obtain predictive models that predict values of an energy control objective and an air quality control objective as a function of control decision variables for the HVAC equipment. The controller executes a multi-objective optimization process using the predictive models to produce multiple sets of optimization results corresponding to different values of the control decision variables, the energy control objective, and the air quality control objective. The controller selects one or more of the sets of optimization results based on the values of the energy control objective and the air quality control objective. The controller operates the HVAC equipment to affect the environmental condition of the building in accordance with the values of the control decision variables corresponding to a selected set of the optimization results.

BACKGROUND
The present disclosure relates generally to a building system in a building. The present disclosure relates more particularly to maintaining occupant comfort in a building through environmental control.
Maintaining occupant comfort and disinfection in a building requires building equipment (e.g., HVAC equipment) to be operated to change environmental conditions in the building. In some systems, occupants are required to make any desired changes to the environmental conditions themselves if they are not comfortable. When operating building equipment to change specific environmental conditions, other environmental conditions may be affected as a result. Maintaining occupant comfort and disinfection can be expensive if not performed correctly. Thus, systems and methods are needed to maintain occupant comfort and provide sufficient disinfection for multiple environmental conditions while reducing expenses related to maintaining occupant comfort and disinfection.
SUMMARY
One implementation of the present disclosure is a controller for heating, ventilation, or air conditioning (HVAC) equipment, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the HVAC equipment is operable to affect an environmental condition of a building. In some embodiments, the controller includes one or more processors and memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to perform operations. In some embodiments, the operations include obtaining one or more predictive models configured to predict values of a carbon emissions control objective and another control objective as a function of control decision variables for the HVAC equipment. In some embodiments, the operations include executing an optimization process using the one or more predictive models to produce multiple sets of optimization results corresponding to different values of the control decision variables, the carbon emissions control objective, and the other control objective. DETAILED DESCRIPTION
Overview
Referring generally to the FIGURES, systems and methods for minimizing energy consumption of an HVAC system while maintaining a desired level of disinfection are shown. The system may include an AHU that serves multiple zones, a controller, one or more UV lights that disinfect air before it is provided from the AHU to the zones, and/or a filter that is configured to filter air to provide additional disinfection for the air before it is provided to the zones. In some embodiments, the system also includes one or more zone sensors (e.g., temperature and/or humidity sensors, etc.) and one or more ambient or outdoor sensors (e.g., outdoor temperature and/or outdoor humidity sensors, etc.).
The controller uses a model-based design and optimization framework to integrate building disinfection control with existing temperature regulation in building HVAC systems. The controller uses the Wells-Riley equation to transform a required upper limit of infection probability into constraints on indoor concentration of infectious particles, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the controller uses a dynamic model for infectious agent concentration to impose these constraints on an optimization problem similar to temperature and humidity constraints. By modeling effects of various types of optional infection control equipment (e.g., UV lights and/or filters), the controller may utilize a combination of fresh-air ventilation and direct filtration/disinfection to achieve desired infection constraints. In some embodiments, the controller can use this composite model for optimal design (e.g., in an off-line implementation of the controller) to determine which additional disinfection strategies are desirable, cost effective, or necessary. The controller can also be used for on-line control to determine control decisions for various controllable equipment (e.g., dampers of the AHU) in real-time to minimize energy consumption or energy costs of the HVAC system while meeting temperature, humidity, and infectious quanta concentration constraints.
The systems and methods described herein treat infection control as an integral part of building HVAC operation rather than a short term or independent control objective, according to some embodiments. While it may be possible to achieve disinfection by the addition of UV lights and filters running at full capacity, such a strategy may be costly and consume excessive amounts of energy. However, the systems and methods described herein couple both objectives (disinfection control and minimal energy consumption) to assess optimal design and operational decisions on a case-by-case basis also taking into account climate, energy and disinfection goals of particular buildings.
The controller can be implemented in an off-line mode as a design tool. With the emergence of various strategies for building disinfection, building designers and operators now have a wide array of options for retrofitting a building to reduce the spread of infectious diseases to building occupants. This is typically accomplished by lowering the concentration of infectious particles in the air space, which can be accomplished by killing the microbes via UV radiation, trapping them via filtration, or simply forcing them out of the building via fresh-air ventilation. While any one of these strategies individually can provide desired levels of disinfection, it may do so at unnecessarily high cost or with negative consequences for thermal comfort of building occupants. Thus, to help evaluate the tradeoff and potential synergies between the various disinfection options, the model-based design tool can estimate annualized capital and energy costs for a given set of disinfection equipment. For a given AHU, this includes dynamic models for temperature, humidity, and infectious particle concentration, and it employs the Wells-Riley infection equation to enforce constraints on maximum occupant infection probability. By being able to quickly simulate a variety of simulation instances, the controller (when operating as the design tool in the off-line mode) can present building designers with the tradeoff between cost and disinfection, allowing them to make informed decisions about retrofit.
A key feature of the design tool is that it shows to what extent the inherent flexibility of the existing HVAC system can be used to provide disinfection. In particular, in months when infectivity is of biggest concern, a presence of free cooling from fresh outdoor air means that the energy landscape is relatively flat regardless of how the controller determines to operate the HVAC system. Thus, the controller could potentially increase fresh-air intake significantly to provide sufficient disinfection without UV or advanced filtration while incurring only a small energy penalty. The design tool can provide estimates to customers to allow them to make informed decisions about what additional disinfection equipment (if any) to install and then provide the modified control systems needed to implement the desired infection control.
The controller can also be implemented in an on-line mode as a real-time controller. Although equipment like UV lamps and advanced filtration can be installed in buildings to mitigate the spread of infectious diseases, it is often unclear how to best operate that equipment to achieve desired disinfection goals in a cost-effective manner. A common strategy is to take the robust approach of opting for the highest-efficiency filters and running UV lamps constantly. While this strategy will indeed reduce infection probability to its lowest possible value, it is likely to do so at exorbitant cost due to the constant energy penalties of both strategies. Building managers may potentially choose to completely disable filters and UV lamps to conserve energy consumption. Thus, the building may end up in a worst-of-both-words situation where the building manager has paid for disinfection equipment but the zones are no longer receiving any disinfection. To remove this burden from building operators, the controller can automate infection control by integrating disinfection control (e.g., based on the Wells-Riley equation) in a model based control scheme. In this way, the controller can simultaneously achieve thermal comfort and provide adequate disinfection at the lowest possible cost given currently available equipment.
Advantageously, the control strategy can optimize in real time the energy and disinfection tradeoffs of all possible control variables. Specifically, the controller may choose to raise fresh-air intake fraction even though it incurs a slight energy penalty because it allows a significant reduction of infectious particle concentrations while still maintaining comfortable temperatures. Thus, in some climates it may be possible to provide disinfection without additional equipment, but this strategy is only possible if the existing control infrastructure can be guided or constrained so as to provide desired disinfection. Alternatively, in buildings that have chosen to add UV lamps and/or filtration, the controller can find the optimal combination of techniques to achieve desired control objectives at the lowest possible cost. In addition, because the constraint on infection probability is configurable, the controller can empower building operators to make their own choices regarding disinfection and energy use (e.g. opting for a loose constraint in the summer when disease is rare and energy use is intensive, while transitioning to a tight constraint in winter when disease is prevalent and energy less of a concern). Advantageously, the controller can provide integrated comfort, disinfection, and energy management to customers to achieve better outcomes in all three areas compared to other narrow and individual solutions.
In some embodiments, the models used to predict temperature, humidity, and/or infectious quanta are dynamic models. The term “dynamic model” and variants thereof (e.g., dynamic temperature model, dynamic humidity model, dynamic infectious quanta model, etc.) are used throughout the present disclosure to refer to any type of model that predicts the value of a quantity (e.g., temperature, humidity, infectious quanta) at various points in time as a function of zero or more input variables. A dynamic model may be “dynamic” as a result of the input variables changing over time even if the model itself does not change. For example, a steady-state model that uses ambient temperature or any other variable that changes over time as an input may be considered a dynamic model. Dynamic models may also include models that vary over time. For example, models that are retrained periodically, configured to adapt to changing conditions over time, and/or configured to use different relationships between input variables and predicted outputs (e.g., a first set of relationships for winter months and a second set of relationships for summer months) may also be considered dynamic models. Dynamic models may also include ordinary differential equation (ODE) models or other types of models having input variables that change over time and/or input variables that represent the rate of change of a variable.
Building and HVAC System
Referring now to FIG. 1 , a perspective view of a building 10 is shown. Building 10 can be served by a building management system (BMS). A BMS is, in general, a system of devices configured to control, monitor, and manage equipment in or around a building or building area. A BMS can include, for example, a HVAC system, a security system, a lighting system, a fire alerting system, any other system that is capable of managing building functions or devices, or any combination thereof. An example of a BMS which can be used to monitor and control building 10 is described in U.S. patent application Ser. No. 14/717,593 filed May 20, 2015, the entire disclosure of which is incorporated by reference herein.
The BMS that serves building 10 may include a HVAC system 100 . HVAC system 100 can include a plurality of HVAC devices (e.g., heaters, chillers, air handling units, pumps, fans, thermal energy storage, etc.) configured to provide heating, cooling, ventilation, or other services for building 10 . For example, HVAC system 100 is shown to include a waterside system 120 and an airside system 130 . Waterside system 120 may provide a heated or chilled fluid to an air handling unit of airside system 130 . Airside system 130 may use the heated or chilled fluid to heat or cool an airflow provided to building 10 . In some embodiments, waterside system 120 can be replaced with or supplemented by a central plant or central energy facility (described in greater detail with reference to FIG. 2 ). An example of an airside system which can be used in HVAC system 100 is described in greater detail with reference to FIG. 2 .
HVAC system 100 is shown to include a chiller 102 , a boiler 104 , and a rooftop air handling unit (AHU) 106 . Waterside system 120 may use boiler 104 and chiller 102 to heat or cool a working fluid (e.g., water, glycol, etc.) and may circulate the working fluid to AHU 106 . In various embodiments, the HVAC devices of waterside system 120 can be located in or around building 10 (as shown in FIG. 1 ) or at an offsite location such as a central plant (e.g., a chiller plant, a steam plant, a heat plant, etc.). The working fluid can be heated in boiler 104 or cooled in chiller 102 , depending on whether heating or cooling is required in building 10 . Boiler 104 may add heat to the circulated fluid, for example, by burning a combustible material (e.g., natural gas) or using an electric heating element. Chiller 102 may place the circulated fluid in a heat exchange relationship with another fluid (e.g., a refrigerant) in a heat exchanger (e.g., an evaporator) to absorb heat from the circulated fluid. The working fluid from chiller 102 and/or boiler 104 can be transported to AHU 106 via piping 108 .
AHU 106 may place the working fluid in a heat exchange relationship with an airflow passing through AHU 106 (e.g., via one or more stages of cooling coils and/or heating coils). The airflow can be, for example, outside air, return air from within building 10 , or a combination of both. AHU 106 may transfer heat between the airflow and the working fluid to provide heating or cooling for the airflow. For example, AHU 106 can include one or more fans or blowers configured to pass the airflow over or through a heat exchanger containing the working fluid. The working fluid may then return to chiller 102 or boiler 104 via piping 110 .
Airside system 130 may deliver the airflow supplied by AHU 106 (i.e., the supply airflow) to building 10 via air supply ducts 112 and may provide return air from building 10 to AHU 106 via air return ducts 114 . In some embodiments, airside system 130 includes multiple variable air volume (VAV) units 116 . For example, airside system 130 is shown to include a separate VAV unit 116 on each floor or zone of building 10 . VAV units 116 can include dampers or other flow control elements that can be operated to control an amount of the supply airflow provided to individual zones of building 10 . In other embodiments, airside system 130 delivers the supply airflow into one or more zones of building 10 (e.g., via supply ducts 112 ) without using intermediate VAV units 116 or other flow control elements. AHU 106 can include various sensors (e.g., temperature sensors, pressure sensors, etc.) configured to measure attributes of the supply airflow. AHU 106 may receive input from sensors located within AHU 106 and/or within the building zone and may adjust the flow rate, temperature, or other attributes of the supply airflow through AHU 106 to achieve setpoint conditions for the building zone.
Airside System
Referring now to FIG. 2 , a block diagram of an airside system 200 is shown, according to some embodiments. In various embodiments, airside system 200 may supplement or replace airside system 130 in HVAC system 100 or can be implemented separate from HVAC system 100 . When implemented in HVAC system 100 , airside system 200 can include a subset of the HVAC devices in HVAC system 100 (e.g., AHU 106 , VAV units 116 , ducts 112 - 114 , fans, dampers, etc.) and can be located in or around building 10 . Airside system 200 may operate to heat, cool, humidify, dehumidify, filter, and/or disinfect an airflow provided to building 10 in some embodiments.
Airside system 200 is shown to include an economizer-type air handling unit (AHU) 202 . Economizer-type AHUs vary the amount of outside air and return air used by the air handling unit for heating or cooling. For example, AHU 202 may receive return air 204 from building zone 206 via return air duct 208 and may deliver supply air 210 to building zone 206 via supply air duct 212 . In some embodiments, AHU 202 is a rooftop unit located on the roof of building 10 (e.g., AHU 106 as shown in FIG. 1 ) or otherwise positioned to receive both return air 204 and outside air 214 . AHU 202 can be configured to operate exhaust air damper 216 , mixing damper 218 , and outside air damper 220 to control an amount of outside air 214 and return air 204 that combine to form supply air 210 . Any return air 204 that does not pass through mixing damper 218 can be exhausted from AHU 202 through exhaust damper 216 as exhaust air 222 .
Each of dampers 216 - 220 can be operated by an actuator. For example, exhaust air damper 216 can be operated by actuator 224 , mixing damper 218 can be operated by actuator 226 , and outside air damper 220 can be operated by actuator 228 . Actuators 224 - 228 may communicate with an AHU controller 230 via a communications link 232 . Actuators 224 - 228 may receive control signals from AHU controller 230 and may provide feedback signals to AHU controller 230 . Feedback signals can include, for example, an indication of a current actuator or damper position, an amount of torque or force exerted by the actuator, diagnostic information (e.g., results of diagnostic tests performed by actuators 224 - 228 ), status information, commissioning information, configuration settings, calibration data, and/or other types of information or data that can be collected, stored, or used by actuators 224 - 228 . AHU controller 230 can be an economizer controller configured to use one or more control algorithms (e.g., state-based algorithms, extremum seeking control (ESC) algorithms, proportional-integral (PI) control algorithms, proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control algorithms, model predictive control (MPC) algorithms, feedback control algorithms, etc.) to control actuators 224 - 228 .
Still referring to FIG. 2 , AHU 202 is shown to include a cooling coil 234 , a heating coil 236 , and a fan 238 positioned within supply air duct 212 . Fan 238 can be configured to force supply air 210 through cooling coil 234 and/or heating coil 236 and provide supply air 210 to building zone 206 . AHU controller 230 may communicate with fan 238 via communications link 240 to control a flow rate of supply air 210 . In some embodiments, AHU controller 230 controls an amount of heating or cooling applied to supply air 210 by modulating a speed of fan 238 . In some embodiments, AHU 202 includes one or more air filters (e.g., filter 308 ) and/or one or more ultraviolet (UV) lights (e.g., UV lights 306 ) as described in greater detail with reference to FIG. 3 . AHU controller 230 can be configured to control the UV lights and route the airflow through the air filters to disinfect the airflow as described in greater detail below.
Cooling coil 234 may receive a chilled fluid from central plant 200 (e.g., from cold water loop 216 ) via piping 242 and may return the chilled fluid to central plant 200 via piping 244 . Valve 246 can be positioned along piping 242 or piping 244 to control a flow rate of the chilled fluid through cooling coil 234 . In some embodiments, cooling coil 234 includes multiple stages of cooling coils that can be independently activated and deactivated (e.g., by AHU controller 230 , by BMS controller 266 , etc.) to modulate an amount of cooling applied to supply air 210 .
Heating coil 236 may receive a heated fluid from central plant 200 (e.g., from hot water loop 214 ) via piping 248 and may return the heated fluid to central plant 200 via piping 250 . Valve 252 can be positioned along piping 248 or piping 250 to control a flow rate of the heated fluid through heating coil 236 . In some embodiments, heating coil 236 includes multiple stages of heating coils that can be independently activated and deactivated (e.g., by AHU controller 230 , by BMS controller 266 , etc.) to modulate an amount of heating applied to supply air 210 .
Each of valves 246 and 252 can be controlled by an actuator. For example, valve 246 can be controlled by actuator 254 and valve 252 can be controlled by actuator 256 . Actuators 254 - 256 may communicate with AHU controller 230 via communications links 258 - 260 . Actuators 254 - 256 may receive control signals from AHU controller 230 and may provide feedback signals to controller 230 . In some embodiments, AHU controller 230 receives a measurement of the supply air temperature from a temperature sensor 262 positioned in supply air duct 212 (e.g., downstream of cooling coil 334 and/or heating coil 236 ). AHU controller 230 may also receive a measurement of the temperature of building zone 206 from a temperature sensor 264 located in building zone 206 .
In some embodiments, AHU controller 230 operates valves 246 and 252 via actuators 254 - 256 to modulate an amount of heating or cooling provided to supply air 210 (e.g., to achieve a setpoint temperature for supply air 210 or to maintain the temperature of supply air 210 within a setpoint temperature range). The positions of valves 246 and 252 affect the amount of heating or cooling provided to supply air 210 by cooling coil 234 or heating coil 236 and may correlate with the amount of energy consumed to achieve a desired supply air temperature. AHU 230 may control the temperature of supply air 210 and/or building zone 206 by activating or deactivating coils 234 - 236 , adjusting a speed of fan 238 , or a combination of both.
Still referring to FIG. 2 , airside system 200 is shown to include a building management system (BMS) controller 266 and a client device 268 . BMS controller 266 can include one or more computer systems (e.g., servers, supervisory controllers, subsystem controllers, etc.) that serve as system level controllers, application or data servers, head nodes, or master controllers for airside system 200 , central plant 200 , HVAC system 100 , and/or other controllable systems that serve building 10 . BMS controller 266 may communicate with multiple downstream building systems or subsystems (e.g., HVAC system 100 , a security system, a lighting system, central plant 200 , etc.) via a communications link 270 according to like or disparate protocols (e.g., LON, BACnet, etc.). In various embodiments, AHU controller 230 and BMS controller 266 can be separate (as shown in FIG. 2 ) or integrated. In some embodiments, AHU controller 230 receives information from BMS controller 266 (e.g., commands, setpoints, operating boundaries, etc.) and provides information to BMS controller 266 (e.g., temperature measurements, valve or actuator positions, operating statuses, diagnostics, etc.). HVAC System with Building Infection Control
Overview
Referring particularly to FIG. 3 , a HVAC system 300 that is configured to provide disinfection for various zones of a building (e.g., building 10 ) is shown, according to some embodiments. HVAC system 300 can include an air handling unit (AHU) 304 (e.g., AHU 230 , AHU 202 , etc.) that can provide conditioned air (e.g., cooled air, supply air 210 , etc.) to various building zones 206 . The AHU 304 may draw air from the zones 206 in combination with drawing air from outside (e.g., outside air 214 ) to provide conditioned or clean air to zones 206 . The HVAC system 300 includes a controller 310 (e.g., AHU controller 230 ) that is configured to determine a fraction x of outdoor air to recirculated air that the AHU 304 should use to provide a desired amount of disinfection to building zones 206 . In some embodiments, controller 310 can generate control signals for various dampers of AHU 304 so that AHU 304 operates to provide the conditioned air to building zones 206 using the fraction x.
The HVAC system 300 can also include ultraviolet (UV) lights 306 that are configured to provide UV light to the conditioned air before it is provided to building zones 206 . The UV lights 306 can provide disinfection as determined by controller 310 and/or based on user operating preferences. For example, the controller 310 can determine control signals for UV lights 306 in combination with the fraction x of outdoor air to provide a desired amount of disinfection and satisfy an infection probability constraint. Although UV lights 306 are referred to throughout the present disclosure, the systems and methods described herein can use any type of disinfection lighting using any frequency, wavelength, or luminosity of light effective for disinfection. It should be understood that UV lights 306 (and any references to UV lights 306 throughout the present disclosure) can be replaced with disinfection lighting of any type without departing from the teachings of the present disclosure.
The HVAC system 300 can also include one or more filters 308 or filtration devices (e.g., air purifiers). In some embodiments, the filters 308 are configured to filter the conditioned air or recirculated air before it is provided to building zones 206 to provide a certain amount of disinfection. In this way, controller 310 can perform an optimization in real-time or as a planning tool to determine control signals for AHU 304 (e.g., the fraction x) and control signals for UV lights 306 (e.g., on/off commands) to provide disinfection for building zones 206 and reduce a probability of infection of individuals that are occupying building zones 206 . Controller 310 can also function as a design tool that is configured to determine suggestions for building managers regarding benefits of installing or using filters 308 , and/or specific benefits that may arise from using or installing a particular type or size of filter. Controller 310 can thereby facilitate informed design decisions to maintain sterilization of air that is provided to building zones 206 and reduce a likelihood of infection or spreading of infectious matter.
Wells-Riley Airborne Transmission
The systems and methods described herein may use an infection probability constraint in various optimizations (e.g., in on-line or real-time optimizations or in off-line optimizations) to facilitate reducing infection probability among residents or occupants of spaces that the HVAC system serves. The infection probability constraint can be based on a steady-state Wells-Riley equation for a probability of airborne transmission of an infectious agent given by:
P := D S = 1 - exp ⁢ ( - Ipqt Q )
where P is a probability that an individual becomes infected (e.g., in a zone, space, room, environment, etc.), D is a number of infected individuals (e.g., in the zone, space, room, environment, etc.), S is a total number of susceptible individuals (e.g., in the zone, space, room, environment, etc.), I is a number of infectious individuals (e.g., in the zone, space, room, environment, etc.), q is a disease quanta generation rate (e.g., with units of 1/sec), p is a volumetric breath rate of one individual (e.g., in m 3 /sec), t is a total exposure time (e.g., in seconds), and Q is an outdoor ventilation rate (e.g., in m 3 /sec). For example, Q may be a volumetric flow rate of fresh outdoor air that is provided to the building zones 206 by AHU 304 .
When the Wells-Riley equation is implemented by controller 310 as described herein, controller 310 may use the Wells-Riley equation (or a dynamic version of the Wells-Riley equation) to determine an actual or current probability of infection P and operate the HVAC system 200 to maintain the actual probability of infection P below (or drive the actual probability of infection below) a constraint or maximum allowable value. The constraint value (e.g., P max ) may be a constant value, or may be adjustable by a user (e.g., a user-set value). For example, the user may set the constraint value of the probability of infection to a maximum desired probability of infection (e.g., either for on-line implementation of controller 310 to maintain the probability of infection below the maximum desired probability, or for an off-line implementation/simulation performed by controller 310 to determine various design parameters for HVAC system 200 such as filter size), or may select from various predetermined values (e.g., 3-5 different choices of the maximum desired probability of infection).
In some embodiments, the number of infectious individuals I can be determined by controller 310 based on data from the Centers for Disease and Control Prevention or a similar data source. The value of I may be typically set equal to 1 but may vary as a function of occupancy of building zones 206 .
The disease quanta generation rate q may be a function of the infectious agent. For example, more infectious diseases may have a higher value of q, while less infectious diseases may have a lower value of q. For example, the value of q for COVID-19 may be 30-300 (e.g., 100 ).
The value of the volumetric breath rate p may be based on a type of building space 206 . For example, the volumetric breath rate p may be higher if the building zone 206 is a gym as opposed to an office setting. In general, an expected level of occupant activity may determine the value of the volumetric breath rate p.
A difference between D (the number of infected individuals) and I (the number of infectious individuals) is that D is a number of individuals who are infected (e.g., infected with a disease), while I is a number of people that are infected and are actively contagious (e.g., individuals that may spread the disease to other individuals or spread infectious particles when they exhale). The disease quanta generation rate indicates a number of infectious droplets that give a 63.2% chance of infecting an individual (e.g., 1−exp(−1)). For example, if an individual inhales k infectious particles, the probability that the individual becomes infected (P) is given by
1 - exp ⁢ ( - k k 0 )
where k is the number of infectious particles that the individual has inhaled, and k 0 is a quantum of particles for a particular disease (e.g., a predefined value for different diseases). The quanta generation rate q is the rate at which quanta are generated (e.g., K/k 0 ) where K is the rate of infectious particles exhaled by an infectious individual. It should be noted that values of the disease quanta generation rate q may be back-calculated from epidemiological data or may be tabulated for well-known diseases.
The Wells-Riley equation (shown above) is derived by assuming steady-state concentrations for infectious particles in the air. Assuming a well-mixed space:
