For example, if the indoor air quality score is between a first or normal range, then the color of the indoor air quality score icon 1204 may be yellow, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, if the indoor air quality score is between a second range or less than a lower value of the first or normal range, this may indicate that the indoor air quality score is poor and the color of the indoor air quality score icon 2104 may be red. In some embodiments, if the indoor air quality score is between a third range or greater than a higher value of the first or normal range, this may indicate that the indoor air quality score is good and the color of the indoor air quality score 2104 may be green.
Referring still to FIG. 21 , the user interface 2100 includes a list 2106 of one or more infectious disease high risk alerts, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the list 2106 includes different items 2108 , each item corresponding to a different zone of the building 10 and an individual infection risk score associated with the different zones. In some embodiments, the items 2108 of the list 2106 are zone-specific and are determined based on the infectious disease risk score for each of the zones of the building 10 . For example, if one of the zones has an associated infectious disease risk score that is below a threshold amount, then that zone may be added with the associated infectious disease risk score to the list 2106 as one of the items 2108 .
Referring still to FIG. 21 , the user interface 2100 also includes a list 2110 of one or more low indoor air quality alerts, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the list 2110 includes different items 2112 , each item corresponding to a different zone of the building 10 and an individual indoor air quality associated with the different zones. In some embodiments, the items 2112 of the list 2110 are zone-specific and are determined based on the indoor air quality for each of the zones of the building 10 . For example, if one of the zones has an associated indoor air quality that is below a threshold amount, then that zone may be added with the associated indoor air quality to the list 2110 as one of the items 2112 .
Referring still to FIG. 21 , the user interface 2100 includes a list 2114 of each of the zones of the building 10 (e.g., organized by zone type, floor of the building 10 , etc.). Each of the items of the list 2114 includes an indication of the zone or floor, an associated infectious disease risk score for the zone or floor, a number of infectious disease risk alerts for the zone or floor, an indoor air quality score for the zone or floor, an indoor air quality trend (e.g., a 30 day trend), a number of indoor air quality alerts, and/or an energy spend versus budget (e.g., for 30 days).
Referring to FIG. 22 , the user interface 2200 includes different widgets 2202 - 2208 indicating the results of the Pareto optimization (e.g., the advisory mode outputs 1240 ) as described in greater detail above with reference to FIGS. 11 - 20 . Specifically, the user interface 2200 includes a current operational state widget 2202 illustrating current energy costs and associated infectious disease risk score with additional air flow, comfort, UV disinfection, and filtration specifics, according to some embodiments. The user interface 2200 includes a widget 2204 illustrating a first option, namely, the Pareto optimal result for optimizing the infectious disease risk score (e.g., minimizing infection risk or infection probability such as the maximum disinfection point 1318 ), a widget 2206 illustrating a second option, namely, the Pareto optimal result for equal priority between disinfection and energy consumption (e.g., the equal priority point 1320 ), and a widget 2208 illustrating a third option, namely, the Pareto optimal result for operating with minimum energy cost (e.g., the minimum energy consumption point 1322 ). Each of the widgets 2204 - 2208 include graphical and/or textual information regarding a corresponding infectious disease risk score, an energy cost per a time period (e.g., a monthly time period), air flow parameters, required operational adjustments, optional design adjustments, etc., for each of the options. In some embodiments, the user or building administrator may select one of the options by selecting one of the widgets 2204 - 2208 .
Referring particularly to FIG. 23 , the user interface 2300 illustrates different operational adjustments for the HVAC system 400 that the building administrator should implement in order to configure the HVAC system 400 to perform the selected option, according to some embodiments. The user interface 2300 includes widgets 2302 a - 2302 d , each of which illustrate a next step that should be performed to implement the selected option, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, each widget 2302 includes a button 2304 which, when selected, navigates the user to a command and control panel where the user or building administrator can perform the specific operational adjustment (e.g., adjusting the supply temperature setpoint). Each widget 2302 also includes a button 2306 which, when selected, marks the task associated with the widget 2302 as completed, according to some embodiments.
Sustainability Metric Techniques
Referring to FIGS. 24 - 30 , various techniques for performing the Pareto optimization based on a sustainability metric are shown, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the sustainability metric can be introduced into the Pareto optimization as a third control objective such that the Pareto optimization considers energy cost, infection risk, and the sustainability metric. In some embodiments, the sustainability metric may replace one of the control objectives discussed above (e.g., replacing energy cost or infection risk) such that the Pareto optimization considers energy cost and the sustainability metric (as shown in FIGS. 26 and 30 ) or considers infection risk and the sustainability metric (as shown in FIG. 24 ).
The sustainability metric may include any of a variety of metrics that quantify the performance of a building, campus, or organization with respect to energy sustainability or environmental sustainability. Some examples of sustainability metrics include carbon dioxide (CO2) related metrics (i.e., carbon equivalents) such as carbon emissions, carbon footprint, carbon credits, carbon offsets, and the like. Other examples of sustainability metrics include greenhouse gas emissions (e.g., methane, nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases, etc.), water usage, water pollution, waste generation, ecological footprint, resource consumption, or any other metric that can be used to quantify sustainable building operations. In some embodiments, sustainability metrics can be expressed on a per unit basis such as carbon per number of widgets produced, carbon per volume of product produced, carbon per meals served, carbon per patients treated, carbon per experiments run, carbon per sales revenue, carbon per items shipped, carbon per emails sent, carbon per unit of data processed, carbon per occupant, carbon per occupied room, carbon per normalized utilization value, etc. In some embodiments, sustainability metrics can be generated on an enterprise-wide basis (e.g., one value for the whole enterprise), on a building-by-building basis, on a campus-by-campus basis, by business unit/department, by building system or subsystem (e.g., HVAC, lighting, security, etc.), by control loop (e.g., chiller control loop, AHU control loop, waterside control loop, airside control loop, etc.), by building space (e.g., per room or floor), or by any other division or aggregation. Sustainability metrics can be calculated or generated based on actual or historical building operations or predicted for future building operations using one or more predictive models.
The techniques described herein with reference to FIGS. 24 - 27 can be performed or implemented by the controller 1110 , the functionality of the controller 1110 as shown in the diagram 1200 , etc., with the one or more sustainability metrics used in the Pareto optimization as an additional parameter (e.g., an additional degree of freedom for the optimization to thereby result in points that define a Pareto optimal surface), in place of the energy cost or consumption, in place of infection risk, or as a post-processing calculation to determine a sustainability metric or carbon equivalence for the various proposed solutions or operating schedules. Advantageously, the sustainability techniques described herein can be used for at least one of (i) an operational optimization to minimize or to inform a building administrator regarding sustainable building operation, or (ii) a design optimization to determine infrastructure (e.g., building equipment, HVAC equipment, etc.) that results in a cost-effective and sustainable (e.g., reduced carbon emissions) HVAC system infrastructure.
It should be understood that the sustainability metric described herein provides an estimation of how sustainable or environmentally friendly a proposed solution is (e.g., in terms of carbon emissions). Therefore, “high” or “maximum” values of the sustainability metric indicate an increased amount of carbon emissions and decreased or minimal environmentally friendliness of the solution, and “low” values of the sustainability metric indicate a decreased amount of carbon emissions and increased or maximal environmentally friendliness of the solution. It should further be understood that while FIGS. 24 - 29 described herein show infection risk being used as one of the optimization objectives (e.g., one of the parameters that is calculated by an objective function), the optimization objectives can also be a combination of the sustainability metric and an energy consumption or energy cost (e.g., as shown in FIG. 30 ).
Referring particularly to FIG. 24 , a diagram 2400 shows the graph 1302 of different decision variables (e.g., supply temperature setpoint and minimum ventilation setpoint), and a graph 2404 that shows corresponding objective function values, shown as points 2408 , for each of the different combinations of decision variables. The decision variables 1306 as shown in the graph 1302 of FIG. 24 may be the same as the decision variables 1306 as shown in the graph 1302 of FIG. 13 or any other decision variables that can be adjusted to influence the objective function values. In the embodiment shown in FIG. 24 , the objective function values are infection risk and a sustainability metric. In other embodiments, the objective function values may be the sustainability metric and energy cost (described in greater detail with reference to FIG. 30 ). It is contemplated that any set of objective function values can be used and the teachings of the present disclosure are not limited to the specific examples provided herein. The sustainability metric can be an estimated amount of CO2 emissions that are predicted to occur due to operation according to the minimum ventilation setpoint and supply temperature setpoint, or any other sustainability metric as described in detail above.
The objective function and corresponding predictive models used to define the sustainability metric and the infection risk can be similar to the objective function and predictive models described above with reference to FIGS. 11 - 20 , with the exception that the sustainability metric is calculated/predicted in place of energy cost or consumption (e.g., as shown in the graph 2404 ). For each combination of the decision variables 1306 (i.e., for cach of the points 1306 a - 1306 l ), the controller 1110 may perform a simulation to determine corresponding values 2408 a - 24081 of the control objectives, as described in greater detail above with reference to FIGS. 13 - 15 and FIGS. 17 - 20 . In this way, the steps of the Pareto optimization as described in greater detail above with reference to FIGS. 13 - 15 can be performed (e.g., by the controller 1110 ) using an objective function that predicts a sustainability metric and an infection risk.
In some embodiments, the value of the sustainability metric is calculated or predicted directly using one or more predictive models that define a relationship between the sustainability metric and building control decisions. For example, a predictive model may define the amount of carbon emissions as a function of operating decisions for building equipment (e.g., equipment on/off decisions, operating setpoints, etc.) over the duration of the optimization period. In other embodiments, the value of the sustainability metric can be calculated based on a corresponding amount of energy consumption. In this scenario, the objective function may be the same as the objective function previously described (e.g., an objective function that predicts energy cost or energy consumption as a function of the supply temperature setpoint and the minimum ventilation setpoint), and the resulting value of the objective function (e.g., energy consumption or cost) can be converted to a value of the sustainability metric (e.g., the carbon equivalence) using a conversion relationship. In some embodiments, the conversion relationship is a linear relationship that is used to map energy cost or energy consumption (e.g., for the HVAC system 200 ) to carbon emissions equivalence or any other sustainability metric.
Referring particularly to FIG. 25 , a graph 2500 shows a relationship between energy cost and carbon equivalence for an operational implementation of the Pareto optimization, according to some embodiments. The graph 2500 includes points 2504 and a trendline 2502 that represents the relationship between the energy cost and the carbon equivalent. In some embodiments, the trendline 2502 is a linear relationship (e.g., y=mx+b) that can be used to convert between energy cost and carbon equivalent in either direction (e.g., to estimate an energy cost based on carbon emissions, or to estimate carbon emissions or carbon equivalent based on energy cost). In some embodiments, the relationship shown in FIG. 25 is used to convert an output of the objective function from energy consumption to the carbon equivalent prior to performing the Pareto optimization described in greater detail above with reference to FIGS. 13 - 15 , in process 1700 , process 1900 , etc. In some embodiments, the relationship shown in FIG. 25 is used when the controller 1110 is implemented in an on-line mode for an operational optimization.
Referring particularly to FIG. 26 , a graph 2600 shows a relationship between total cost (e.g., a sum of capital expenses for purchase and installation of equipment, and energy cost associated with operating the equipment) and carbon equivalent is shown, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the relationship shown in FIG. 26 is used for an off-line implementation of the controller 1110 (e.g., when the functionality of the controller is implemented as a design tool or used to determine what equipment should be purchased). The graph 2600 includes points 2604 and a curve fit 2602 that illustrates the relationship between the total cost and the carbon equivalent (e.g., a curve fit approximation of the points 2604 ). In some embodiments, the relationship between total cost and the carbon equivalent is used by the controller 1110 when the capital cost is affected by a decision variable or depends on a decision variable (e.g., when the controller 1110 is used to determine what equipment should be purchased or used, or to provide a recommendation to a building administrator regarding what equipment should be purchased). In some embodiments, the relationship as shown in FIG. 26 illustrates that as the carbon equivalent increases, a significant tradeoff between carbon emissions and total cost may occur (e.g., the total cost may be significantly reduced but cause increasingly higher carbon equivalents).
Referring to FIG. 27 , the diagram 1200 that illustrates the functionality of the controller 1110 (see e.g., FIG. 12 , above) is shown as diagram 2700 , modified to account for sustainability instead of energy cost or energy consumption, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the components of the diagram 2700 are the same as the components of the diagram 1200 but with an additional sustainability conversion 2702 that is performed either (i) using an output of the dynamic model simulator 1232 to convert the resulting objective function values into a sustainability metric (e.g., CO2 emission or carbon equivalent), (ii) using an output of the Pareto optimizer 1236 to convert the optimized values to a sustainability metric (e.g., CO2 emission or carbon equivalent) so that at least one of the optimized values in terms of energy cost or energy consumption or the carbon equivalent is provided to the user as the advisory mode outputs 1240 or the analysis mode outputs 1234 , or (iii) using a different generic model simulation 1230 that predicts the sustainability metric as a function of one or more decision variables, or incorporates a conversion between energy consumption or cost and the sustainability metric.
As shown in FIG. 27 , the sustainability conversion 2702 can be implemented using an output of the dynamic model simulator 1232 to convert the objective function values from being in terms of energy cost or energy consumption to being in terms of the sustainability metric. In some embodiments, the sustainability conversion 2702 is configured to receive values of the objective function from the dynamic model simulator 1232 (e.g., values of energy cost or energy consumption) and determine a corresponding or equivalent value of a sustainability metric such as carbon or CO2 emissions. In some embodiments, the sustainability conversion 2702 or any of the other sustainability conversions described herein is/are implemented using the linear relationship shown in FIG. 25 or using the curve-fit relationship as shown in FIG. 26 . In some embodiments, the linear relationship shown in FIG. 25 is implemented when the controller 1110 operates to perform operational optimizations, and the curve-fit relationship as shown in FIG. 26 is implemented when the controller 1110 operates to perform building design and operational optimization. In some embodiments, the sustainability conversion 2702 is implemented using outputs of the Pareto optimizer 1236 , or as part of a post-process when providing the analysis mode outputs 1224 or the advisory mode outputs 1240 to the user.
Referring still FIGS. 27 , 4 - 5 , and 11 , the functionality of the sustainability conversion 2702 can be performed in an on-demand manner in response to a user input, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the user can provide an input to the controller 1110 to transition use of the sustainability conversion 2702 or to toggle the controller 1110 from operating using an objective function that predicts energy consumption or energy cost, and an objective function that predicts the sustainability metric. In this way, the dynamic model simulator 1232 can be transitioned between performing a simulation for energy consumption or energy cost (e.g., the objective function values) and performing a simulation for a sustainability metric. In some embodiments, the functionality of the sustainability conversion 2702 is performed as a display feature. For example, the Pareto optimal values may be provided to the user (e.g., via the display device 422 , a user interface, a display screen, etc.) in terms of energy consumption or energy cost, and can be toggled (e.g., in response to a user input) to the sustainability metric (e.g., using the linear relationship shown in FIG. 25 ) in response to a user input. In this way, the user can use either energy consumption, energy cost, or the sustainability metric to determine which control decisions to select. In some embodiments, the controller 1110 operates to provide both the sustainability metric and the energy cost or consumption to the user (e.g., via the display device 422 ) without requiring a user input.
Referring to FIGS. 13 and 24 , all of the infection risk, the energy cost or consumption, and the sustainability metric can be used to determine objective function values based on one or more decision variables, according to some embodiments. Specifically, while FIGS. 13 and 24 show only two objective function values (e.g., predicted energy cost/consumption and predicted infection risk in FIG. 13 , and predicted sustainability metric and predicted infection risk in FIG. 24 ), the objective function values may be combined so that more than two objective function values are used to assess Pareto optimality of the different combinations of decision variables. In some embodiments, the sustainability metric, the energy cost or consumption, and the infection risk are calculated using several different objective functions to determine a surface of points (e.g., each point having a value of the sustainability metric, the infection risk, and the energy cost or consumption). The subsequent steps of determining feasible points, and the various Pareto optimal points can be performed by the controller 1110 similarly as described above but using the surface graph. In some embodiments, the equal priority point is an equal priority between the sustainability metric, the infection risk, and the energy cost or consumption, and may be an inflection point of the surface of feasible points that is identified by the controller 1110 .
Referring particularly to FIG. 28 , a process 2800 shows the process 1700 modified to use the sustainability metric in place of the energy cost or energy consumption, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the process 2800 is the same as the process 1700 but includes an additional step 2802 performed using the outputs of the simulation performed in step 1704 . Process 2800 includes converting values of the energy cost and infection risk to values of a sustainability metric and infection risk (step 2802 ), according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, step 2802 includes using either of the relationships shown in FIGS. 25 and 26 to convert the energy cost or energy consumption resulting from the simulations into a corresponding value of carbon emissions (e.g., the sustainability metric).
Process 2800 also includes modified steps 2804 , 2806 , and 2808 , and steps 1712 - 1716 of process 1700 , according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the modified step 2804 is the same as the step 1706 but is performed based on the sustainability metric instead of the energy cost. Similarly, step 2806 can be the same as or similar to the step 1708 but performed to determine Pareto optimal solutions based on the sustainability metric. Finally, step 2808 can be the same as the step 1710 of the process 1700 but performed to determined various of the Pareto optimal points (e.g., a minimum sustainability metric solution, a maximum disinfection solution, and an equal priority sustainability/disinfection solution), according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the step 2802 is incorporated in the step 1704 , or the simulation is performed to determine sets of values of the sustainability metric and the infection risk directly. In such an implementation, step 2802 can be performed to determine energy cost or energy consumption based on the determined values of the sustainability metric.
Referring particularly to FIG. 29 , a process 2900 for performing a Pareto optimization while accounting for the sustainability metric of an HVAC system, the energy cost, and an infection risk is shown, according to some embodiments. Process 2900 includes steps 2902 - 2916 and can be the same as or similar to the steps 1702 - 1716 of process 1700 . Process 2900 differs from the process 1700 in that the process 2900 is performed for three objective function values (the energy cost, the sustainability metric, and the infection risk) instead of only two objective function values (the energy cost and the infection risk).
Particularly, process 2900 includes performing a simulation for each set of the values of the control decision variables to determine sets of values of energy cost, a sustainability metric, and infection risk (step 2904 ), according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, step 2904 is performed by the controller 1110 similarly to step 1704 but for several objective function values (e.g., optimization objectives). In some embodiments, step 2904 is performed using multiple objective functions, namely, an objective function that estimates energy cost based on the control decision variables, an objective function that estimates a sustainability metric based on the control decision variables, and an objective function that estimates or predicts infection risk based on the control decision variables. In some embodiments, the objective function used to predict the sustainability metric is the same as the objective function used to predict the energy cost but with an additional conversion factor or function to convert the energy cost to the sustainability metric.
Process 2900 includes determining which of the sets of values of energy cost, the sustainability metric, and the infection risk are infeasible and which are feasible (step 2906 ), according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the sets of values of energy cost, sustainability metric, and the infection risk are used to construct a surface or 3-d plot. In some embodiments, the step 2906 includes comparing various values of the control decision variables, or values of any of the energy cost, the sustainability metric, or the infection risk to constraints (e.g., user-specified constraints, system operating constraints, etc.) to determine which of the sets of values of the energy cost, the sustainability metric, or the infection risk are feasible or infeasible.
Process 2900 includes determining which of the feasible sets of values of energy cost, the sustainability metric, and the infection risk are Pareto optimal solutions (step 2908 ), according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, step 2908 is performed similarly to step 1708 of process 1700 but also accounting for the sustainability metric. In some embodiments, the Pareto optimal solutions are curves that define multiple Pareto optimal solutions. Process 2900 includes determining, based on the Pareto optimal solutions, a minimum energy cost solution, a maximum disinfection solution, a minimum sustainability metric solution, and an equal priority solution (step 2910 ), according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, step 2910 is similar to step 1710 but also accounts for the sustainability metric. In some embodiments, the Pareto optimal solutions are curves that define multiple Pareto optimal solutions along the surface graph in terms of the minimum energy cost solution, the maximum disinfection solution, the minimum sustainability metric solution, and the equal priority solution. In some embodiments, the equal priority solution is an equal priority between the energy cost, the infection risk, and the sustainability metric.
Process 2900 includes steps 2912 - 2916 that are the same as or similar to steps 1712 - 1716 but also including display and accordingly user selection of options that take into account the sustainability metric. In some embodiments, only one of the sustainability metric or the energy cost is displayed to the user via the display screen, and the user may toggle between the sustainability metric and the energy cost for the different proposed solutions to facilitate proper selection.
Referring to FIG. 30 , another diagram 3000 shows a graph 3002 of different decision variables, and a graph 3004 of corresponding objective function values for each of the different decision variables. The graph 3002 can be the same as or similar to the graph 1302 as described in greater detail above with reference to FIG. 13 . As shown in FIG. 30 , the graph 3002 shows different combinations for a first decision variable (the Y-axis) and a second decision variable (the X-axis) for the HVAC system 300 , illustrated as points 3006 , according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the first decision variable and the second decision variable are minimum temperature setpoint and minimum ventilation setpoint for the HVAC system 300 . It should be understood that the decision variables 3006 are not limited to the minimum temperature setpoint and the minimum ventilation setpoint and may be any other setpoints, operating parameters, etc., such as temperature setpoints, humidity setpoints, comfort parameters, HVAC operating parameters, etc. The points 3006 are shown to include points 3006 a - 30061 , each point corresponding to a different pair of objective function values.
In some embodiments, a simulation is performed using one or more dynamic models to determine one or more corresponding values of Pareto optimization objectives (e.g., values of the sustainability metric and the energy cost) for each of the decision variables, represented by the points 3006 . In some embodiments, the corresponding values of the Pareto optimization objectives are shown as points 3008 , including points 3008 a - 30081 . Each of the points 3008 a - 30081 correspond to one of the points 3006 a - 30061 . In some embodiments, the one or more dynamic models include models that predict energy cost and/or the sustainability metric as a function of both the first decision variable and the second decision variable. In some embodiments, the points 3008 are determined by the dynamic model simulator 1232 based on the different values of the first decision variable and the second decision variable using one or more dynamic models.
The points 3008 can be used by the Pareto optimizer 1236 or the Pareto optimizer 1112 to determine which of the points 3008 are feasible and in-feasible, and to further determine which of the feasible points 3008 are Pareto optimal points in terms of sustainability (e.g., a Pareto optimal point having a lowest value of the sustainability metric), energy cost (e.g., a Pareto optimal point having a lowest value of energy cost), or an equal priority Pareto point that optimizes both the sustainability metric and the energy cost equally, according to some embodiments. In some embodiments, the sustainability metric accounts for operational carbon emissions (e.g., if the Pareto optimization is performed in the context of an operational tool) or accounts for carbon emissions resulting from both operation of the HVAC system 300 and/or installing equipment in the HVAC system 300 (e.g., if the Pareto optimization is performed in the context of a design tool). In some embodiments, the points 3008 are used for selection or determination of the various Pareto optimal points. These Pareto optimal points may be automatically selected for use by the HVAC system 300 or may be presented to a building administrator for selection thereof. Each of the Pareto optimal points corresponds to different values of the decision variables or schedules of decision variables over a time period (e.g., setpoints over a future time period) and selection of one of the Pareto optimal points of the points 3008 results in the selection of the corresponding decision variables or schedules of the decision variables.
Once a particular Pareto optimal point of the Pareto optimal points 3008 are selected, the controller 1110 or the controller 310 generates control signals for the HVAC system 300 to operate the HVAC system 300 according to the selected Pareto optimal point (e.g., according to the corresponding combination of decision variables or the corresponding schedule of the decision variables over a time horizon such as a future time horizon).

Claims
What is claimed is:
1. A controller for heating, ventilation, or air conditioning (HVAC) equipment operable to affect an environmental condition of a building, the controller comprising:
one or more processors; and
memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to perform operations comprising:
obtaining one or more predictive models configured to predict values of an energy control objective and an air quality control objective as a function of control decision variables for the HVAC equipment;
executing a multi-objective optimization process comprising performing multiple different optimizations using the one or more predictive models to produce multiple sets of optimization results, wherein each of the multiple different optimizations is performed using a different set of constraints and produces a different set of the optimization results comprising different values of the control decision variables, the energy control objective, and the air quality control objective;
selecting one or more of the sets of optimization results based on the values of the energy control objective and the air quality control objective; and

### 📜 Full Specification & Deep Scrape Text
Title
Multi-objective optimization operation method of active distribution network considering 5G base station access

Abstract
The invention discloses an Active Distribution Network (ADN) multi-objective optimization operation method considering 5G base station access, which comprises the following steps: taking the minimum system operation cost and the minimum carbon emission as objective functions, and constructing an ADN multi-objective optimization model according to 5G base station operation constraint conditions, renewable Energy (RES) power generation capacity constraint conditions, distribution network tide constraint conditions and system operation safety constraint conditions; adopting an interval analysis method to process the objective function and each constraint condition, and converting the ADN multi-objective optimization model into a deterministic multi-objective optimization model; and solving the deterministic multi-objective optimization model by adopting a non-dominant ordering genetic algorithm to obtain an ADN multi-objective optimization operation scheme considering 5G base station access. According to the scheme, the RES and the 5G base station equipment in the ADN are jointly scheduled, and uncertainty of RES output and communication load is considered by adopting an interval method, so that simultaneous optimization and scientific compromise of system economy and low-carbon benefit can be realized.

Description
Multi-objective optimization operation method of active power distribution network considering 5G base station access
Technical Field
The invention relates to the technical field of energy optimization and scheduling, in particular to a multi-objective optimization operation method of an active power distribution network considering 5G base station access.
Background
At present, the improvement of the duty ratio and the utilization efficiency of Renewable Energy (RES) in terminal energy consumption and the construction of a novel power system mainly based on new energy become important subjects of the construction of an energy system in China under the targets of carbon reaching peak and carbon neutralization. In recent years, an Active Distribution Network (ADN) technology creates good conditions for large-scale distributed renewable energy grid connection, but is inherently limited by the current distribution network structure and renewable energy intermittence, in order to realize full utilization of RES under an ADN framework, a large amount of flexible resources must be mined to participate in operation scheduling of a power system so as to stabilize the influence of power generation and massive access of RES on system power balance.
With the rapid popularization of the fifth generation mobile communication technology, the 5G base station has gradually developed into an important emerging load in the power distribution network. In the operation process, through carrying out scientific scheduling management to power supply and consumer in the 5G basic station, interactive response potential that the 5G basic station contains can be fully exerted, considerable flexibility support is provided for the electric wire netting, and finally the purpose that the distribution network consumes renewable energy and carbon emission reduction is improved when reducing basic station self electricity consumption cost is reached. At present, the problem of optimizing operation of the active power distribution network containing the RES at home and abroad does not relate to the influence of the 5G base station and the flexibility potential thereof. To effectively exert the low-carbon enabling potential of the 5G base station in the operation of the active power distribution network, the influence of the information domain attribute on the operation of the 5G base station needs to be deeply considered, and a refined description model facing to the adjustable characteristic of the operation of the 5G base station under the energy and information multi-domain coupling is established. Furthermore, to ensure the effectiveness of the resulting operating scheme, prior studies mostly employ stochastic optimization or robust optimization methods to account for uncertainties in ADN, such as RES-forces or fluctuations in load demand. In practical applications, random optimization must use a large amount of reliable historical data to extract accurate descriptions about uncertainty factors, while robust optimization generally focuses on uncertainty scenes that are most unfavorable for system target implementation, and the resulting operation strategies tend to be too conservative. The above-described approach does not meet well the need for ADN operation decisions that are aimed at facilitating RES utilization as a primary goal.
Therefore, a multi-objective interval optimal scheduling method for improving low-carbon benefits of the ADN by using the operation flexibility of the 5G base station is needed, and the cooperative optimization of the system economy and the low-carbon benefits is achieved by jointly scheduling RES in the ADN and 5G base station equipment.
Disclosure of Invention
Therefore, the invention provides a multi-objective optimization operation method of an active power distribution network considering 5G base station access, which integrates the flexibility of the energy consumption management of the 5G base station and the flexible scheduling capability of an internal energy storage battery into ADN operation scheduling by considering the energy consumption management of the 5G base station and the flexible scheduling capability of the internal energy storage battery, and utilizes an interval method to account for the influence of RES output and communication load uncertainty on an operation strategy so as to achieve collaborative optimization of system economy and low-carbon benefits.
The invention provides a multi-objective optimization operation method of an active power distribution network considering 5G base station access, which comprises the following steps:
step 1: establishing a 5G base station operation characteristic model comprising the energy consumption characteristic, the communication characteristic and the internal energy storage battery characteristic of the 5G base station;
step 2: obtaining 5G base station operation constraint conditions according to the 5G base station operation characteristic model, obtaining renewable energy power generation output constraint conditions according to the output value of the renewable energy distributed power supply, obtaining active power distribution network parameters, and obtaining power distribution network tide constraint conditions;
Step 3: taking the minimum running cost and the minimum carbon emission of the active power distribution network with the 5G base station as objective functions, and constructing an active power distribution network multi-objective optimization model with uncertainty parameters according to the 5G base station running constraint condition, the renewable energy power generation output constraint condition, the power distribution network tide constraint condition and the system running safety constraint condition;
step 4: processing the objective function and each constraint condition by adopting an interval analysis method, and converting the multi-objective optimization model of the active power distribution network containing uncertainty parameters into a deterministic multi-objective optimization model;
step 5: and solving the deterministic multi-target optimization model by adopting a non-dominant ordering genetic algorithm to obtain a multi-target optimization operation scheme of the active power distribution network considering 5G base station access.

According to the scheme, the multi-target interval optimization operation method of the active power distribution network with low-carbon energization of the 5G base station is considered, the influence of uncertainty in the RES output and the 5G communication load is comprehensively considered, and the cooperative scheduling of a distributed power supply in a system, a start-stop plan of 5G base station equipment and an energy storage battery is realized, so that the ADN operation economy and the low-carbon benefit are optimized. Because the response characteristic of the 5G base station is influenced by the number of base station transceivers to be started, the operation parameters of the energy storage battery and other factors, on the premise of meeting the service quality of user communication, the ADN tide distribution can be improved, the network loss can be reduced, and the consumption space of the power grid to the RES can be enlarged by carrying out joint optimization on the operation states of the base station equipment and the energy storage battery. The interval optimization method is adopted in the scheme, so that the obtained decision scheme is flexible, has optimality and risk resistance capacity and has good engineering value on the basis of fully respecting subjective preference of a decision maker.

Detailed Description
Exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure will be described in more detail below with reference to the accompanying drawings. While exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure are shown in the drawings, it should be understood that the present disclosure may be embodied in various forms and should not be limited to the embodiments set forth herein. Rather, these embodiments are provided so that this disclosure will be thorough and complete, and will fully convey the scope of the disclosure to those skilled in the art.
The massive access of 5G base stations provides new possibilities for the low-carbon development of future power systems. By exciting the 5G base station to participate in demand response and incorporating the 5G base station into an existing Active Distribution Network (ADN) operation framework, the consumption and efficient utilization of Renewable Energy Sources (RES) can be promoted while the self electricity cost of the 5G base station is reduced. In this regard, a multi-objective optimization operation method of an active power distribution network considering 5G base station access is provided. On the basis of in-depth analysis of interaction modes of the 5G base station and the power distribution network, an ADN multi-objective optimization operation model containing the 5G base station is constructed. The model can realize simultaneous optimization and scientific compromise of system economy and low-carbon benefits by jointly scheduling RES and 5G base station equipment in ADN and taking uncertainty of RES output and communication load into consideration by adopting an interval method. And solving the problem by combining an equivalent transformation and non-dominant sorting genetic algorithm based on interval analysis, wherein the result of the calculation example analysis proves the effectiveness of the method.
The equipment of the 5G base station mainly comprises a communication device and a power supply device. The communication equipment mainly comprises an Active Antenna Unit (AAU), a baseband processing unit (BBU) and signal transmission equipment (such as optical fibers), and the power supply equipment mainly comprises a power supply and an energy storage battery which are connected with the power distribution network. The energy storage battery can ensure the reliability of communication service to be used as an emergency working power supply when the power supply of the power grid is interrupted, so that a wide space is provided for the 5G base station to participate in the power grid interaction. Specifically, on one hand, the 5G base station operator can adjust its own power consumption in real time through various operation control means (such as transceiver start-stop arrangement, power regulation and control, etc.) to participate in the power demand side response; on the other hand, the 5G base station can also utilize an internal energy storage battery to charge and discharge, participate in the power grid optimization operation on the premise of guaranteeing the self power supply and communication service quality, and improve the digestion capability of the system to RES.
In order to determine the action mechanism of the flexibility of the 5G base station on ADN carbon emission reduction, a System Dynamics (SD) method can be adopted to analyze key influence factors and correlations of the key influence factors on the ADN low-carbon benefits of the 5G base station, so that an ADN multi-objective optimization operation model considering the low-carbon energization of the 5G base station is constructed. The SD theory considers that the dynamic structure and feedback mode of the system determine the action mode and the characteristics of the system, the system evolves according to a certain rule under the action of internal and external power and constraint factors, and the model constructed by the SD method can effectively reflect the influence relation of dynamic feedback among the factors of the system.
By quantifying the costs involved in the subject, and expressing the causal relationships as a function, an SD model can be built, and fig. 1 shows a causal relationship diagram with 5G base station ADN low carbon benefits according to one embodiment of the present invention. As shown in fig. 1, "+" is that variable X increases (decreases) resulting in variable Y increasing (decreases); "-" is that the variable X increases (decreases) resulting in the variable Y decreasing (increases). It can be seen that the expected carbon emission of the ADN containing the 5G base station is mainly influenced by endogenous factors such as RES generating capacity, 5G base station energy consumption, and charging/discharging of the 5G base station energy storage battery in the system; in addition, the system is closely related to external factors such as policies and system operation policies. The above factors act together so that the carbon emission reduction effect of the 5G base station interaction response on ADN can be summarized in 3 aspects:
1) The self energy efficiency is improved, and the system load demand is reduced
The huge electricity consumption generated by the operation of the massive 5G base stations can obviously increase the overall load demand of the power distribution system, and further the carbon emission of the power generation side is increased. The 5G base station can reduce the self electricity consumption requirement and improve the system energy efficiency by technical management means such as base station dormancy, transceiver shutdown, downlink power control and the like under the condition of ensuring the communication service quality, thereby indirectly reducing the carbon emission of the power generation side.
2) Improving the power flow distribution of the power grid and improving the power transmission efficiency
Large scale RES generation grid-connection exacerbates power and voltage fluctuations in the distribution network. This aspect will affect the level of loss of the distribution network; on the other hand, to ensure that grid security constraints are met, system operators sometimes have to resort to wind/light curtailment, thereby reducing RES resource utilization. By carrying out power management and flexible charging and discharging of the energy storage battery on the 5G base station, the power flow/voltage distribution in the power distribution network can be obviously changed, the network loss can be reduced, the electric energy transmission efficiency can be improved, the line blockage can be effectively relieved, and the grid-connected digestion capacity of the power distribution network to RES power generation can be improved.
3) Improving the matching of power supply and demand and promoting the utilization of renewable energy sources
For partial RES power generation (such as wind power), the output has obvious anti-load regulation characteristics in time sequence. Under ADN, this timing mismatch of power supply and demand will seriously hamper the system's efficiency of the consumption and utilization of renewable energy sources. And the interaction potential of the 5G base station is utilized in operation scheduling, the base station is enabled to increase electricity purchasing from a power grid in the RES output peak period through the energy storage battery, and the electricity purchasing from the power grid is reduced in the RES power generation valley period, so that the utilization efficiency of the RES can be effectively improved, and further the system is promoted to realize carbon emission reduction.
Fig. 2 shows a flow diagram of an active distribution network multi-objective optimization operation method 100 that considers 5G base station access according to one embodiment of the invention.
As shown in fig. 1, an active power distribution network multi-objective optimization operation method 100 considering 5G base station access starts with step S110, and a 5G base station operation characteristic model including a 5G base station energy consumption characteristic, a communication characteristic, and an internal energy storage battery characteristic is established.
The energy consumption related to the 5G base station comprises two aspects of static power consumption and dynamic power consumption. The static power consumption refers to the energy demand independent of the service load and the output transmission power, and mainly consists of the fixed loss of a power supply system and a BBU baseband unit signal processing and cooling system; while dynamic power consumption refers to the energy requirements associated with the 5G traffic load as a function of the 5G base station output transmission power. And then, executing step S130, and constructing an active power distribution network multi-objective optimization model containing uncertainty parameters according to 5G base station operation constraint conditions, renewable energy power generation output constraint conditions, power distribution network trend constraint conditions and system operation safety constraint conditions by taking the minimum operation cost and the minimum carbon emission of the active power distribution network containing 5G base stations as objective functions.
In view of the flexibility of the 5G base station and the potential contribution of the 5G base station to the low-carbon development of a future power distribution network, the scheme takes the effect of the participation interaction response of the 5G base station on promoting the consumption of the distributed RES into consideration, considers the 5G base station as a flexible resource to be brought into a power distribution network operation scheduling model, and determines the optimal coordinated operation strategy of the distributed power supply and the 5G load resource in the power distribution network by combining factors such as the power supply cost, the operation safety and the carbon emission of the system.
For power distribution network operators, the optimized operation of ADN is required to reduce the economic cost of system operation as much as possible, and the utilization of RES is also required to be increased as much as possible, so that the carbon emission of the system is reduced. Under the prior art level and market conditions, the economic efficiency and the carbon emission reduction target implementation have natural contradiction, so that the economic efficiency and the carbon emission reduction target implementation can be generalized into a typical multi-target optimization problem to actively comprise a 5G base stationThe minimum running cost and the minimum carbon emission of the power distribution network are double targets, a multi-target optimization model is built, and the objective functions comprise a minimum running cost objective function min C OPT And a minimum target function min C of carbon emission CA ：
The operation cost of the 5G base station ADN mainly comprises the electricity purchasing cost of the external market, the electricity purchasing cost of the internal distributed power generation and the energy storage loss cost of the 5G base station, and the specific calculation formula is as follows:
Wherein C is OPT For the system operation cost, T is the operation period, N DG In the case of a distributed set of power supply nodes, cost of purchasing power for distributed power supply in period t, < >> Electricity price for the time t from the external market,/-for> For the actual output value of the a-th distributed power supply node in the period t, P t Grid For the power purchase of the power distribution network in the period t, deltat is the duration of a single period, the unit is hours, and Sigma ch 、σ dis The loss cost corresponding to the charge and discharge of the energy storage battery in the 5G base station is respectively +.> And respectively charging and discharging power of the energy storage battery of the ith base station in the period t.
In order to comprehensively reflect carbon emission reduction benefits brought by the participation demand response of the 5G base station to the power distribution system, the minimum carbon emission of the system is taken as another target of the optimized operation model. The carbon emission of the system is directly related to the fossil fuel consumption at the power generation side, the CO2 emission in the operation scheduling period is equal to the electricity purchased from the external market multiplied by the coal consumption coefficient of unit power generation and the carbon emission coefficient at the power generation side, and the specific calculation formula is as follows:
wherein C is CA For the CO2 emission in the operation scheduling period, epsilon represents the carbon emission corresponding to the unit coal consumption power generation; f is a coal consumption coefficient corresponding to unit power generation amount in the external power grid.
The constraint conditions of the multi-objective optimization model mainly comprise 4 aspects of 5G base station operation characteristic constraint, RES power generation output constraint, system tide constraint and operation safety constraint. Decision variables in the model include: electric power purchase P from external market by ADN of each period t Grid Power of RES generation Control parameter related to 5G base station operation +.> α i,j,t 、 And 5G base station energy storage battery charging and discharging power +.> To solve the multi-objective optimization model of the active power distribution network, the numerical value of each parameter in the model needs to be determined in advance. For some of the parameters, such as the energy storage battery damage cost, the carbon emission coefficient, the coal consumption coefficient and the like, the value of the parameters can be determined by a scientific prediction method. For another part of parameters, such as RES power generation capacity and user real-time communication load, due to the limitation of prediction means and prediction precision, a decision maker often has difficulty in obtaining accurate predicted values of the parameters in advance, so that significant uncertainty is brought to model solving.
The two most common methods currently used to address the problem of optimization of uncertainty-containing parameters are stochastic optimization and robust optimization. The random optimization is to refine feature distribution about uncertainty factors by using a statistical method on the basis of a large amount of historical data, and accordingly represent the influence of the uncertainty factors on system decisions by generating a series of deterministic scene sets. But scheduling control in both power and traffic will be involved for 5G containing base station ADN operation. The user's data usage behavior is more random, either in time or space, than in power demand. In addition, the complex characteristics of high heterogeneity, dynamic evolution with time and the like are also shown. It is often difficult for system operators to obtain accurate probability distributions for data demand parameters, which causes the random optimization approach to face significant hurdles in the research herein. The most unfavorable uncertainty scene is realized on the system target by the robust optimization method, and the obtained result is generally conservative, so that the low-carbon enabling potential of the 5G base station resource is difficult to fully mine.
Aiming at the problems, the invention adopts an interval method to model each uncertainty factor (namely RES power generation output and communication load) in the system operation.
And then, executing step S140, and processing the objective function and each constraint condition by adopting an interval analysis method to convert the active power distribution network multi-objective optimization model containing the uncertainty parameters into a deterministic multi-objective optimization model.

Through the processing, the original multi-objective interval optimization model containing uncertain parameters is converted into a conventional deterministic multi-objective optimization problem.
And finally, executing step S150, and solving the deterministic multi-objective optimization model by adopting a non-dominant sorting genetic algorithm to obtain the multi-objective optimization operation scheme of the active power distribution network considering the 5G base station access.
FIG. 3 illustrates a flow chart for solving a multi-objective optimization model using a non-dominant ordered genetic algorithm and interval analysis, according to one embodiment of the invention. The flow is as follows:
1) And initializing parameters. And reading input data of a system, and setting relevant parameters of a non-dominant sorting genetic algorithm NSGA-II, wherein the relevant parameters comprise population scale, maximum evolutionary algebra, crossover factors, mutation factors and the like.
2) A population is randomly generated. The initial population, i.e., the initial solution set, is generated by a random function.
3) For each group of individuals, the interval analysis method is adopted to calculate the interval upper and lower boundaries of each objective function and constraint conditions.
4) And calculating the midpoint and the radius of the objective function and the possibility of all constraints, and realizing deterministic conversion of the original model.
5) And aiming at the transformed deterministic multi-objective optimization problem, calculating the fitness of individuals in various groups. In NSGA-II, individual fitness includes the number of non-dominant layers and the degree of congestion of each individual layer. Layering the population by adopting a rapid non-dominant sorting method, namely selecting all non-inferior solution individuals in the current population as a 1 st non-dominant layer; searching for a new non-inferior solution in individuals outside the dominant layer as a 2 nd non-dominant layer; this process is repeated until all population individuals have completed the hierarchical ordering and the number of non-dominant layers is determined therefrom. On this basis, the crowdedness of each individual layer is calculated using the following formula:
n d ＝n d +f m (p+1)-f m (p-1)
wherein f m (p+1),f m (p-1) is the value of the objective function m corresponding to population individuals p+1 and p-1, respectively, n d Is the distance between individuals in the population.
6) And judging whether a convergence condition is reached. Taking the maximum evolution algebra as a convergence condition, and outputting a Pareto optimal solution set if the evolution algebra reaches the specified value; otherwise, selecting, crossing and mutating the parent population to form offspring population individuals; and then forming a next generation population according to individual fitness based on elite retention strategy, and returning to the step 3) until convergence condition is reached. And finally, obtaining the multi-objective optimal operation scheme of the active power distribution network considering the 5G base station access.
The invention comprehensively considers the influence of uncertainty in the RES output and the 5G communication load, and achieves the simultaneous optimization of ADN operation economy and low-carbon benefit by the cooperative scheduling of the start-stop plan and the energy storage battery of the distributed power supply and the 5G base station equipment in the system. The specific effects are as follows:
1) Under the existing power generation structure, the ADN containing the 5G base station has specific contradiction between the operation economic cost and the carbon emission, and the flexible response capability of the 5G base station is utilized to participate in power grid side dispatching, so that the power system can be helped to improve the renewable energy consumption and utilization efficiency, and considerable low-carbon benefits are brought.
2) The response characteristic of the 5G base station is influenced by the number of base station transceivers to be started, the operation parameters of the energy storage battery and other factors, and on the premise of meeting the service quality of user communication, the ADN tide distribution can be improved, the network loss can be reduced, and the consumption space of the power grid to the RES can be enlarged by carrying out joint optimization on the operation states of the base station equipment and the energy storage battery.
3) The interval optimization method can make the obtained decision scheme flexible and have optimality and risk resistance capability on the basis of fully respecting subjective preference of a decision maker, and has good engineering value.

### 📜 Full Specification & Deep Scrape Text
Title
A distributed drive electric vehicle drive system multi-objective optimization method and system

Abstract
Translated from Chinese
The invention relates to a multi-objective optimization method and system for a drive system of a distributed drive electric vehicle. The method includes: obtaining the optimal torque distribution model; obtaining the current longitudinal speed of the vehicle, and determining the current torque value of each hub motor of the vehicle according to the optimal torque distribution model; completing the energy consumption calculation of the whole vehicle in real time according to the torque value of the hub motor, and at the same time The unsprung mass is obtained, and the energy consumption of the whole vehicle and the calculated unsprung mass are used as optimization goals to achieve the optimal matching design of the size of the front and rear hub motors of the vehicle. The present invention aims at the demand for economy and power of the distributed drive electric vehicle, comprehensively considers the test working conditions, the target performance requirements of the whole vehicle and the optimal torque distribution control strategy, and reasonably selects the power of the four hub motors through a multi-objective optimization design method And size configuration, in order to achieve the optimal matching design of the drive system of distributed drive electric vehicles while meeting the requirements of the vehicle's maximum speed, maximum gradeability, acceleration capability and energy consumption.

Description
Multi-objective optimization method and system for driving system of distributed driving electric automobile
Technical Field
The invention relates to the field of optimization of electric automobile driving systems, in particular to a multi-objective optimization method and system for a distributed driving electric automobile driving system.
Background
In the prior art, various optimization matching methods are disclosed for an electric vehicle driving system. In the prior art, aiming at the process of matching test of a power system of a biaxial drive electric vehicle, a test method and a test device for matching of the power system of the biaxial drive electric vehicle are provided (patent CN 106525450A). According to vehicle configuration parameters, a vehicle dynamic model is constructed, and vehicle load is calculated according to the current rotating speed and torque; according to the target speed, the required torque is calculated, whether the vehicle enters a driving state or a mechanical or regenerative braking state is judged, throttle signals of all driving motors are distributed to achieve the target speed, or the mechanical braking torque is simulated and is superposed with the vehicle load, and the regenerative braking torque distributes braking depth signals of all motors to achieve the target speed.
However, the scheme only considers the vehicle working state, does not carry out optimal design on a driving system according to the test working condition, and does not consider the optimal distribution strategy of the hydraulic-electric composite braking torque. This method is not applicable to distributed drive configuration vehicles.
A power matching method for an electric vehicle is also disclosed in the prior art (patent CN 103568868A), which first determines the number of motors according to the driving mode adopted by the vehicle type. And then listing main parameters including vehicle parameters, motor parameters and battery parameters. And then carrying out preliminary power matching according to the parameters in the list. And then, determining the number of the battery modules according to the primary matching result, and then determining the transmission ratio of the transmission system to finish the power matching of the pure electric vehicle.
However, the scheme does not carry out drive system optimization design according to test working conditions, and is only suitable for a single-motor centralized drive electric automobile.
In a parameter matching method (patent CN 107862325A) of a double-basic-speed motor of a pure electric truck disclosed in the prior art, firstly, the whole vehicle parameters of the pure electric truck are obtained, and then the matching of the rated parameters of a low-basic-speed motor is completed, wherein the matching comprises the rated power P v Rated speed n b Rated torque T high (ii) a Finally, matching the peak parameters of the high-base-speed motor, including the peak power P max Peak torque T max Peak rotational speed n max (ii) a And completing the parameter matching of the double-base-speed motor.
However, the scheme aims at parameter matching of the pure electric truck double-base-speed motor, the parameter matching is only carried out through the design target performance of the whole truck, and the actual test working condition is not considered. This method is not applicable to distributed drive configuration vehicles.
In the electric vehicle matching optimization method based on multi-objective programming (patent CN 109033531A) disclosed in the prior art, firstly, the whole vehicle performance index and key parameters of the electric vehicle are determined; then, performing initial model selection calculation on the power system through a physical formula, and determining various model selection schemes of the power system by combining factors such as market and the like; and then, evaluating the whole vehicle performance corresponding to different power matching schemes by using cruise software simulation.
However, the scheme performs drive system optimization design according to the test working condition, an optimal torque distribution strategy is not adopted, and meanwhile, the scheme is not suitable for a distributed drive electric automobile.
The parameter matching and optimizing scheme of the electric logistics vehicle driving motor disclosed in the prior art (patent CN 108491670A) includes the following basic steps: the method comprises the following steps of primarily selecting basic parameters of a driving motor according to the dynamic requirement of the electric logistics vehicle and the requirement of the driving working condition; establishing a driving motor parameter multi-target optimization model which takes dynamic property and economy as optimization targets and takes rated power, rated rotating speed and rated torque of a driving motor as optimization variables; and solving the multi-target optimization model of the parameters of the driving motor by using an artificial ant colony algorithm to obtain a parameter optimization matching scheme of the driving motor.
However, the optimal design of the driving system is carried out according to the test working condition and the performance requirement of the whole vehicle, the optimal torque distribution strategy is not considered, and the method is not suitable for distributed driving electric vehicles.
In summary, the matching method of the existing electric vehicle driving system only considers the test working condition and the target performance requirement of the whole vehicle, and is only suitable for the single-motor or double-motor driving scheme.
Therefore, a multi-objective optimization scheme of a distributed driving electric vehicle driving system is provided, so that the optimal matching design of the distributed driving electric vehicle driving system is realized while the requirements of the highest vehicle speed, the maximum climbing gradient and the acceleration capability of the vehicle and the optimal energy consumption under different test working conditions are met, and a technical problem to be solved in the field is urgently solved.
Disclosure of Invention
The invention aims to provide a multi-objective optimization method and a multi-objective optimization system for a distributed driving electric automobile driving system, which aim to achieve optimal matching design of the distributed driving electric automobile driving system by taking optimal energy consumption and unsprung mass under different test working conditions as targets while meeting the highest vehicle speed, the maximum climbing gradient and the acceleration capacity of a vehicle.
In order to achieve the purpose, the invention provides the following scheme:
a multi-objective optimization method for a driving system of a distributed driving electric automobile comprises the following steps:
obtaining an optimal torque distribution model; the optimal torque distribution model takes the longitudinal speed of the automobile as input and takes the torque of each hub motor of the automobile as output;
acquiring the current longitudinal speed of the automobile, and determining the current torque value of each hub motor of the automobile according to the optimal torque distribution model;
determining the energy consumption and unsprung mass of the whole vehicle according to the torque value of each hub motor, and determining the size of each hub motor by taking the energy consumption and the unsprung mass of the whole vehicle as optimization targets;
and finishing the control of the automobile driving system according to the size of each hub motor.

and determining the torque demand of the whole vehicle according to the test working conditions (generally standard test working conditions such as NEDC, WLTC and the like), target whole vehicle dynamic design index parameters (the highest vehicle speed, the maximum climbing gradient and the acceleration time of 0-100 km/h) and a vehicle model. Determination of the torque requirement of the whole vehicle: according to the speed and acceleration sampling points in the test working condition, inputting a vehicle model to obtain the longitudinal force demand of the whole vehicle, and substituting the longitudinal force of the whole vehicle into a single-wheel dynamic model to obtain the total torque demand of the whole vehicle.

Determination of the motor efficiency model: the motor efficiency model of the invention is the motor efficiency Map and the loss Map, on the premise of not changing the topology scheme of the existing hub motor, the hub motor with different peak output torques can be obtained by changing the axial and radial sizes of the motor stator, and the efficiency and the loss Map characteristics are basically unchanged, and the stretching transformation is only carried out in the torque axis direction, and the motor quality can also be determined according to the axial and radial sizes of the stator.
For given sizes (axial and radial sizes) of the front and rear hub motors, a front and rear hub motor efficiency model can be obtained, then according to the total torque (including driving and braking torques) requirements of the whole vehicle output by the vehicle model and the front and rear hub motor efficiency model, the total energy consumption of the four motors is the minimum as an optimization target, the front and rear hub optimal torque distribution strategy is determined, and the optimal torque distribution Map is obtained.
