TECHNICAL FIELD This patent relates to quantum computing, and more particularly to preparing and evolving arrays of atoms for quantum computing.
BACKGROUND Fully controlled coherent many-body quantum systems as quantum simulators can provide unique insights into the role of strongly interconnected quantum systems and quantum entanglement, allowing the realization and study of new states of matter, even far from equilibrium. These systems also form the basis for the realization of quantum information processors. The basic building blocks of such processors have been demonstrated in systems of several coupled qubits, but it is challenging to increase the number of coherently coupled qubits to perform tasks beyond the reach of modern classical machines. Moreover, existing systems lack the coherence and/or quantum nonlinearities to achieve fully quantum dynamics.
Neutral atoms can serve as building blocks for large-scale quantum systems, as described in more detail in US Pat. No. 5,399,363 entitled "NEUTRAL ATOM QUANTUM INFORMATION PROCESSOR." The large-scale quantum systems can be well isolated from the environment, allowing for long-lasting quantum memory. Initialization, control, and readout of the internal and motional states of the large-scale quantum systems are achieved by resonant methods developed over the past 40 years. Arrays with many identical atoms can be rapidly assembled while maintaining optical control of single atoms. These bottom-up approaches are complementary to methods involving optical lattices loaded with ultracold atoms prepared by evaporative cooling, typically resulting in atomic separations of a few micrometers. Controllable interactions between atoms can be introduced to use these arrays for quantum simulations and quantum information processing. This can be achieved by coherent coupling to highly excited Rydberg states, which exhibit strong, long-range interactions. This approach provides a powerful foundation for many applications, such as rapid multiqubit quantum gates, quantum simulations of Ising-type spin models with up to 250 spins, and studies of collective behavior in mesoscopic ensembles. The short coherence times and relatively low gate fidelity associated with such Rydberg excitations are challenging. This imperfect coherence may limit the quality of quantum simulations and cloud the prospects for neutral atomic quantum information processing. Limited coherence is also evident at the level of single isolated atomic qubits.
US Patent No. 5,999,336 describes exemplary methods and systems for quantum computing. These systems and methods may include first trapping individual atoms and arranging them into a specific geometric configuration of multiple atoms, for example using an acoustic optical deflector. This precise arrangement of the individual atoms assists in encoding the quantum computing problem. One or more of the arranged atoms may then be excited into a Rydberg state, which may cause interactions between the atoms in the array. The system may then be developed in a controlled environment. Finally, the state of the atoms may be read out to observe the solution to the encoded problem. Further examples include providing high fidelity and coherent control of assembled arrays of atoms.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION Optimization algorithms are used to find the best solution given a particular criterion for a particular problem. Combinatorial optimization involves identifying the optimal solution to a problem given a finite set of solutions. Quantum optimization is a technique for solving combinatorial optimization problems by using the controlled dynamics of quantum many-body systems, such as a 2D array of individual atoms, where each of the individual atoms can be referred to as a "qubit" or "spin." Quantum algorithms can combinatorially solve difficult optimization problems by encoding such problems into classical ground states of programmable quantum systems, such as spin models. The quantum algorithms are then designed to use quantum evolution to drive the system to this ground state, so that subsequent measurements reveal the solution. In other words, the problem can be encoded by placing qubits in a desired configuration with desired interactions, which encode the constraints dictated by the optimization problem. If properly encoded, the ground state of the many-body system contains the solution to the optimization problem. Thus, the problem can be solved by driving the many-body system to its ground state by an evolution process.
Without being bound by theory, assuming perfect control of the interactions between qubits, it is possible to encode nondeterministic polynomial ("NP")-complete optimization problems into the ground states of such systems. However, in most realizations, not all interactions are fully programmable. Instead, such interactions are determined by properties of the specific physical realization, such as but not limited to locality, geometric connectivity, or controllability, which either constrain the types of problems that can be efficiently realized or mean that substantial overhead is required for their realization. Thus, one of the challenges in understanding and evaluating quantum optimization algorithms involves designing methods for encoding specific and larger classes of combinatorial problems in physical systems in an efficient and natural way.
In some implementations, quantum optimization may involve (1) encoding a problem by controlling the positions of individual qubits in a quantum system given a particular type and strength of interaction between pairs of qubits, and (2) manipulating the dynamics of the qubits in the quantum system through an evolution process, so that their evolved final state provides a solution to the optimization problem. Manipulating the dynamics of the qubits to a ground state solution to the optimization problem may be achieved through a number of different processes, such as, but not limited to, the adiabatic principle in quantum annealing algorithms (QAA), or more general variability approaches, such as, but not limited to, quantum approximate optimization algorithms (QAOA). Such algorithms may tackle computationally challenging problems that are beyond the capabilities of classical computers. However, the heuristic nature of these algorithms poses challenges in predicting their actual performance, requiring experimental testing. Moreover, such systems, in their full generality, are inefficient and difficult to implement due to the practical constraints mentioned above, and may be used for only a subset of optimization problems.
Some aspects of the present disclosure relate to systems and methods for arranging qubits in a programmable array that can encode or approximately encode a wider set of optimization problems in an efficient manner. In some embodiments, an even number of chains of nearby "ancillary" qubits are used to encode interactions between distant qubits by linking distant qubits with chains of ancillary qubits, e.g., as described in more detail with respect to FIG. 2A. As described in more detail throughout this disclosure, these chains of "ancillary" qubits can be used to encode interactions between specific "vertex" qubits rather than other vertex qubits, and can be used to reduce the strength of long-range interactions between two vertex qubits that are not intended to be linked by an edge. In some embodiments, the effects of long-range interactions can be further reduced by introducing detuning parameters into the selected control technique to selectively control the interactions between specific qubits. For example, for corner and junction qubits, the detuning patterns described in this disclosure can reduce the effects of long-range interactions such that the ground state of the system is an optimal solution to the encoded problem. The techniques described herein may enable efficient encoding of a larger set of optimization problems beyond simple unit pie graphs.
Some further or alternative aspects of the present disclosure relate to systems and methods for coherently manipulating the internal states of qubits, including excitations. In some embodiments, techniques are disclosed that can be used to evolve encoded problems and find optimal (or approximately optimal) solutions. For example, embodiments of the present disclosure relate to optimal variability parameters and strategies for implementing quantum approximate optimization algorithms ("QAOA"), some embodiments of which are described, for example, with respect to FIG. 14A. For example, embodiments include heuristics for classical feedback loops that can improve performance of brute-force QAOA implementations. In some embodiments, these strategies are implemented at least as well, if not better, than existing algorithms. Although some aspects of the present disclosure focus on implementations that use QAOA to solve MaxCut combinatorial problems, the disclosed techniques are not limited thereto.
Exemplary Optimization Problems and Encodings In some embodiments, certain types of optimization problems may be encoded using an arrangement of qubits. For example, FIGS. 1A-1E show exemplary diagrams for encoding and finding solutions to optimization problems using an array of qubits according to some embodiments. FIG. 1A shows aspects of the Rydberg blockade mechanism and maximal independent set on a unit circle graph according to some embodiments. One exemplary optimization problem that may be solved using the techniques described in this disclosure is the maximal independent set ("MIS") problem. Given a graph G having vertices V and edges E, an independent set may be defined as a subset of vertices whose pairs are not connected by an edge. FIG. 1A shows an exemplary graph having vertices such as 102, 104. The vertices 102, 104 may be connected via edges such as edge 106. The computational task of the MIS problem is to find the largest such set, called a maximal independent set (MIS). As shown in the graph of FIG. 1A, the maximal independent set is indicated via the black vertices, such as 102, none of which are connected. In the example of FIG. 1A, the size of the maximum independent set is 6. Determining whether the size of the MIS is greater than a given integer a for any graph G is a well-known NP-complete problem. Moreover, even approximating the size of the MIS is an NP-hard problem. In some embodiments, the MIS problem is also equivalent to the maximum clique problem and the minimum vertex cover problem. Thus, a solution to the MIS problem constitutes a solution to the corresponding maximum clique problem and the minimum vertex cover problem.
Without being bound by theory, the embodiment of FIG. 1A may be referred to as a unit circle ("UD") graph. A UD graph is a geometric graph in which vertices are arranged on a 2D plane and are connected if their pairwise distance is less than a unit length r. In other words, a UD graph is a graph in which any two vertices within distance r of each other are connected by an edge, e.g., vertices 102, 104 are connected via edge 106. Vertex 108 is too far from vertices 102, 104 to be connected to it using an edge. The MIS problem on UD graphs (UD-MIS) is still NP-complete and can be used to find real-world situations in various industrial domains ranging from, e.g., wireless network design to map labelling.

By changing the detuning and Rabi frequency over time, a quantum evolution can occur that changes the system from an initial state to a final state, which may contain a solution (or one or more approximate solutions) to the encoded problem. As noted above, under such conditions, for qubits closer than r B (the Rydberg blockade radius), it is energetically favorable for one of the qubits to remain in the |0> state. For example, when U>Δ>0, the Hamiltonian H P energetically favors each spin to be in state |1>, unless the pair of spins is connected by an edge (i.e., within the Rydberg radius). Thus, in the ground state of the Hamiltonian H P , only the vertices in the MIS are in state |1>. Such states may be referred to as MIS-states, and H P may be referred to as the MIS-Hamiltonian. In some embodiments, the NP-complete decision problem of MIS amounts to determining whether the ground state energy of H 2 P is lower than −αΔ.
In some embodiments, a quantum annealing algorithm ("QAA") can be used to evolve a quantum state from an initial state to a final state that encodes a solution to an optimization problem. For example, a simple QAA can be used to evolve a quantum state from an initial state to a final state that encodes a solution to an optimization problem.

The present invention describes the transition between spin states |0> and |1> controlled by a laser beam having a detuning Δ<0. For detuning Δ<0, the ground state of the Hamiltonian H P is a trivial state in which all qubits are in the |0> state. For detuning Δ>0, the ground state of H P is an MIS state in which qubits in state |1> form an MIS. By slowly varying Ω and Δ in a time-dependent manner, for example as shown in FIGS. 1E and 1D, respectively, the trivial ground state (Δ<0, Ω=0) in which all qubits are in |0> can be adiabatically coupled to a final state (Δ>0, Ω=0) that encodes an MIS, and the qubits remain in the solution to the optimization problem. Note that in general, such a procedure may include transitions across vanishing energy gaps, as discussed in more detail throughout this disclosure. Exemplary and non-limiting aspects of the simulation are described in more detail below in the section entitled "Quantum Annealing for Random UD-MIS".
In some embodiments, MIS problems can be implemented using Rydberg interactions between individual atoms. For example, as discussed in more detail in PCT/US18/42080, graphs such as those shown in FIG. 1A can be implemented using a two-level qubit, the state of which is shown in FIG. 1B according to some embodiments. Using optical tweezers, atoms (qubits) can be individually and deterministically positioned in fully programmable arrays in one, two and even three dimensions. Such systems can use individually trapped, uniformly excited neutral atoms that interact via the so-called Rydberg blockade mechanism. Each atom is a qubit with an internal ground state |0> and a highly excited, long-lasting Rydberg state |1>.
, which can be coherently manipulated by an external laser field. If two atoms are both in this Rydberg state and are within the Rydberg blockade radius, the two atoms will interact via a strong van der Waals interaction, which is energetically unfavorable. This may allow encoding the UD-MIS problem using qubits as vertices and a circle size set by the Rydberg radius, as described in more detail below. Figure 9 shows an example solution to the UD-MIS problem, where, according to some embodiments, some qubits 904 are found in an internal ground state |0> and other qubits 902 are found in a long-lived Rydberg state |1>.

In some embodiments, for an isotropic Rydberg state, the interatomic interaction strength depends only on the relative atomic distance x,
where C is a constant. The strong interaction at short distances occurs when the two qubits are separated by a Rydberg blockade radius, as shown in FIG. 1C.
The Rydberg Hamiltonian H Ryd energetically precludes two qubits from being in state |1> at the same time if they are within a certain distance of the Rydberg blockade radius, resulting in a so-called blockade mechanism according to some embodiments. This may provide a link between the Rydberg Hamiltonian H Ryd and the solution to the UD-MIS problem. In other words, the Rydberg blockade makes nearby qubits within the Rydberg radius (r B ) energetically favorable but does not allow both to be in the Rydberg state |1>. As in the UD graph, in some embodiments of this configuration, the qubits cannot both be found in state |1> if they are separated by a distance shorter than the Rydberg blockade radius.
The MIS-Hamiltonian H P shares some features with the Rydberg Hamiltonian H Ryd in the classical limit Ω v =0. In some embodiments, for example, when arbitrary graphs are allowed for H P , the main difference is in the achievable connectivity of pairwise interactions. We can consider a special limited class of graphs that are most closely related to the Rydberg blockade mechanism. These so-called unit circle (UD) graphs are constructed as described above, where vertices can be assigned to coordinates in a face, and only pairs of vertices that are within a unit distance r are connected by edges. Thus, the unit distance r plays a role similar to the Rydberg blockade radius r B in H Ryd . In other words, the spatial proximity of qubits is used to encode edges in the UD-MIS problem. MIS is NP-complete even when restricted to such unit circle graphs. Although embodiments of the present disclosure discuss 2D problems and 2D arrangements of qubits, those skilled in the art will understand based on the present disclosure that the problem encoding aspects described herein are applicable to other spatial structures, such as one-dimensional or three-dimensional structures.

Exemplary Qubit Placement and Detuning Although the Rydberg interaction decays significantly beyond the Rydberg radius, there is still a long-range interaction tail between distant qubits such as 102 and 108, as shown in FIG. 1A. The interaction tails, either alone or collectively, can reduce the likelihood that the system will be found to be in solution after drives such as those shown in FIGS. 1D and 1E. Thus, runs such as those shown in FIG. 1A may not always perfectly encode NP-complete MIS problems. Furthermore, the range of NP-complete problems that can be encoded using the techniques described with respect to FIG. 1A is limited to those associated with the unit circle.
In some embodiments, one or more of these problems can be solved by choosing the atomic positions in two dimensions and the laser parameters such that the low-energy region of the Rydberg Hamiltonian H Ryd simplifies to the (NP-complete) MIS-Hamiltonian H P on a planar graph with a maximum degree of three. In some aspects of the present disclosure, antiferromagnetic order can be found in the ground state of the (quasi-)1D spin chain of ancillary qubits at positive detuning due to the Rydberg blockade mechanism. Such a configuration can effectively send blockade binding between distant vertex qubits. In other aspects of the present disclosure, detuning patterns {Δ v } can be introduced to eliminate the effects of undesired long-range interactions without changing the ground state spin configuration. Some embodiments allow efficient encoding of NP-complete problems in the ground state of an array of trapped neutral atoms. Without being bound by theory, the ground state energy of Rydberg interacting atoms in a 2D array in such embodiments is NP-hard (and NP-complete when Ω v =0).
Exemplary Qubit Arrangements Using Ancillary Qubits As described with respect to FIGS. 2A and 2B, NP-complete problems may be encoded using “ancillary” qubits or vertices that implement edges between “vertex” qubits, where, according to some aspects, the vertex qubits have a maximum degree of three. For example, as shown in FIG. 2A, a number of vertex qubits 202, 204, 212, 214, and 216 may be arranged in a graph. Edges between pairs of vertex qubits, such as vertex qubits 202 and 204, may be implemented using an even number of ancillary qubits 206, each of which is separated by a unit length r. This technique may be used to embed a planar grid graph with a maximum degree of three into a UD graph. For example, a planar graph with a maximum degree of three may be encoded using a grid (with grid units g) by introducing an even number of ancillary vertices along each edge, as shown in FIG. 2A according to some aspects.

According to some embodiments, it may be desirable to implement approximately the same density of ancillary qubits along any given edge to ensure that the interactions forming each vertex are approximately equal in strength.
In the example of vertex qubits 202 and 204, vertex qubit 202 may interact with the left-most ancillary qubit 206 as if it were vertex qubit 204, and vertex qubit 204 may interact with the right-most ancillary qubit 206 as if it were vertex qubit 202. In this manner, edges may be implemented between vertex qubits outside the Rydberg radius and in a manner that cannot be implemented purely as a unit circle graph. Furthermore, in a unit circle graph such as the one discussed with respect to FIG. 1A, it is not possible to have some vertices separated by the same distance connected by edges (e.g., vertex qubits 202, 204) while other vertices separated by the same distance are not connected by edges (e.g., vertex qubits 212, 214), although such configurations may be realized using the ancillary vertices described in this disclosure.

In some embodiments, the implementation can be extended beyond unit circle graphs to more general graphs. Such implementations can be referred to as "stroboscopic" implementations, which can include any graphs implemented without ancillary qubits as described with respect to FIG. 2A. For example, in some embodiments, various optical techniques can be used to expand the types of problems that can be addressed in these systems. One exemplary approach includes encoding qubits in hyperfine ground states rather than basis-Rydberg qubit encoding, and selectively exciting various types, such as Rydberg S and P states, into Rydberg states (e.g., with individual addressing of qubits). In this example, the strong, long-range bipolar interactions between Rydberg states with different parities S and P can be used to efficiently realize a rotation of a single qubit controlled by its multiple neighbors. For example, Rydberg S and P states can be used to realize a multi-qubit-controlled rotation. Rotations (or qubit flips) can be used to evolve a quantum state from an initial state to a final MIS-state. By controlling these interactions, it is possible to ensure that the evolution of the system does not violate the independent set constraint, for example by ensuring that two qubits, when linked by an edge, do not evolve such that they are both in the Rydberg state. In some examples, all neighbors of a given (central) qubit are in the state
The qubits can be selectively excited from the Rydberg state to the S-state. A two-step transition between the two hyperfine states of the central qubit and an intermediate step in the Rydberg P-state can then perform multi-qubit-controlled rotations. Combined with Trotterized time evolution (e.g., splitting the entire Hamiltonian evolution into small discontinuous steps), these techniques provide a means to go beyond UD graphs and perform various quantum optimization algorithms for MIS problems on arbitrary graphs. In some embodiments, the techniques can perform arbitrary graphs, which may include a broader range of graphs than those depicted in FIG. 2A. In some embodiments, "stroboscopic execution" (selective and sequential excitation of qubits to Rydberg states) enables the performance of multi-qubit-controlled rotations. This selective excitation can facilitate controlled rotations according to graph structures, which are not necessarily limited to unit circle geometry.

As described throughout this disclosure, it is possible to exploit the direct connection of computational complexity theory to many-body problems of spins interacting via van der Waals interactions. With individual control over the positions of such spins, NP-complete optimization problems are directly encoded in such quantum systems. This result can be obtained from a simplification from MIS on planar graphs with a maximum degree of 3. Quantum optimizers based on the techniques described in this disclosure in combination with techniques for trapping and manipulating neutral atoms can address NP-hard optimization problems as an improvement over traditional computational techniques.

Exemplary Parameter Optimization for QAOA Aspects of the present disclosure detail techniques for efficiently optimizing QAOA variability parameters. In some examples, assuming a set of qubits in a particular configuration, QAOA proceeds by applying a series of operations to the qubits, each operation having at least two variability parameters. The evolved state of the qubits is measured, which is fed back to an optimization routine (such as a classical algorithm) to adjust the variability parameters. The process is then repeated for the qubits until the measured state of the qubits is determined to be a solution or an approximation to the encoded problem. In some embodiments, techniques for classical optimization routines are disclosed. These techniques are suboptimal in the sense that they typically yield a known global optimum and generally require 2 O(p) brute-force optimization runs to beat performance. Aspects of the present disclosure also disclose the implementation of QAOA using such optimization techniques, for example, an example includes a 2D physical array of hundreds of Rydberg-interacting atoms that shows potential advantages over classical algorithms to solve the MaxCut problem.

Designing an algorithm that guarantees a minimum approximation ratio of is NP-hard.
According to some embodiments, QAOA provides several benefits. For certain cases, it achieves a guaranteed minimum approximation ratio when p=1. Moreover, under some reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions, QAOA cannot be efficiently simulated by any classical computer even when p=1, which lends the candidate algorithms to "quantum supremacy," i.e., the ability of quantum computers to perform calculations that classical computers cannot. Dynamically evolving square-pulse ("bang-bang") ansatu, of which QAOA may be an example, may be optimal, assuming a constant quantum computer computation time. In general, the performance of QAOA may improve as p increases, achieving r→1 for p→∞, because the performance of QAOA may approximate adiabatic quantum annealing via Trotterization. This monotonicity makes QAOA more attractive than quantum annealing, whose performance may degrade with increasing run time.

Exemplary heuristics for parameter optimization Some embodiments of the present disclosure relate to techniques for optimizing variability parameters. As described in more detail below, patterns in optimal parameters can be utilized to develop heuristic optimization strategies to more quickly identify optimal variability parameters. In some examples described below, parameters identified for level p QAOA can be used to more quickly optimize parameters for level -(p+1) QAOA, which can generate a good starting point for optimization. These techniques provide improvements over brute force techniques. In some embodiments, parameters identified for level -q QAOA for any q<p can be used to more quickly optimize parameters for level p QAOA. Additionally, some examples discuss randomly generated examples of u3R and w3R, but similar results can be found when applying these techniques to u4R and w4R graphs, as well as complete graphs with random weights (or the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass problem). These other exemplary u3R, w3R, u4R, and w4R graphs are regular graphs, meaning, for example, that each vertex has the same number of neighbors (3 or 4, respectively). The letters u and w may refer to what a human would consider an unweighted or weighted graph, respectively. In some embodiments, these graphs are useful as test samples. The patterns in the optimal parameters identified herein are used to develop exemplary heuristic strategies that can efficiently find sub-optimal solutions in O(poly(p)) times.

As discussed above, the heuristic approach described in this disclosure constitutes a significant improvement over brute-force QAOA techniques. A non-limiting comparison of exemplary implementations is discussed below in the following sections.
Based on this disclosure, one skilled in the art will understand that the disclosed heuristic strategy can be implemented on multiple technical bases. In the following section entitled "Exemplary QAOA Implementation", the MaxCut problem is considered as an example, but it can also be applied to solve other interesting problems.
Exemplary Implementations with Quantum Systems In some embodiments, large size problems lend themselves to implementation on quantum systems. Two aspects of such implementations (reducing the interaction range and the example using Rydberg atoms) are discussed in more detail below.
First, regarding reducing the interaction range, in some quantum implementations, as discussed above, each vertex can be represented by a qubit. For large problem sizes, the main challenge to encoding general graphs is the required range and versatility of interaction patterns (between qubits). Embedding a random graph into a physical implementation with 1D or 2D geometry may require very long-range interactions. By relabeling the graph vertices, it is possible to reduce the required range of interactions. Without being bound by theory, this can be formulated as the graph bandwidth problem: Given a graph G=(V, E) with N vertices, the vertex numbering is a bijective map from the vertices to distinct integers
Vertex numbering bandwidth
This can be understood as the length of the longest edge (in 1D). The graph bandwidth problem is then to find the minimum bandwidth among all vertex numberings, i.e. B(G) = min f B f (G); that is, it is to minimize the length of the longest edge by vertex renumbering.
In general, finding the minimum graph bandwidth is NP-hard, but good heuristic algorithms have been developed to reduce the graph bandwidth. Figures 20A-20E show a simple example of bandwidth reduction according to some aspects. Figures 20A, 20B show vertex renumbering using a 5-vertex graph. Figure 20E shows a histogram of graph bandwidth for 1000 random 3-regular graphs, each with N=400. Using the Cuthill-McKee algorithm, the graph bandwidth is approximately
This may still require a very long interaction range in 1D, but the bandwidth problem can also be generalized to higher dimensions. In a 2D configuration, the interaction radius is
, which is possible for quantum devices. Figures 20C and 20D show the sparse patterns of the adjacency matrix before and after vertex renumbering for one example graph. In this example example, the vertex renumbering technique is applied to the MaxCut problem, but those skilled in the art will understand based on this disclosure that the same technique can be used for other combinatorial optimization problems, such as the maximum independent set problem.
In some embodiments, a general construction can be used to encode arbitrarily long-range interactions into local fields by including additional physical qubits and gauge constraints. It is also possible to restrict to special graphs that exhibit some geometric structure. For example, the unit circle graph is a geometric graph in the 2D plane, where vertices are connected by edges only if they are within unit distance. These graphs can be encoded into 2D physical implementations, and the MaxCut problem is still NP-hard on the unit circle graph.
In some embodiments, the above discussion of QAOA is platform independent and applicable to any modern platform. Exemplary platforms include neutral Rydberg atoms, trapped ions, and superconducting qubits. The following discussion focuses on implementations of QAOA involving neutral atoms interacting via Rydberg excitations, where high-fidelity entanglement has recently been demonstrated, although other implementations are contemplated.
In some embodiments, it is possible to implement control of the interactions between individual atoms according to a predefined graph. In some embodiments, in this manner, it is possible to control what type of problem is being solved. Since the interactions can specify the problem, controlling the interactions is one way to control the problem. As discussed in more detail above, in an exemplary Rydberg implementation, the hyperfine ground state in each atom is the qubit state
The state is at the Rydberg level to induce the interaction.

Selecting an appropriate gate time for the second step, e.g.

In some embodiments, a further advantage of the Rydberg blockade mechanism is its ability to implement multi-qubit collective gates in parallel. This can reduce the number of 2-qubit manipulation steps from the number of edges to the number of vertices, N, which means a factor of N reduction for dense graphs with ∼N2 edges. Although the reduction in Rydberg interactions may limit the distance at which two qubits can interact, MaxCut problems of interesting size can still be implemented by renumbering vertices on or focusing on the unit circle graph, as discussed above. Furthermore, implementing ancillary vertices as discussed in this disclosure can be used to increase the length of the interaction.
Without being bound by theory, in some embodiments, for the general problem of a 400-vertex regular graph, the interaction range may be roughly 5 atoms in 2D. This may be determined by assuming a minimum interatomic separation of 2 μm, which implies an interaction radius of 10 μm, which may be achieved using high Rydberg levels. Maximum Independent Sets for Unit Circle Graphs Without being bound by theory, this section addresses some aspects of the MIS problem on unit circle graphs that can be solved according to the techniques described in this disclosure. Figure 5 illustrates a unit circle graph with vertices 502, 504, represented by a circle 508, according to some embodiments, some of which are connected by edges 506 if they are within a radius r of each other. The problem is
This problem can be proven NP-complete by simplifying the problem from an MIS on planar graphs of up to degree 3. Model Detuning for Corners and Junctions Without being bound by theory, to illustrate the application of the above simplifications to an implementation using Rydberg interactions, a simple model may be implemented to illustrate some implementation aspects. This model may be used to illustrate some aspects and benefits of the embodiments of the present disclosure, including but not limited to the treatment of specific vertices. For example, a Hamiltonian similar to the MIS-Hamiltonian H UD for a UD graph may be considered introducing interactions beyond the unit circle radius. Similar to the situation in the Rydberg system, these additional interactions may cause energy shifts that may cause changes in the ground state, thus invalidating the encoding of the MIS. In other words, such additional interactions may cause the ground state of the encoded MIS problem to be mismatched with the solution to the MIS problem. To solve this problem, local detuning may be used to offset the additional interactions.

Without being bound by theory, in some embodiments, the detuning model described above can be applied to the case of the Rydberg Hamiltonian, thereby showing that it is NP-complete to determine whether the ground state energy of H Ryd is below a certain threshold when Ω v =0, where atoms can be positioned arbitrarily in at least two dimensions. While the main ideas are similar, the infinite range Rydberg interaction warrants more explanation.
As noted above, in some embodiments, it is possible to apply detuning patterns that separate length and interaction scales. This is possible in part because the Rydberg interaction decays quickly, such that interactions between nearby qubits can be decoupled from interactions between qubits that are far apart on the graph G. For example, interactions between distant qubits can be ignored if a large enough k is chosen. In such embodiments, individual substructures of the system can be treated separately for the purposes of theory.
In some embodiments, the low-energy region of the Rydberg Hamiltonian can be mapped to a much simpler effective spin model. For example, clusters of qubits can be addressed with a specific detuning pattern such that only two configurations are associated with each cluster. In some embodiments, the resulting effective pseudo-spin is described by an MIS Hamiltonian. This allows the MIS problem to be encoded into a planar graph with a maximum degree of three, such that the ground states of the Rydberg Hamiltonian are MIS solutions. The discussion in this section establishes the details of the mapping to the effective model.
First, with regard to the separation of length scales, the Rydberg interaction may decay with distance as a power law and therefore does not define a length scale at which the interaction ceases to exist. Nevertheless, in some embodiments, an exemplary qubit arrangement introduces two length scales: (1) the closest distance d between the two qubits, and (2) the grid length g. These length scales are separated by a factor g=d(2k+1), which can be expressed as

Behavior at Low Energy Without being bound by theory, aspects of the ground state of the Rydberg Hamiltonian are described below. Exemplary aspects of the Rydberg Hamiltonian show that at lower energies, the ground state corresponds to an MIS solution to the encoded problem. Thus, in an exemplary implementation, if a problem is properly encoded, transitioning the corresponding qubit to a lower energy state can result in a system in a ground state that corresponds to a solution to the encoded problem. Without being bound by theory, the discussion of such transitions can be aided by reference to "pseudospin" discussed in a previous section.

The ground states of correspond to maximal independent sets on the relevant UD graph when the detuning of each spin is selected according to the techniques described herein. A maximal independent set refers to an independent set to which no vertex can be added without violating the independence property (e.g., two neighboring vertices cannot both be in state |1>). The largest maximal independent set is a maximal independent set. For a configuration corresponding to such a set, two neighboring spins cannot be in state |1> (independence) and a spin cannot be in state |0> if all its neighbors are in state |0> (maximality).

Exemplary QAOA Implementation In some embodiments, further considerations are related to the implementation of the QAOA techniques described in this disclosure. However, the QAOA framework is general and can be applied to a variety of technology platforms for solving combinatorial optimization problems.
Finite Measurement Samples In some embodiments, quantum fluctuations (such as projection noise) may result in finite precision, since finite precision may be obtained by averaging a finite number of measurements that can only take on discrete values. Therefore, there may be a trade-off between measurement cost and optimization quality: finding a good optimum may require good precision at the expense of many measurements. Furthermore, large variations in the objective function values may require more measurements, but may help improve the chances of finding a near-optimal MaxCut configuration.
Without being bound by theory, by way of example, the effect of measurement projection noise can be illustrated by a full Monte Carlo simulation of QAOA on some exemplary graphs, where the objective function is evaluated by iterative projection measurements until its error falls below a threshold. Details of an exemplary run of this numerical simulation are discussed in the section entitled "Exemplary Simulation with Measurement Projection Noise".

Since 102 measurements can be taken to obtain a sufficiently accurate estimate of the objective function,
A ground state probability of 10 2 means that the ground state can be found without much parameter optimization. In some embodiments, for larger problem sizes with 10 2 -10 3 qubits, the ground state probability from a general QAOA/QA protocol without optimization can decrease exponentially with the size of the system, while the measurement cost of optimization simply increases polynomially with the problem size. The results here show that the parameter patterns and heuristic strategies disclosed are useful guidelines for implementation purposes in practical implementations of QAOA that enhance optimization to significantly increase the probability of finding a ground state.
Execution for Large Problem Sizes Execution of the solution to the MaxCut problem by a quantum machine may be limited by quantum coherent time and graph connectivity. In some embodiments, with respect to coherent time, QAOA is highly advantageous: the hybrid nature of QAOA and its short and medium depth circuit parameterizations makes QAOA useful for quantum devices. Furthermore, QAOA is generally not limited by small spectral gaps, which indicates that interesting problems can be solved (or at least approximated) in coherent time.

Beyond adiabatic mechanisms: case studies
To understand the behavior of QAOA, we can address in more detail examples of graphs that are difficult for adiabatic QA. For example, we use a representative example to explain how aspects of QAOA and adiabatic QA can overcome the adiabatic limit. As illustrated in Fig. 18A, QAOA can learn to exploit diabatic transitions at anticrossings to avoid the difficulties caused by very small graphs in QA. Fig. 18A shows a schematic diagram of how QAOA and the interpolated annealing pathway can overcome the small minimum gap limit by nonadiabatic transitions (small dashed lines). The naive adiabatic quantum annealing pathway leads to an excited state that passes through the point of anticrossing (large dashed lines).

According to some embodiments, this annealing path allows one to trace the instantaneous eigenstate population during the quantum annealing process, as shown in FIG. 18F. In particular, FIG. 18F shows the instantaneous eigenstate population under the annealing path given in FIG. 18E. Note that the instantaneous ground state and the first excited state are exchanged at the point of anticrossing. In contrast to adiabatic QA, the state population leaks out of the ground state and accumulates in the first excited state before the point of anticrossing, where the gap is at its minimum. Using a nonadiabatic transition at the anticrossing, the two states can exchange populations, and a large ground state population is obtained at the end. The final state population from the constructed annealing path may differ slightly from that of QAOA, for example due to trotalization and interpolation, but without being bound by theory, the underlying mechanism may be interpreted as the same, which may also be considered to be the cause of the nonadiabatic bump seen in FIG. 18C. In addition to the transformations used in the equations above, other criteria can be used to construct annealing paths from the QAOA parameters, and the qualitative characteristics are not likely to change.
Without being bound by theory, these results show that QAOA is closely related to a dexterously optimized nonadiabatic QA pathway that can overcome the limitations set by the adiabatic theorem. Aspects of the present disclosure show that quantum algorithms can be implemented to solve computationally difficult problems with a coherent quantum optimizer with minimal resource and execution overhead, which is not limited by the number of ancillary qubits required, but may include additional depth of quantum circuitry required, etc.
Aspects of the present disclosure show that NP-complete combinatorial optimization problems can be precisely encoded in quantum systems, even when taking into account undesirable interactions between qubits.
Aspects of the present disclosure show that quantum algorithms can be performed by applying optical pulses having non-constant durations and non-constant optical phases to at least some of the multiple qubits.
An aspect of the present disclosure is that a heuristic optimization strategy is required over a brute force approach that uses many initial guesses for parameters.
Without resources,
We show that it is possible to find suboptimal variability parameters in a variability quantum algorithm in just 100 times.
Aspects of the present disclosure show that a quantum approximation optimization algorithm exploits nonadiabatic mechanisms to overcome challenges associated with vanishing spectral gaps.
Aspects of the present disclosure show that renumbering the vertices of a combinatorial optimization problem allows quantum systems to implement examples of a much broader class of problems.

### 📜 Full Specification & Deep Scrape Text
Title
Quantum Approximate Optimization

Abstract
In a general aspect, a computing system is configured to execute a quantum approximate optimization algorithm. In some aspects, a control system identifies a pair of qubit devices in a quantum processor. The quantum processor includes a connection that provides coupling between the pair of qubit devices. ZZ coupling between the pair of qubit devices is activated to execute a cost function defined in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. The cost function is associated with a maximum cut problem, and the ZZ coupling is activated by allowing the pair of qubits to evolve under a natural Hamiltonian for a time period τ. One or more of the pair of qubit devices is measured to obtain an output from an execution of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm.

Description
CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS
This application claims priority to U.S. Provisional Application No. 62/469,877 entitled “Quantum Approximate Optimization” and filed Mar. 10, 2017 which is hereby incorporated by reference.
BACKGROUND
The following description relates to quantum approximate optimization.
Quantum computers can perform computational tasks by executing quantum algorithms. Quantum algorithms are often expressed in terms of quantum logic operations applied to qubits. A variety of physical systems have been proposed as quantum computing systems. Examples include superconducting circuits, trapped ions, spin systems and others.

FIG. 2 is a block diagram on an example quantum information processor.
FIG. 3 is a diagram of an example quantum logic circuit.

FIG. 5 is a diagram of an example pulse sequence.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
In some aspects of what is described, a computing system can execute a quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). The computing system can include hardware that is programmed for a certain problem or class of problems that can be encoded in the cost function of the QAOA. For example, the computing system may include quantum processor hardware configured to provide qubit interactions that match the cost function of the QAOA. In some of the examples described here, a quantum processor includes special purpose logic circuitry that can efficiently execute quantum logic operations of a QAOA, for example, quantum logic operations corresponding to the cost function associated with the maximum cut problem. For instance, the quantum processor can be designed such that a graph structure and cost function of a maximum cut problem can be readily mapped to, and efficiently executed by, the quantum processor hardware.
In some implementations, a quantum processor includes many interconnected qubit devices, where the physical connections between the qubit devices in the quantum processor are designed based on the graph structure of the maximum cut problem. The connections can be specified according to a particular graph structure or a class of graph structures to be solved. In some implementations, the physical connections provided in the quantum processor provide physical interactions that closely match or otherwise correspond to a cost function Hamiltonian of the maximum cut problem. For example, the cost function for the maximum cut problem can be expressed in the form of ZZ operations acting pairwise on the states of connected vertices in a graph, and the quantum processor hardware can be configured to provide ZZ interactions acting pairwise on the quantum states of connected qubit devices. In such cases, the connections in the quantum processor can be used to directly apply the cost function Hamiltonian to the qubits defined by the connected pairs of qubit devices.
Accordingly, the techniques described here can provide technical advantages and improvements over existing technologies. The system can operate more efficiently for certain problems, for instance, by reducing computational overhead and by providing faster quantum logic operations. As an example, the computational overhead required to map a specific problem to a physical system hardware can be reduced or eliminated when the physical system hardware matches the structure of the problem. As another example, quantum logic transformations that are typically required to express a cost function Hamiltonian in terms of quantum logic operations provided by a quantum processor architecture can be reduced or eliminated when the cost function Hamiltonian matches the natural Hamiltonian provided by the quantum processor. As another example, swap gates and other operations required to shuttle information within the quantum processor can be reduced or eliminated when the qubit interactions specified by a quantum logic circuit match the qubit connections provided by the quantum processor. Other technical improvements and advantages may be achieved in some cases.
FIG. 1 is a schematic diagram of an example quantum computing system 100 . The example quantum computing system 100 shown in FIG. 1 includes a control system 110 , a signal delivery system 106 , and a quantum information processor 102 . A quantum computing system may include additional or different features, and the components of a quantum computing system may operate as described with respect to FIG. 1 or in another manner.
In some implementations, the quantum computing system 100 can perform quantum computation by storing and manipulating information within individual quantum states of a composite quantum system. For example, qubits (i.e., quantum bits) can be stored in and represented by an effective two-level sub-manifold of a quantum coherent physical system. Control devices (e.g., coupler devices) can be used to perform quantum logic operations on single qubits or conditional quantum logic operations on multiple qubits. In some instances, the conditional quantum logic can be performed in a manner that allows large-scale entanglement within the quantum computing device. Control signals can manipulate the quantum states of individual qubits and the joint states of multiple qubits. In some instances, information can be read out from the composite quantum system by measuring the quantum states of the individual qubits.
The example quantum computing system 100 shown in FIG. 1 can perform quantum computational tasks by executing quantum algorithms such as, for example, quantum approximate optimization. In some implementations, the quantum computing system 100 can operate using gate-based models for quantum computing. For example, quantum algorithms may be executed by applying quantum logic gates to qubits defined in the quantum computing system 100 . In some implementations, the quantum computing system 100 is constructed and operated according to a scalable quantum computing architecture. For example, in some cases, the architecture can be scaled to a large number of qubits to achieve large-scale coherent quantum computing.
The example quantum information processor 102 shown in FIG. 1 includes qubit devices that are used to store and process quantum information. The quantum information processor 102 shown in FIG. 1 can be implemented, for example, as the quantum information processor 200 shown in FIG. 2 , the quantum processors 600 A, 600 B shown in FIG. 6 , or in another manner. In some cases, the quantum information processor 102 includes a superconducting circuit, and the qubit devices are implemented as circuit devices that include one or more Josephson junctions (e.g., in the form of superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) loops or otherwise).
In the example quantum information processor 102 , the qubit devices each store a single qubit (a bit of quantum information), and the data qubits can collectively define a computational state for a quantum computation. The quantum information processor 102 may also include readout devices that interact with the qubit devices to detect their quantum states. For example, the readout devices may generate readout signals that indicate the computational state. The quantum information processor 102 may also include coupler devices that selectively operate on individual qubits or pairs of qubits. For example, the coupler devices may be operated to produce entanglement over two or more qubits in the quantum information processor 102 .
In some implementations, the example quantum information processor 102 can process the quantum information stored in the qubit devices by applying control signals to the qubit devices or to other control devices in the quantum information processor 102 . In some examples, the operations can be expressed as single-qubit gates, two-qubit gates, or other types of logical gates that operate on one or more qubits. A sequence of quantum logic operations can be applied to the qubits to perform a quantum computation. The quantum computation may correspond to the quantum approximate optimization algorithm or another type of quantum algorithm.
In the example quantum computing system 100 shown in FIG. 1 , the control system 110 controls operation of the quantum information processor 102 . The example control system 110 may include data processors, signal generators, interface components and other types of systems or subsystems. In some cases, the control system 110 includes one or more classical computers or classical computing components.
In some implementations, the control system 110 generates a quantum logic control sequence based on a quantum computation to be performed. The quantum logic control sequence can include a sequence of quantum logic operations that can be executed by the quantum information processor 102 . In some cases, the control system 110 generates a quantum logic control sequence for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. The quantum logic control sequence may be converted to control signals (e.g., microwave control signals, optical control signals, DC bias control signals, etc.) that are delivered to the quantum information processor 102 , and upon delivery, cause the quantum information processor 102 to execute the quantum computation.
In the example shown in FIG. 1 , the signal delivery system 106 provides communication between the control system 110 and the quantum information processor 102 . For example, the signal delivery system 106 can receive control signals (e.g., qubit control signals, readout control signals, coupler control signals, etc.) from the control system 110 and deliver the control signals to the quantum information processor 102 . In some instances, the signal delivery system 106 performs preprocessing, signal conditioning, or other operations to the control signals before delivering them to the quantum information processor 102 .
The signal delivery system 106 may include signal lines, signal processing hardware, filters, feedthrough devices, or a combination of these and other types of components. In some implementations, the signal delivery system 106 provides connections between different temperature and noise regimes. For example, the quantum computing system 100 may include a series of temperature stages between a higher temperature regime of the control system 110 and a lower temperature regime of the quantum information processor 102 .
The quantum information processor 102 , and in some cases all or part of the signal delivery system 106 , can be maintained in a controlled environment. The environment can be provided, for example, by shielding equipment, cryogenic equipment, and other types of environmental control systems. In some examples, the components in the quantum information processor 102 operate in a cryogenic temperature regime and are subject to very low electromagnetic and thermal noise. For example, magnetic shielding can be used to shield the system components from stray magnetic fields, optical shielding can be used to shield the system components from optical noise, thermal shielding and cryogenic equipment can be used to maintain the system components at controlled temperature, etc.
In some implementations, a computer device 120 can access the quantum computing system 100 , for instance, over a communication channel 122 . The computer device 120 can be an access node that operates local to, or remote from, the control system 110 or other components of the quantum computing system 100 . In some cases, the computer device 120 can be integrated with the control system 110 or other components of the quantum computing system 110 . In some cases, the computer device 120 has a local data connection to the control system 110 and communicates directly with the control system 110 through the local data connection. For instance, the communication channel 122 can be a local data connection that is provided by a wireless Local Area Network, an Ethernet connection, a USB connection, or another type of wired or wireless connection. In some cases, the computer device 120 has a remote data connection to the control system 110 and communicates with the control system 110 through the remote data connection. For instance, the communication channel 122 can be a wide area network, such as, for example, the Internet or another type of wide area communication network. In some cases, communication channel 122 is another type of remote data connection (e.g., satellite-based connections, a cellular network, a private network, etc.).
In some instances, the control system 110 may initiate and control a quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) executed by the quantum computing system 100 . In other instances, the computer device 120 initiates the execution (e.g., by providing instructions or inputs for the QAOA), and the control system 110 controls the execution of the QAOA according to instructions or inputs provided by the computer device 120 . In response to the computer device 120 , the quantum computing system 100 can provide an output of the execution to the computer device 120 . The computer device 120 may initiate an execution of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm and receive the output of the execution by communicating with the quantum computing system 100 over the communication channel 122 or otherwise.
The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is an example of a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm. For example, the QAOA may be executed in a quantum computing system or a hybrid quantum-classical computing system that includes a quantum processor and one or more classical processors. For instance, the QAOA may be executed in the quantum computing system 100 shown in FIG. 1 . As an example, the control system 110 may include, or may access, a classical co-processor that performs certain operations of the QAOA.
In some implementations, constraint satisfaction problems can be encoded in a QAOA, and optimizing certain parameters (usually described as “angles,” for example, the set of angles ({right arrow over (β)}, {right arrow over (γ)}) in the quantum logic circuit 300 shown in FIG. 3 ) in the QAOA leads to distributions that allow efficient sampling of (approximately) optimal solutions to the encoded constraint satisfaction problem. For example, the number of samples needed to find a feasible solution can be substantially smaller than the full exponential state space. Accordingly, the QAOA can be configured to maximize a cost function associated with a constraint satisfaction problem. More precisely, the QAOA can be configured to maximize the cost function

FIG. 2 is a block diagram showing an example quantum information processor 200 . The example quantum information processor 200 includes a two-dimensional device array, which includes qubit devices 204 arranged in a lattice structure. Sixteen qubit devices are shown in FIG. 2 . The example quantum information processor 200 may include additional devices; for example, the lattice structure may include additional rows or columns of qubit devices, coupler devices arranged between neighboring pairs of the qubit devices, readout devices arranged in proximity to the qubit devices, or a combination of these.
In the example shown in FIG. 2 , the qubit devices 204 are arranged in a rectilinear (e.g., rectangular or square) array that extends in two spatial dimensions (in the plane of the page), and each qubit device 204 has four nearest-neighbor qubit devices. In some implementations, the qubit devices 204 can be arranged in another type of ordered array (e.g., triangular, hexagonal, etc.). In some instances, the rectilinear array also extends in a third spatial dimension (in/out of the page), for example, to form a cubic array or another type of three-dimensional array. The quantum information processor 200 may include additional devices, including additional qubit devices, coupler devices and other types of devices.
The example quantum information processor 200 is configured to apply entangling quantum logic operations 206 to neighboring pairs of the qubit devices 204 . In some cases, the entangling quantum logic operations 206 are quantum logic gates that can be applied to two target qubits to produce an entangled state on the target qubits. Examples include the controlled-not (CNOT) gate, the controlled-phase (C-Phase) gate, and others.
In some cases, the entangling quantum logic operations 206 are executed by activating ZZ couplings between neighboring pairs of the qubit devices 204 . For instance, in some superconducting quantum circuits, each neighboring pair of superconducting qubit devices i and j have a natural Hamiltonian that includes a ZZ coupling term (a term proportional to σ i z ⊗σ j z , where σ u z represents the z Pauli operator applied to qubit i, and σ j z represents the z Pauli operator applied to qubit j), and the ZZ coupling term produces an interaction between the qubits when the qubits evolve under the natural system Hamiltonian. In some contexts, the ZZ coupling term may be expressed in terms of the number operators (e.g., â † â for each qubit) or other quantum operators that are proportional to the z Pauli operator
σ

)
for each qubit. The ZZ coupling term may be expressed with a scaling factor (e.g., the coupling strength χ) that characterizes the rate of the coupling between the qubits defined by the two qubit devices.
In some cases, quantum information processor 200 can be implemented as a superconducting circuit, qubit devices 204 may be implemented as circuit devices that include one or more Josephson junctions (e.g., superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) loops or other circuit structures). Pairs of the qubit devices can be coupled to each other through a capacitor, an inductor, or another mode of coupling. In some examples, a transition frequency of a qubit device is tunable, for example, by application of an offset field. For instance, a tunable qubit device (e.g., a tunable transmon qubit device, a fluxonium qubit device, etc.) may include a superconducting loop (e.g., a SQUID loop) that is tunable by application of magnetic flux. In some examples, the transition frequency of a qubit device is not tunable by application of an offset field and is independent of magnetic flux experienced by the qubit device. For instance, a fixed-frequency qubit device may have a fixed transition frequency that is defined by an electronic circuit of the qubit device. As an example, a superconducting qubit device (e.g., a fixed-frequency transmon qubit) may be implemented without a SQUID loop. In some examples, a fixed-frequency qubit device is coupled to one or more tunable-frequency qubit devices.
In the example shown in FIG. 2 , the qubit devices 204 can each be encoded with a single bit of quantum information. Each of the qubit devices has two eigenstates used as computational basis states (“0” and “1”), and each qubit device can transition between its computational basis states or exist in an arbitrary superposition of its basis states. In some implementations, connections between the qubit devices 204 in the quantum information processor 200 allow the qubits to be selectively coupled on-demand, for instance, to apply a driver Hamiltonian, to apply a cost function Hamiltonian, or to perform other types of operations.
In some instances, information is encoded in the qubit devices 204 , and the information can be processed by applying a quantum logic control sequence. For instance, input information can be encoded in the computational states or computational subspaces defined by data qubits encoded in some of all of the qubit devices. The information can be processed, for example, by applying the quantum logic control sequence to the input information. The quantum logic control sequence may be represented as quantum logic gates or other quantum logic operations. For instance, a quantum computation may be executed by a combination of single-qubit gates and two-qubit gates. In some cases, information is processed in another manner. Processing the information encoded in the qubit devices 204 produces output information that can be extracted from the qubit devices. The output information can be extracted, for example, by performing state tomography or individual readout operations.
In some instances, the quantum information processor 200 executes a quantum approximate optimization algorithm. In some cases, a quantum approximate optimization algorithm can be used as a benchmark or metric for assessing the performance of the quantum information processor 200 . For instance, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm can be implemented on quantum information processors of varying sizes—from very small (e.g., 2-qubit systems) to very large (e.g., hundreds or thousands of qubits). In some cases, the output of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm can be compared against a standard or benchmark value as a standardized assessment of the quantum information processor 200 . For instance, the algorithm may be used to evaluate hardware performance or other attributes of the quantum information processor 200 .
FIG. 3 is a diagram of an example quantum logic circuit 300 . The example quantum logic circuit 300 shown in FIG. 3 represents p iterations of a quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). The quantum logic circuit 300 can be executed by a computing system, for example, by the example quantum computing system 100 shown in FIG. 1 . In some cases, a general purpose quantum processor executes the quantum logic circuit 300 . In some cases, a special purpose quantum processor executes the quantum logic circuit 300 .
In the example shown in FIG. 3 , the quantum logic circuit 300 is applied to n qubits; the quantum logic circuit 300 can be adapted for application on any number of qubits (e.g., two qubits, ten qubits, hundreds or thousands of qubits). As shown in FIG. 3 , the qubits are initialized to the computational basis state 10 )®n, where each individual qubit is in the |0
state. Each iteration (s) of the QAOA includes unitary evolution under the unitary driver operator for iteration (s)
U(Ĥ Driver ,β s )
that is parameterized by an angle β s and a driver Hamiltonian Ĥ Driver ; followed by unitary evolution under the unitary cost operator for iteration (s)
U(Ĥ Cost ,γ s )
that is parameterized by an angle γ s and a cost function Hamiltonian Ĥ Cost . The values of the angles (β s , γ s ) that parameterize the unitary driver operator and the unitary cost operator, respectively, are updated for each iteration.
As shown in FIG. 3 , p iterations of the QAOA evolves the n qubits defined in the quantum processor to the output state |ψ F ({right arrow over (β)}, {right arrow over (γ)})
. The output state can be measured, for example, by performing projective measurements on the n qubits or by another type of measurement. Measuring the qubit devices provides an output from an execution of the QAOA (e.g., an execution of one or more iterations of the QAOA). The quantum logic circuit 300 can be iterated to sample the distribution of computational basis states in the output state |ψ F ({right arrow over (β)}, {right arrow over (γ)})
. For example, each iteration can produce a bitstring representing one of the computational basis states of the n qubits.
In some implementations, a co-processor (e.g., a classical co-processor) selects values for the set of angles ({right arrow over (β)}, {right arrow over (γ)}), and a quantum processor then executes the quantum logic circuit 300 to prepare the output state |ψ F ({right arrow over (β)}, {right arrow over (γ)})
based on the selected values for the set of angles and the cost operator (the cost operator represents the problem for which an optimal solution is sought). The output state is then measured to obtain a set of bitstrings (e.g., a projective measurement can be used to obtain classical bitstrings).
The quantum logic circuit 300 shown in FIG. 3 can be configured to find solutions to the maximum cut problem by defining a cost function Hamiltonian Ĥ Cost associated with the maximum cut problem. For instance, the maximum cut problem can be encoded in the QAOA by defining the cost function Hamiltonian

FIG. 4 is a diagram of example graphs associated with a maximum cut problem. As shown in FIG. 4 , the maximum cut problem is defined over a graph that includes vertices connected by edges. The maximum cut problem can be described as a binary shading problem over a graph, where the solution to the maximum cut problem is the set of vertex shading assignments that maximize the score of all edges in the graph (where each vertex is shaded either black or white). As shown at 400 , constraints can be defined with an arbitrary graph. As shown at 402 , when the vertices connected by an edge are shaded different from each other, the edge connecting the vertices is assigned a score of +1; and when the vertices connected by an edge are shaded alike, the edge connecting the vertices is assigned a score of 0.
As shown in FIG. 4 , the cost function for an edge connecting vertices i and j in the graph can be expressed C ij =(½)(1−Z i Z j ). And the cost function over the full graph can be expressed

FIG. 5 is a diagram of an example pulse sequence 500 . The example pulse sequence 500 shown in FIG. 5 can be used to implement an iteration of the QAOA having a cost function associated with the maximum cut problem. The operations 502 shown in the top row of FIG. 5 are applied to one qubit device; the operations 504 shown in the bottom row of FIG. 5 are applied to another qubit device. The pulse sequence 500 shown in FIG. 5 for two qubit devices can be adapted for maximum cut problems defined over any number of qubits. In some implementations, a control system is configured to execute the pulse sequence 500 ; for example, the control system may store a quantum program that, when executed by the control system, causes the control system to initiate the operations shown in FIG. 5 .
As shown in FIG. 5 , a first pair of pulses R γ π/2 apply a π/2 rotation about the Y-axis to each respective qubit device. After the first pair of pulses R γ π/2 , a ZZ coupling is activated between the two qubit devices. In the example shown in FIG. 5 , the ZZ coupling is activated by allowing the qubit devices to evolve under their natural coupling Hamiltonian for time period τ=γ/χ. Here, the angle γ is a parameter provided for the QAOA algorithm, and χ is the coupling strength of the ZZ coupling between the qubit devices.
In the example shown in FIG. 5 , the ZZ coupling is activated for the time period τ with the coupling strength χ, to evolve the pair of qubits devices under the unitary operator
